sections.title: Analysis
sections.text: Once you have assembled your analysis dataset ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)), you are ready to analyse. This section stays register-specific and practical : when to use what, which packages, and a minimal example - it does not teach statistical theory. For depth, see the Epidemiologist R Handbook, [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) and the introductory R course hosted by the Danish Diabetes and Endocrinology Academy (DDEA) (see [Learning resources](learning-resources.qmd)).

sections.title: Analysis
sections.heading: Pages in this section
sections.text: Pick the pages that fit your study - not every study uses all of them. A usual order is: choose the analysis, describe the population (Table 1), fit the main model (regression, time-to-event or rates), then the sensitivity analyses and figures. Read the output-control box below before you start. Output control decides what you can compute, not just what you can send. Only aggregated results leave DST, and cells below the threshold (3 or 5 observations, depending on your project) may not be repatriated at all. That shapes the analysis itself: how finely you may stratify a table, whether a subgroup is worth running, whether a figure can show what you want. Plan for it here rather than discovering it at the end. The rules and the threshold are on Phase 14 - Export and repatriation.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.text: Use this page to build your study population, once you know which registers your study needs and before you extract any covariates. You decide who could have entered the study at all (the source population), find the exposed people or cases, give each of them an index date, and exclude those who already had the outcome. When you are done you have a cohort: a table with pnr and index_date per person, which every later phase builds on ([Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd) to Phase 13). Finding exposed people or cases in hospital data uses the LPR extraction pattern from Extract from LPR, so read that page first. What you do after this page depends on your study design, see [the end of this page](#what-now-choose-your-design). Index date is the point in time that marks the start of follow-up for a given person. Exposed: the date the person received the exposure (e.g. surgery date, diagnosis date, first prescription dispensed) Comparator cohort: the index date assigned from the matched exposed person Everything that follows - outcome date, covariates at baseline, follow-up time - is calculated relative to index date. The definition of index date is crucial for study validity. The

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Step 1 - Define the source population
sections.text: Before you look for the exposed, decide who could have entered the study at all. That is the source population, and two things decide it: your data delivery and a residence criterion. Your data delivery sets the outer limit. DST only delivers data on the population your project is approved for. If your delivery is "persons in BEF 2005-2024", then a person who only lived in Denmark in 2003 does not exist in your extract at all - and no code can pull them in. Check your project guide first. The registers below can make the timing of residence precise within your delivery, but they cannot add people to it.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: BEF alone cannot decide residence
sections.text: BEF (the population register) is a snapshot: one picture per reference time point (quarterly since 2008, yearly before that - see Overview of registers). That means BEF gets it wrong in both directions: Too many included: the person is in that year's snapshot, but had emigrated or died by your index date. Too few included: the person is not in that year's snapshot, but was genuinely resident on the index date. That happens if they had emigrated at the time of the snapshot and moved home later the same year. You can filter your way out of the first error, but not out of the second: a filter can only remove people from the pool BEF already found, never add the ones missing from it. So residence has to be decided on events, not on snapshots.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Use BEF and VNDS together
sections.text: You need both registers, plus the death register: BEF: the population and demographics: who exists, date of birth and sex. Use all snapshots in your study window combined (the union), not one year at a time. VNDS (migrations): the events: immigrations and emigrations with dates. VNDS holds only migration events, so a person born in Denmark who never left has no rows in VNDS. Absence of events is the normal case, not an error. DOD (deaths): the date of death, applied on top. The rule is therefore a default with exceptions: resident since birth, unless VNDS says otherwise. For each person, find the latest VNDS event before the index date: That start date is what you measure a continuous residence requirement from (e.g. "at least 5 years in Denmark before index"). It is not the same as the earliest year the person appears in BEF: someone seen in BEF in 2005, but living abroad 2006-2012 and moving home in 2013, has only two years of continuous residence at an index date in 2015. Check these six things before you trust the rule. The event codes: run count(indud_kode) on your own VNDS. The guide uses "I" and "U" , but confirm the values in your delivery. Immigration before 1971:

sections.heading: Code: the source population at study start
sections.text: Does each person have their own index date? Then the same rule applies, but it has to be used where the date exists, not here. The index date is not a property of the person: The exposed get their index date in Step 2 (the exposure date). Residence is therefore decided for them when you prepare the exposed on [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd). Comparison persons are only assigned an index date at the match itself, and the same person can be a candidate at several different index dates - and be resident at one but not the other. So residence is decided per (person, index date) at match time on Comparison cohort, never once and for all. So the source population here is at person level, while eligibility at index is at the level of person and date.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Step 3 - Exclude prevalent cases
sections.text: People who already had your outcome before the index date must be excluded, otherwise they count as new cases even though they are not. The convention used throughout this guide: a diagnosis on or before the index date is prevalent ( <= ), and only one after it is an outcome ( > ). This applies to all designs, including a prevalence study without a comparison group, so it belongs here where you build the exposed cohort. Count how many drop out at each exclusion step, so you can describe the attrition and later draw a STROBE flow diagram (also called a participant or attrition diagram; see the [STROBE checklist](https://www.strobe-statement.org/checklists/)). The generic N-counting template is in Phase 6.

See [Good coding practice](good-coding-practice.qmd). Planning a comparison cohort? Extract the outcome (and exposure) dates for the whole population here rather than just for the exposed, and reuse them: restricted to the exposed as above, and later for the comparison pool (see Comparison cohort). Filtering the diagnosis codes returns everyone with the diagnosis anyway, so it saves a second query against the registers. If that comparison group is matched with replacement, know what distinct(pnr) %>% pull(pnr) excludes. prior_outcome_pnrs() checks each row against that row's own index_date (the inner_join before the filter), but the final distinct(pnr) collapses the result to a plain list of people, so filter(!pnr %in% prevalent) drops every row for that pnr , not just the one where they had a prevalent outcome. If the same person is matched to a different case with an earlier index_date , where they did not yet have the outcome, that instance gets excluded too. That may be the conservative rule

sections.heading: Participant flow diagram (STROBE)
sections.text: The N counts you made in Step 2 and Step 3 come together in a STROBE flow diagram: a figure showing how many people were in from the start, how many were excluded at each step and why, and how many ended up in the study population. How each step maps to the data: Source registers: the whole population's LPR data (you have no cohort list yet). LPR2 and LPR3 are opened lazily with read_register() , see Step 2 above. Step 3 (exclusion): prevalent cases (people with the outcome before their index date) are found in the LPR diagnoses and removed. That is the n_before - nrow(exposed) shown in the exclusion box. Final study population: pnr + index_date per person, ready for [Phase 11 - Extract variables](extract-variables.qmd). If you build a comparison cohort, Comparison cohort comes before the last step. sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Next step depends on your design
sections.text: Prevalence study / cohort without a comparison group: after this page you are done: you have your study population with an index date. Continue to Phase 11 - Extract variables and [Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset](data-manipulation.qmd). Cohort study with a comparison cohort: continue to [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd), where you build a match pool and risk-set match a comparison group. (Nested) case-control: continue to Case-control, where your "exposed" group above is instead your cases, and you sample controls who were at risk when the case had the outcome. Self-controlled or family-based design: the person, or the family, is their own control - see [Self-controlled and family-based designs](special-designs.qmd).

sections.title: Case-control
sections.text: Use this page when your study is a nested case-control study inside the register population. It comes after [Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd), and it reuses the person table built on Comparison cohort, so you need Steps 1 and 2 there even though you will not match a comparison cohort. The group you identified is here your cases (those who developed the outcome), and their index date is the outcome date. For each case you sample controls: people without the outcome who were at risk exactly when the case had the outcome. When you are done you have a matched dataset of cases and controls with a matched-set id. Case-control is especially efficient when the outcome is rare, or when a covariate is expensive to extract for the whole cohort. The design choice between cohort and case-control is in [Phase 1 - what type of study](plan-your-study.qmd#study-type). The examples show the shape of each step. They have not yet been run end to end on real register data , so treat them as a starting point: check the column names against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan. Confirm too that heaven::incidenceMatch() and Epi::ccwc() are

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: The principle: incidence-density sampling
sections.text: Controls are selected by risk-set (incidence-density) sampling: for each case you draw controls who, on the case's index date (= the outcome date), (1) have not yet developed the outcome and (2) meet the inclusion criteria. A person can be a control for one case and later become a case themselves. That is correct in this design: excluding people who later become cases from the controls biases the estimate ([Lubin and Gail 1984](https://doi.org/10.2307/2530744)). It is the same mechanic as the matching in [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) - only the "event" has changed: here it is the outcome (case), not an exposure. So this page also reuses the person table from there.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Step 1 - Build the dataset for matching
sections.text: Identifying cases and excluding prevalent cases are done on [Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd). Here you need one row per person with matching variables and the dates eligibility depends on. Reuse the pool from [Comparison cohort, Step 2](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-2---build-the-comparison-pool) (demographics + death date + first exit + first outcome date) and the migration events vnds_ev from Step 1 there, for the entry (residence) date. For case-control, though: Exposure is not an eligibility criterion here: unlike the comparison cohort, where a control must be exposure-free at index. In case-control, exposure is what you study: you measure it for both cases and controls afterwards and do not use it to decide who can be a control. A control just needs to be outcome-free (and meet your other criteria) at the case's index. Who is a case, and when: the outcome date is the index date.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Step 2 - Sample controls
sections.text: Two routes. Both do incidence-density sampling; pick one. Route A: heaven::incidenceMatch() . The sibling of exposureMatch() from Comparison cohort, but the "event" is the outcome. Route B: Epi::ccwc() . Simple risk-set sampling from entry and exit times; not counter-matching). Confirm arguments with ?Epi::ccwc . Same rules as in Comparison cohort: apply inclusion and exclusion criteria before sampling and to everyone (cases and pool), and set a seed . A control can be drawn for several cases, and a person can be a control before becoming a case; both follow from sampling from the risk set, so do not remove them. incidenceMatch() itself handles the risk-set time dimension via case.index + end.followup .

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Analysis: conditional logistic regression
sections.text: The analysis itself belongs to Regression (Phase 13); here only briefly, so you know where this leads. Matched case-control data can be analysed with conditional logistic regression ( survival::clogit() with a strata() term per matched set), so the matching is respected; the odds ratio from an incidence-density design estimates the rate/hazard ratio. This is the standard approach for matched case-control studies. Before the analysis you attach exposure and covariates to the matched persons (from Phase 11/[Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)). Measure exposure in a window defined relative to each matched set's index date (the case's outcome date), the same window for the case and its controls. The matched-set id is called case.id (Route A) or Set (Route B).

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.text: Use this page to find the test or model that fits your outcome before you start the analysis, and the R command for it. It is a quick pointer to the right test, not the final word: always check the test's assumptions and your analysis plan, and look things up if in doubt. Start with your question. First state your research question and null hypothesis - they drive everything else. In the R commands in the tables, x , y , group , m0 etc. are placeholders - replace them with your own variable and value names. Commands written as package::function (e.g. survival::coxph , epitools::riskratio ) come from a package that must be installed on DST; the rest are base R (the stats package, always available). Regression and time-to-event are expanded in Regression and Time-to-event. Prefer a flowchart? Antoine Soetewey's [decision tree for choosing a statistical test](https://statsandr.com/blog/what-statistical-test-should-i-do/) is an excellent visual companion to the tables here - you click through data type, number of groups, paired/unpaired and distribution. Find the right test - three questions: 1. What data type is your outcome? Numeric (a number), binary (yes/no) or

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.heading: Concepts in brief
sections.text: New to statistics? Expand for the concepts the tables build on. The data type decides which table you need: Numeric (continuous): a number, e.g. age, BMI or blood pressure. Binary (dichotomous): yes/no, e.g. whether a person got a diagnosis or not. Time-to-event: the time until an event happens, where not everyone reaches it during follow-up (censoring) - e.g. time to diagnosis or death. A normal distribution is bell-shaped: most values lie in the middle, with few very small or very large ones. A skewed (or irregular) distribution does not - it may have a long tail to one side. !Two distributions (simulated data): a bell-shaped normal distribution and a right-skewed one. Most parametric tests (e.g. t-test) assume the data are roughly normal; if they are clearly skewed, that points to a nonparametric test. Check the shape with a histogram ( hist() ) or a Q-Q plot ( qqnorm() + qqline() ). The mean can be pulled by extreme values (outliers), while the median (the middle value) is more robust. In a right-skewed distribution the mean therefore sits to the right of the median: !Right-skewed distribution (simulated data) with the mean and median marked; the mean lies

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.text: Every test rests on some assumptions. Some you can test or inspect in the data; others are design questions you must judge from how the data were collected. Here are the ones named in the tables: Normal distribution (t-tests, linear regression, ANOVA). That the values - or for regression the model's residuals - are roughly normally distributed. Check: visually with a histogram ( hist() ) and Q-Q plot ( qqnorm() + qqline() ); optionally a formal test ( shapiro.test() ), but it is oversensitive in large samples, so trust the visual most. With large samples, t-tests and means are also robust (the central limit theorem). Normally distributed paired differences (paired t-test). It is the differences (e.g. before minus after) that should be roughly normal - not each group separately. Check: histogram/Q-Q plot of the differences. Symmetric distribution (Wilcoxon signed-rank). The test assumes the distribution of the values (about the median) or of the paired differences is symmetric - not necessarily normal. Check: histogram of the values/differences; if it is clearly skewed, a sign test may be more appropriate. Equal variance (homoscedasticity) (unpaired t-test,

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis plan has comorbidity at baseline as a covariate. It helps you decide between adjusting for individual conditions and adjusting for one combined measure, and whether to define a condition from hospital diagnoses, dispensed prescriptions or both. It then shows the extraction of diagnoses before index. It builds on [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd) and Medication (ATC), and you end with one 0/1 flag per condition per person, saved as .rds .

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Individual conditions or one combined measure?
sections.text: Which comorbidities to adjust for belongs to your analysis plan and typically follows from your DAG (directed acyclic graph, see [Phase 1 - Choose your covariates using a DAG](plan-your-study.qmd#covariates-dag)). There are two approaches: 1. Individual comorbidities as separate covariates, for example the specific diagnoses you identified as confounders in your DAG. You extract these as ordinary diagnosis variables, with the same LPR pattern as on Outcomes. This gives the most control and transparency, but you have to know in advance which conditions are confounders. 2. One combined measure of comorbidity burden: a count or an index built from hospital diagnoses, sometimes together with prescriptions. It is practical when many conditions are potential confounders, or when you want to describe the burden in Table 1. The Charlson Comorbidity Index is one such index; two packages that compute it from LPR diagnoses are listed on Algorithms & special packages. The Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI) is not a measure of comorbidity burden. Despite its name it is a score built to predict 5-year mortality. Use it when your question is mortality risk, and not as the combined measure in

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Diagnoses, prescriptions, or both?
sections.text: Whether a condition is defined from hospital diagnoses, from dispensed prescriptions, or from both is a design decision you make per condition, and it changes who counts as having it. Some conditions are captured well by LPR (the National Patient Register) on its own: the ones that reliably bring people to hospital, such as myocardial infarction or hip fracture. Others are mostly treated outside hospital. Hypertension is an example: people managed entirely in general practice never appear in LPR with an I10 diagnosis, but they do collect antihypertensives and so appear in LMDB, the prescription register. Both single-source definitions fail, in opposite directions: Diagnoses only miss everyone treated outside hospital: they look healthy. Prescriptions only catch everyone on the drug, including those taking it for something else. Antihypertensives are also prescribed for heart failure and angina, so a definition of hypertension from ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) codes alone over-counts. If you combine the two, the halves normally need different rules: A single dispensing is weak evidence of treatment, because some people fill a prescription once and stop. The pattern for

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: regmorbidity: many conditions from editable code lists
sections.text: regmorbidity is an R package in development for deriving many conditions at once from Danish register data. It is on GitHub only (not on CRAN), and parts of it have not been run on DST yet: read the package README for what has been tested before you rely on it. It computes no score and does not implement a published index. If you have code lists to contribute, get in touch. Conditions live in plain CSV code lists, not in R code. One row per code, with columns for the condition, the vocabulary ( ICD10 or ATC ), the code and, for medication, the minimum number of dispensings and the window in days. One condition can therefore mix diagnoses and prescriptions, and the definitions can be edited and version-controlled without touching the code that runs them. Medication conditions take a configurable count and window , and the onset date is the date of the qualifying dispensing. Results are written to disk one file per condition , so a long run over the full register can resume after an interruption. The bundled code lists take Prior et al. (2016) (doi:10.1093/aje/kwv324) as their starting point. They are meant to be revised for your own study and are not an implementation of that

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.text: Use this page when your study compares exposed people with a matched group of unexposed people from the population. It comes after [Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd), where you identified the exposed and excluded prevalent cases (the object exposed with pnr , index_date and exposed = 1 ). Here you build the comparison group: people who are not exposed, resemble the exposed on the variables you match on, and were at risk on the index date they are assigned. When you are done you have full_cohort.rds with both groups, a matched-set id and the index date per row. If you would rather not match and instead adjust for confounders in the analysis, go to Without matching near the end of the page. The examples show the shape of each step. They have not yet been run end to end on real register data , so treat them as a starting point: check the column names against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan. Confirm too that heaven::exposureMatch() is available on your project.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Risk-set sampling: who can be a comparison person
sections.text: A comparison group gives you the counterfactual experience: what would have happened to the exposed had they not been exposed. The main rule: a comparison person is assigned the exposed person's index date and must be at risk on exactly that date: alive, resident in Denmark, free of your outcome and meeting your criteria. This is the core of risk-set (incidence-density) sampling , and it is what prevents immortal time bias (assigning someone follow-up time during which they could not possibly have had the outcome). A person can be a comparison person now and become exposed themselves later; that is correct (see the crossover fold-out below).

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: What "risk set" means, and why the index date decides everything
sections.text: Study start vs. index date. Study start is the common date the study begins to look at data (e.g. 1 January 2010) - the same for everyone. The index date is a person's own start of follow-up: for an exposed person it is the exposure date, and a comparison person is assigned the exposed person's index date. It therefore varies from one exposed person to the next, and each comparison person is judged on exactly that date. Requiring "at risk" on the index date rather than at study start is what stops you including someone who had already died or emigrated by the time the exposed person was exposed. The risk set is a term from survival analysis: at each index date it is everyone still at risk right then - alive, outcome-free, under observation. Comparison persons are sampled from that set. An unexposed person stays in it until they themselves become exposed, then leaves it (and can become a case). Risk-set sampling captures that movement, because eligibility is judged on the index date rather than once and for all. !Risk-set sampling: on the case's index date (dashed line) comparison persons are sampled from those still at risk. sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: The design choices
sections.text: Matching variables are typically sex and birth year, but can also be index date/calendar year, SES and municipality. Whether a person may be reused is decided below. Whether to match at all is the other decision, and it is a different route through the page - see [Without matching](#without-matching-an-unmatched-comparison-group) after the four steps. In a risk-set design a future-exposed person is allowed to be a comparison person until their own exposure date. So do not exclude everyone who ever becomes exposed: that conditions on the future and can overestimate the effect (immortal-time or selection bias). Instead store a crossover_date = the date the person themselves becomes exposed, and decide how to handle it: censor at crossover, or let the person switch group. Crossover is explained briefly here; the censoring itself is done when follow-up time is calculated, in Link your extracts. General population: maximal contrast, but a risk of confounding by indication (the exposed differ systematically from the background population). sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: With or without replacement
sections.text: When you sample comparison persons, decide whether the same person may be used more than once. The choice affects both the matching and the analysis afterwards, so decide it before you match. Default: sample with replacement (risk-set sampling). A person can be matched to several exposed (and themselves become exposed/a case later). In Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2018, sampling with replacement did not bias the comparators' outcome risk, whereas 5:1 sampling without replacement biased it in older, high-risk cohorts, and chronological sampling without replacement failed to fill the matching ratio. exposureMatch() and the manual loop below both sample with replacement by default. Without replacement (each person used at most once) is not recommended even when the pool is large. If you have a specific reason to use it, the manual loop has a WITHOUT_REPLACEMENT switch - then check the match rate in Step 4, and expect bias in older or high-risk cohorts. With replacement, use clustered standard errors in the analysis. Standard models assume each row is an independent observation. sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 1 - Prepare the exposed for matching
sections.text: Identifying the exposed and excluding prevalent cases are done on [Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd). Here you attach sex and birth date from BEF (needed if you want to match on age or birth year), derive the variables you need (e.g. age at index), and apply your inclusion criteria. The same criteria are applied to the pool in Step 2. Deriving a variable. A new column is computed from existing ones with mutate() . Age at index is the days between index and birth over 365.25 (a year is 365.25 days because of leap years): The same applies to other derived measures, e.g. mutate(bmi = weight_kg / (height_m^2)) . Compute it once and reuse it, so the matching age and Table 1 always agree - see Link your extracts. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers - see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. The requirement is that the person has lived in Denmark continuously for at least 5 years up to their index date: years_resident >= 5 , where resident_since is the start of the current residence period. resident_since is the date of the latest immigration before index, or the date of birth if the person

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 2 - Build the comparison pool
sections.text: Now you build the pool that the comparison group will be drawn from. A member must satisfy two things: (1) be in BEF in the relevant years (i.e. resident in Denmark), and (2) meet your inclusion and exclusion criteria. The criteria depend on dates from several registers (death, emigration, exposure, outcome), so you join several tables to assemble the pool. The focus now shifts from the exposed to the whole population. On [Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd) the exposure definition gave you data for the exposed only. A comparison person can be anyone in the background population, so the variables that decide eligibility - demographics, death date, migration events, exposure date, outcome date, lookback - must be available for the whole population. That is why bef_py / demographics were pulled for everyone in Step 1, and why the dates here are extracted for the population too. The time-varying criteria (alive, exposure-free and outcome-free ON the assigned index date) cannot be filtered out here - they are decided at match time in Step 3: in Route A via end_fu (the date a person stops being eligible as a control), in Route B via the eligibility filters in

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Code: build the pool
sections.text: Exclusion happens before sampling, and on both groups. This is not a separate step but a rule: all inclusion and exclusion criteria (age, residency, prevalent outcome) must be applied to BOTH the exposed and the pool, each relative to its own/assigned index date, BEFORE you sample. Excluding after matching changes the population the exposed are matched to and introduces selection bias. See [Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30310326/) on correct comparison-cohort sampling.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 3 - Match the comparison group
sections.text: Always set a seed before sampling, so the matching is reproducible. Route A and Route B do the same single step; pick one. A package like exposureMatch() replaces only the sampling loop. Everything else (prepare the exposed, build the pool, exclusions, assemble and validate) you do either way. If you take Route A, skip the manual loop and the performance fold-out.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Route A: heaven::exposureMatch()
sections.text: Route A is the one to start with for most studies. exposureMatch() is built for a comparison cohort: a case is a person who becomes exposed at index, and a control is one who is not yet exposed at the case's index. ( incidenceMatch() is the sibling for case-control; riskSetMatch() is the internal engine under both.) First we combine the exposed and the pool into ONE table ( all_persons ) in the format exposureMatch() needs: an event indicator (1/0), a case.index date and an end.followup date. This prepares the match pool; the sampling itself is only the function call afterwards. (The manual Route B uses exposed and pool directly and does not need this assembly.) Route A cannot model someone moving back. exposureMatch() gives each person one end_fu , i.e. a single continuous risk interval. Someone who emigrates in 2008 and moves back in 2010 therefore leaves the risk set in 2008 and never re-enters, even though they were genuinely resident from 2010. The consequence is lost person-time, not a wrong inclusion, so the direction is conservative - but it is there. If return migration matters in your population (e.g. many migrants or long follow-up), use Route B

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Route B: manual risk-set loop
sections.text: It also shows what exposureMatch() does under the hood. The manual loop gives full control, but you handle every step yourself, so there are more places it can go wrong; Route A is the safer starting point. Route B is needed when Route A cannot express what you need, e.g.: Interval / caliper matching: exposureMatch() only matches exactly on fixed factor variables (e.g. same birth year). If you want to match within an interval around the case's value - e.g. birth year ±1, age ±2 years or BMI ±5 - that cannot be written as exact matching, so you have to loop yourself. (You can put e.g. age into groups and match exactly on the group in Route A; only a rolling ± around each case's value needs the loop.) Matching criteria computed relative to the case: criteria that date.terms / duration.terms cannot express. Custom sampling: e.g. counter-matching or special replacement rules, or your own per-matched-set variables. The package is not available: heaven is missing on your project. For standard register matching (sex, birth year, calendar time, alive/resident/outcome-free/exposure-free at index, comorbidity timing) Route A is enough. Chronological order. We sort the exposed by

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Without matching: an unmatched comparison group
sections.text: A comparison group does not have to be matched. Matching and adjustment are two ways to handle the same confounders: Matching (design): you balance the groups on e.g. sex, age and calendar year before you look at the outcome (that is what Step 3 does). The cost is that a matched variable can no longer be studied as an exposure of its own, and a narrow pool can be depleted. Adjustment (analysis): you take a broader unexposed group without matching and instead control for the same variables in the analysis. If you "just" want a comparison group that is not matched on anything: 1. Define the eligible unexposed group with the same inclusion and exclusion criteria as the exposed (alive, resident, outcome-free and exposure-free at their index). This is still the pool from Step 2. 2. You need no matching function: just combine exposed and unexposed with an exposed indicator (1/0). 3. Assign a start of follow-up (index) to the unexposed, so follow-up begins at a comparable point. This is the hard part: do it so you avoid immortal time (e.g. using calendar time as the time axis, or assigning index dates from the exposed persons' distribution). 4. Adjust in the analysis for the

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Checklist before you trust the matched cohort
sections.text: Every one of these is something you cannot repair after the fact: At risk ON the assigned index date (not just at study start) - otherwise immortal time bias. Exclusion BEFORE sampling and on both groups (exposed + pool). Exposure-free ON index, not "never exposed": do not exclude everyone ever exposed (crossover). Exclude prevalent outcome in both groups, each relative to its own index date. set.seed() before sampling: otherwise the matching is not reproducible. Compute age ONCE ( /365.25 ) and reuse the variable, so matching age and Table 1 agree. One row per person: deduplicate (duplicate person-year rows produce duplicate matches). Avoid over-matching: match only on confounders. With replacement (or crossover) → clustered standard errors in the analysis. Several comparison cohorts can share individuals - analyze each separately, do not pool them.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Next step: extract outcomes and covariates for both groups
sections.text: You have full_cohort.rds : one row per person (per matched set, if drawn more than once) with pnr and index_date for both groups (exposed and comparison group). Use it in all subsequent extractions: cohort_pnrs thus contains the pnr's for both exposed and comparison persons, not just the exposed. Extraction of outcomes and covariates must cover the entire study population.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.text: This guide is continuously evolving, and many researchers have solved the same classic problems each in their own project - without the code or the experience ever being shared. If we share, we all save time. There are two kinds of contribution we are especially looking for: knowledge (recurring problems, methods and packages we should cover) and code (concrete, reusable solutions). You do not need anything finished - drafts and good pointers are gold too.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: Share your knowledge
sections.text: Where do register researchers keep hitting the same things? Point us in the right direction: #### Recurring problems Which pitfalls do you meet again and again? (immortal time, exclusion order, prevalent vs. incident, time-varying confounding ...) - so we can describe them in one place. #### Epidemiological methods Designs, bias and analysis approaches specific to register data - and how to explain them simply for beginners. #### Packages that already exist Do you know an R package that solves a register problem? (e.g. heaven , Epi , MatchIt , EpiForsk , comorbidity ...) Then we point to it instead of reinventing. Do you know the "stamdata" register? The National Centre for Register-based Research works with an external dataset of that name, and we have no description of it. If you know what it contains or how it is obtained, we would like to hear from you.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: Share your code
sections.text: Concrete, reusable solutions. It does not need to be validated - we are happy to work on from a draft: #### Ethnicity Deriving ethnicity/origin and generations from BEF/IEPE. #### Medication and medication use Exposure measures from LMDB: DDD, weighted use, PDC/MPR, insulin dosing, lag time and long-term prescriptions. Medication (ATC) explains why dispensings are not intake, but stops short of the code. #### Family linkage Linking parents, children and siblings via CPR/family id, e.g. to carry exposures or covariates across generations. [Special designs](special-designs.qmd) covers the design side; the linkage code itself is what we are missing. #### Socioeconomic classification Education, income and employment, e.g. by SEPLINE. We have a [starter page](socioeconomic-variables.qmd) - validated code welcome. #### Time-varying variables Variables that change over follow-up - blood tests, BMI, weight. We have a starter page - worked examples from real projects welcome. It does not need to be finished or validated - we are happy to work further with drafts. If you have something else entirely that solves a general problem in register data, you are very welcome to get in touch as well.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: How to contribute
sections.text: Two ways - pick whichever suits you: Email us (easiest): saras@clin.au.dk. Send code, a draft, or just an idea - we'll add it. You need neither git nor GitHub. Open a pull request on GitHub (if you're comfortable with it): The guide's source files live in a GitHub repository: github.com/steno-aarhus/registers-guide. Every page in the guide is a .qmd file, and the website itself is built automatically from them. A pull request is a proposal of concrete changes to those files that we can review and merge. A pull request is only a proposal - it is never merged automatically. We are notified, review the change, and merge it only once we have approved it. An outside contributor can therefore propose a change but cannot alter the page directly; only people we have explicitly given write access can merge. So nothing goes live behind our backs. 1. Create a (free) GitHub account if you don't have one. 2. Find the file. Every page is a .qmd file in the repository root, and the filename is shown in the address bar : the page at .../understand-lpr.html is the file understand-lpr.qmd (the part before .html is the .qmd name). 3. sections.text: Register data on DARTER is loaded with fastreg::read_register("name") - exactly as in the general guide. You just point fastreg at DARTER's parquet folder once per script; see [Loading templates](darter-register-paths-datastores.qmd#load-templates). Before running a script: verify that path_output at the top of each script points to your workspace folder (defined under [Base paths in Register paths and datastores](darter-register-paths-datastores.qmd#base-paths)).

sections.text: This page only holds what is specific to the DARTER delivery. Everything that applies to all projects is in the general guide; the list at the bottom points to the general pitfalls that also bite on DARTER.

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 1. How far the parquet files reach
sections.text: Most registers are as of 2026 updated to end of 2024 . Check each register you use against your study period with the general coverage check. If a register stops too early, exposed people and comparators whose events fall after its end date look like nothing happened to them, which affects censoring and matching with no error message. If the parquet file does not cover your study period: You need to extract data from the raw SAS file on DST. Contact your data manager - they can help with raw data access and conversion. Deaths are the known case: dod is not in cleaned-data on DARTER. See Register paths and datastores for how to read it.

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 2. Surgery and procedures
sections.text: Procedure codes are split across two registers by period: lpr_sksopr (parquet-registers) - procedures and surgery 1996--2018, joined to lpr_adm via recnum procedurer_kirurgi (parquet-external) - 2019 and onwards, joined to lpr_a_kontakt via dw_ek_forloeb dw_ek_kontakt is NA for all rows in procedurer_kirurgi . Use dw_ek_forloeb - not dw_ek_kontakt - to fetch pnr from lpr_a_kontakt , or better, use lpr_a_procregistrering , which also exists on DARTER and joins on dw_ek_kontakt like lpr_a_diagnose does. The full column list, why the key is empty, and the fallback code are in [Register paths and datastores](darter-register-paths-datastores.qmd#procedurer-kirurgi).

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 3. LPR3: DARTER's LPR2 stops a quarter early
sections.text: The general guide filters lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" to avoid counting LPR2 contacts twice (see general pitfall 13). On DARTER, that filter currently drops a real quarter of contacts, not just duplicates. DST's LPR2 files end 31 March 2019 (the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019), but DARTER's lpr_adm / lpr_diag delivery available under cleaned_data currently stops 31 December 2018 , a full quarter earlier (confirmed directly, not DST's documented date). The LPR2-tagged rows still sitting in lpr_a_kontakt for January-March 2019 are the only record of those contacts anywhere in this delivery: filtering to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" removes them entirely, not just de-duplicates them. Direct measurement confirms the loss is bounded to that one quarter: practically no rows carry an LPR2-tagged start date after 31 March 2019, so this is not an open-ended problem spanning years. Do not just drop the lprindberetningssystem filter to get the missing quarter back - that also brings back the real 2017-2018 duplicates the filter exists to remove. The fix is a date cutover: keep genuine LPR3

sections.title: Register paths and datastores
sections.heading: Critical notes
sections.text: lpr_sksube has no procedure code on DARTER. The parquet holds three columns and no more: DST documents this register with c_opr , c_oprart , c_osgh and c_tilopr for every year 1999-2019, the same shape as lpr_sksopr . None of them are here, so the table can tell you that a procedure happened and on what date, but not which procedure. There is no filtering trick that recovers them. If you need examinations and non-surgical treatments, ask for the columns to be added to the delivery. Surgical procedures are unaffected: lpr_sksopr has c_opr and d_odto as documented. Deaths: dod is not in cleaned-data. You do not need a separate extraction on DARTER: the raw file reads directly. Do the range check. The file is named dod2024 , and the row above says 1970-2024, but nobody on the DARTER team has confirmed the start year of this extract . sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.text: You arrive at this phase with separate RDS files: your cohort from [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd) and the variables you extracted in [Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd) - outcomes, socioeconomics and comorbidity (plus demographics from Phase 6 if relevant). You leave with one analysis-ready dataset ready for [Phase 13 - Analysis](analysis.qmd). Before you can analyse, you need to: 1. Shape each extract into one row per person (most registers are in long format with many rows per person) 2. Assemble them into one analysis-ready dataset with left_join() That is what this phase is about. The technique for step 1 is either group_by() + slice() or pivot_wider() - the choice depends on what you want out of the register. Step 2 is a left_join() onto the cohort, so everyone in the cohort is kept.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: What is an analysis-ready dataset?
sections.text: An analysis-ready dataset has one row per person and one column per variable - what we call wide format : The example uses a cohort study with exposure , outcome and followup_years - the column names every Phase 13 page uses (the full list, including time_days and status_code , is built in [Link your extracts](joins.qmd#follow-up-time)). For a prevalence study the column structure will look different - typically without follow-up time, but with a cross-sectional date and covariates measured at that point. The techniques in this phase (joins, pivots, group_by() + slice() ) are the same regardless of study design. The registers you extract from - LPR, LMDB, BEF - are almost always in long format with many rows per person. This phase shows how to reshape and assemble them.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: What have you already saved?
sections.text: Each extraction from Phases 6, 9 and 11 should be saved as its own RDS file - one register, one topic. Example of what you typically have: Date of death and emigration have no file of their own here: [Link your extracts](joins.qmd) reads them from DOD and VNDS when it attaches them. The goal of this phase is to assemble them into one dataset with left_join() - one new column per file. The cohort is the backbone: each extract is joined on via pnr (or pnr + index_date when the value is measured at index) and adds its columns - all cohort members are kept, and people with no match get NA . Assemble only what you need. It is tempting to keep all columns "just in case". Do not. Always end with select() and explicitly choose the columns the analysis requires. A dataset with only the necessary columns is far easier to debug and understand.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: Two tools for shaping data
sections.text: The two central operations in this phase are pivots and joins - they sound similar but do fundamentally different things: Rule of thumb: Use pivot when you want to change the shape of one table. Use join when you want to combine two tables.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: This phase's pages
sections.text: Two core pages take you from separate extracts to one analysis-ready dataset: 1. Long ↔ wide format: get each extract down to one row per person . Understand the difference between long and wide format, and use either group_by() + slice() (one representative value per person) or pivot_wider() (several time points side by side). 2. Link your extracts: join the extracts on pnr ( left_join() , inner_join() , semi_join() , anti_join() ), stack two versions of the same register vertically ( bind_rows() ), validate the join, and calculate follow-up time and event variable. This is where the final dataset is assembled. The order is deliberate: reshape first, then join . You cannot join predictably until each extract has one row per person. Two optional add-on pages you only take if your project needs them: Missing data: how to understand and handle missing values, including multiple imputation. Time-varying variables: what to do when a variable changes during follow-up (and when you do not need to do anything).

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.text: DST's variable lists describe a register. Your project gets a delivery : a copy of the registers that someone ordered, converted and placed on your project's drive. The two can differ. Columns can be missing, keys renamed or empty, years cut off, and registers left out of the parquet folder. None of this causes an error. Your code runs, and the result is quietly wrong. So before you build a cohort, spend an hour running the checks on this page against your own delivery. Each check comes with an example of what it catches. The examples are examples. Each one is a problem that turned up in one real project's delivery. They show what can happen, not what is in yours. Another project, or a newer delivery for the same project, may look completely different. That is the reason to run the checks yourself rather than rely on anyone's list of known issues, this one included. All the code reads registers with read_register() from fastreg. Without fastreg, use open_dataset("path/to/<register>/") instead; the rest is the same.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 1. Does each register reach the end of your follow-up?
sections.text: Check the first and last year or date of every register you use against your study period. The code is in Inspect your data. Example: in one delivery, the LPR2 contact register lpr_adm stopped on 31 December 2018, a full quarter before DST's own LPR2 files end (31 March 2019; the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019). Contacts from those three months existed only in the LPR3 tables, so the standard LPR3 filter quietly removed them. See [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#lpr3-filter-caveat) for how to check where your LPR2 stops.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 2. Does each register have the columns DST documents?
sections.text: Compare the column names in your delivery with DST's variable list for that register (Overview of registers links to each one). If a column you need is not there, no amount of filtering will bring it back. Ask your data manager whether it can be added to the delivery. Example: in one delivery, lpr_sksube (examinations and treatments) had only three columns: recnum , d_odto and year . DST documents it with the procedure code c_opr and three more. The table could say that a procedure happened and when, but not which procedure.
sections.code: read_register lpr_sksube replace register you need rename_with tolower colnames columns actually have

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 3. Are the join keys named as documented?
sections.text: Joins fail, or join nothing, when a key has a different name than the code expects. Look for the key columns before you write a join. Example: in one delivery, the psychiatric LPR2 tables used v_cpr instead of pnr and k_recnum / v_recnum instead of recnum . See [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd) for how to rename them only when your delivery needs it.
sections.code: read_register t_psyk_adm rename_with tolower colnames person key pnr contact recnum

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 4. Are the join keys actually filled in?
sections.text: A key column can exist and still be empty. Count the missing values in every key you plan to join on. Some missing keys can be by design: in LPR3, a procedure attaches either to a contact or to a whole course, and the other key is left empty. A key that is missing on every row is not by design. Example: in one delivery, a project-specific LPR3 procedure table had the contact key dw_ek_kontakt empty on every single row, so joining it to the contacts returned nothing. The general LPR3 procedure register, lpr_a_procregistrering , had the key filled in and was the way out.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 5. Is there one row per key, as documented?
sections.text: Registers that are documented as one row per person per year (or per family per year) do not always arrive that way. Duplicates make every join grow without an error. Example: in one delivery, FAIK (family income) from 2022 onward also carried pnr and repeated each family's row once per family member. See Socioeconomic variables for the full check and the fix. BEF can do the same with quarterly snapshots.

sections.heading: 6. Is every register in the parquet folder?

If a register is missing, ask your data manager where it is. Reading a raw SAS file and converting it are covered in [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet). Example: in one delivery, the death register dod was only a raw SAS file, while dodsaars was converted and easy to load. dodsaars stops in 2001 (see pitfall 1), so anyone who took the convenient one treated everyone who died after 2001 as alive.

sections.heading: When you find something
sections.text: Write it down where your project keeps its notes, with the date and the check that found it, and tell your data manager. The next person on the project will otherwise find it again the hard way. Re-run the checks when a new delivery arrives: problems can be fixed, and new ones can appear.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.text: A Table 1 describes your study population: age, sex and other baseline variables, usually split by exposure. It is almost always the first table in a register-based paper. This page builds one from the analysis-ready dataset with the gtsummary package, adds a crude incidence rate per group, and writes the table to a file you can take through output control. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. gtsummary - and huxtable , if you want to export to Excel - must be installed in your R environment on DST; if they are not, contact your data manager.

sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: You start from your analysis-ready dataset with one row per person ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)), or one row per person and index date if your comparison group was matched with replacement.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Build the table with tbl_summary()
sections.text: tbl_summary() summarises the variables you point it at. With by = you split the table into columns by a group (e.g. exposure). tbl_summary() detects the variable type itself from the column's contents and picks a suitable statistic: factor and character variables - and numeric variables with fewer than 10 unique values - become categorical and are shown as {n} ({p}%) (count and percentage); other numeric variables become continuous and are shown as {median} ({p25}, {p75}) (median and quartiles, i.e. IQR); variables coded 0/1 , yes/no or TRUE/FALSE become dichotomous and are shown with only the one ("yes") row. statistic = is therefore optional. Omit the line entirely and you get exactly the default display above. It is only included to show how you change it - for mean instead of median, write all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})" . In gtsummary the tilde ~ means "assign": what ~ value . E.g. age ~ "Age (years)" gives the age variable the label "Age (years)", and all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})" sets that statistic for all continuous variables. all_continuous() / all_categorical() mean "all continuous" resp. "all categorical" variables, so

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Crude incidence rate (per 1000 person-years)
sections.text: Register papers often report the crude incidence rate per exposure group alongside Table 1: the number of events divided by the total follow-up time (person-years), scaled to per 1000 person-years. It needs outcome (1 = event, 0 = censored) and followup_years from your analysis-ready dataset (built in [Phase 12](joins.qmd#follow-up-time)). This is a descriptive rate with no adjustment. The number of events is a cell like any other, so check it against the small-cell rule before export. To compare the groups with control for confounding, see [Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)](rates-poisson.qmd) for an adjusted rate ratio or Time-to-event, where a Cox model gives a hazard ratio.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Export the table (for output control)
sections.text: Anything leaving DST must go through output control, and the rules are on Phase 14 - Export and repatriation. Before you write the file, check three things in the table: Small cells. Every count, including the "Missing" row, must be at or above your project's threshold (3 or 5). Hidden numbers. If you hide a count, the Overall column and the N in the header can give it back. See [a hidden number must not be possible to work out](export.qmd#back-calculation). Median and quartiles. DST allows percentiles only when they cannot point to a person. In a large group that is not a problem; in a small subgroup, report mean (SD) or leave the row out. See [min, max, median and percentiles](export.qmd#min-max-median). If huxtable or flextable is not available on DST, use the CSV route (base R, no packages needed) or contact your data manager.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.text: This page collects the errors that most frequently catch new users of DST registers. What they have in common: the error messages are either confusing, or there is no error message at all - the result is just silently wrong.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 1. Four death registers - dodsaars stops in 2001
sections.text: Four registers have confusingly similar names, and the one most people reach for first is the one that ends a quarter of a century ago: Coverage is from [DST's own register overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html). Two separate things are going on. The date of death lives in dod , which covers the whole period on its own. The cause of death is split across the three others, each picking up where the last stopped, so a study spanning 1995 to 2024 needs all three chained together and none of them alone will tell you it is incomplete. If you censor on dodsaars , everyone who died after 2001 looks alive. There is no error and no warning. They stay in your risk set until the end of follow-up, so your survival curves are too good and your rates are too low. For a study running past 2001, which is nearly all of them, use dod . Two things to check on your own project before you rely on this. Is dod in your delivery, and does it reach far enough back? Your project received the years it ordered, not necessarily all of 1970-2025. Check with read_register("dod") %>% summarise(min(doddato), max(doddato)) %>% collect() . Is it
sections.code: fastreg read_register dplyr semi_join select collect death censoring dod dodsaars rename_with tolower death_person tibble pnr cohort_pnrs copy only cohort death_date doddato d_dodsdto

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 2. RAM is shared - clean up after large extractions
sections.text: You are on a shared server with shared RAM. When the memory bar in RStudio turns red, everyone on the server experiences slowdowns - and DST automatically kills processes when RAM is close to full, so an oversized extraction can cost you your unsaved work. To find out which object is filling the memory, see [Seeing your memory use from inside R](good-coding-practice.qmd#see-ram-in-r) - gc() for the session total and object.size() for the culprit. More practical habits (save often, partial loading, Task Manager) in [Mind your RAM in the shared environment](good-coding-practice.qmd#mind-your-ram), and DST's official advice in [DST guide: Reducing RAM use in the shared environment (PDF, Danish)](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=4500415120635&fo=0&ext=forskning).

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 3. rename_with(tolower) must be called on each register
sections.text: Raw column names vary by register and year: PNR , pnr , Pnr , V_CPR . If you forget it, semi_join(..., by = "pnr") silently fails with "Column pnr not found" - even though the column is there. The rule: every open_dataset() or read_register() call ends with %>% rename_with(tolower) as the first step in your pipe. See [Extracting data step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd) for explanation and example.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 4. Date columns are not always in Date format
sections.text: DST registers store dates in multiple formats - they look the same but behave differently. The rule: always check class() on a date column before using it in calculations. A datetime and a date are two different types, and on a lazy table (before collect() ) the engines do not reliably convert between them. Tested on lpr_a_kontakt on the DST server (fastreg 0.14.1, duckdb 2.0.0, arrow 21.0.0.1, duckplyr 1.2.2): filter(as.Date(kont_starttidspunkt) >= as.Date("2023-01-01")) on a table from read_parquet_dataset() ran without an error but returned 0 rows , although millions of rows match. Others have seen a rapi error from the same pattern. The same line on a table from read_parquet_duckdb() stops with This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB . Comparing the column with a datetime created before the pipe gave the same, correct count on both. Convert to a plain date with as.Date() after collect() , when the data are in R. After any date filter, compare count() before and after to confirm that the filter did what you meant - a filter that keeps nothing, or everything, is the warning sign.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 5. BEF is a status snapshot - not a live register
sections.text: BEF is a status register : it records the composition of the population at a given reference time - not continuously. DST classifies every register as one of four reference types: Status (a snapshot on one date, which is BEF), Statusperiode (population fixed on a date, values accumulated over a period), Forløb (rows with a start and an end date) and Hændelse (one row per event, with one date). Knowing which type you are holding tells you what a row actually means. DST's reference time is ultimo (typically 31 December for an annual snapshot). Since 2008, BEF is also delivered quarterly (March, June, September, December). year == 2020 meaning 1 January 2020 is a project convention. In many projects BEF snapshots are renamed so that year == 2020 refers to the population composition as of 1 January 2020, but that does not follow from DST's delivery naming. Confirm the convention in your project guide. See DST's official BEF documentation: [statistikdokumentation/befolkningen →](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/befolkningen) A person is in a BEF file only if they were alive and living in Denmark on that file's reference date. DST's file

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 6. The "a" in lpr_a_diagnose does not mean A-type diagnoses
sections.text: The table is called lpr_a_diagnose - DST describes the LPR_A tables as an "LPR analyse model" in [its release note from June 2025](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2025/nyt-om-grunddata-2-kvartal-2025), which is the likely origin of the "a". It does not mean the table only contains A-type (action) diagnoses. LPR3 has two diagnosis types, and the table holds both: A (action diagnosis) and B (secondary diagnosis). G (underlying condition) is an LPR2 type and is not reported in LPR3. The six LPR2 types and their years are in [Understand LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#diagtype). You still need to filter on diag_kode_type :

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 7. Categorical codes are not consistent across registers
sections.text: The same variable can have different coding in different registers - different type (numeric vs. character), different values, or both. The worst case is ICD-10. LPR stores it with a Danish D in front ( DE119 ), the cause-of-death registers and the cancer register store the plain WHO code ( E119 ). A code list built for one matches nothing in the other, and the habit of stripping the D turns E119 into 119 . See [ICD codes and the D-prefix](understand-lpr.qmd#d-prefix-not-everywhere). In practice you extract demographic variables (sex, age) from BEF and rarely need to compare the same variable in another register. But if you do, always check with table() and class() before using the variable:

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 8. !! (bang-bang) forgotten in lazy evaluation
sections.text: When filtering with a local R vector inside a lazy query, dplyr first looks for a column with that name; only if there is none does it copy in the values of your R object. Usually that just works - the trap is a name clash : if your local object has the same name as a column, the column wins and you get a wrong result or a confusing message. !! is a recommended safeguard for all local R objects used inside filter() , mutate() etc. on lazy Arrow/DuckDB connections - typically code or year lists ( %in% !!codes , >= !!min_date ). If instead you filter on pnr against the whole cohort, use semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) : it takes a local table directly and needs no !! . See [Functions guide](function-guide.qmd#bang-bang-two-exclamation-marks) for full explanation.
