sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 9. nmi_count ≠ nmi
sections.text: These two variables are not the same and are not interchangeable: If you use nmi_count in your regression model instead of nmi , you are adjusting for something different than you think - and you get no error message.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 10. Immortal time bias - exposure defined using the future
sections.text: No error message, no warning - just an effect estimate that looks too good. Immortal time bias arises when a person is given follow-up time during which they could not, by construction, have had the outcome. It is the classic register mistake, because register data let you define groups retrospectively , looking back at what eventually happened. A concrete example. Question: does bariatric surgery lower mortality in people with type 2 diabetes? You take everyone diagnosed with T2D in 2010, split them into a surgery group (had surgery at some point during follow-up) and a no-surgery group, and start counting follow-up for everyone at the diagnosis date. The trap: to land in the surgery group, a person had to survive long enough to be operated . Say the average wait from diagnosis to surgery is 2 years. Those 2 years are immortal : anyone who died in that window never reached surgery and so fell into the no-surgery group instead. You have handed the surgery group \~2 years of guaranteed-alive person-time and labelled it "surgery" time. Correctly aligned, the 4,000 pre-surgery person-years count as no-surgery time, and the rates are identical (3.0) - surgery does nothing.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 11. year is a folder name, not a date
sections.text: In a fastreg converted register (to parquet), year says which yearly file a row came from. Filtering on it is what makes a query against a billion rows finish in seconds - but it does not tell you when anything happened. year == 2020 in BEF does not say which quarterly snapshot you have. When the timing matters, use the register's own date column ( hf_vfra in UDDA, d_inddto in lpr_adm , referencetid in BEF). The two uses look identical in the code. And it is only a year at all if the register arrived as one file per year. Some registers arrive as a single file covering everything, and then every row carries the same year whatever its date. dodsaars spans 1970 to 2001 and says 2024 on every row. lpr_a_kontakt is worse, because it is the consolidated LPR_A table: one file holding every contact that ended in 2017 or later, so counting by year puts LPR1, LPR2, MiniPAS (records from private hospitals) and LPR3 contacts all in the same single year, and it looks as though four reporting systems ran at once. Check with count(year) before you filter on it. One value means the column labels the delivery, not the data, and a year filter will return everything or nothing.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 12. DST's own published totals do not agree with each other
sections.text: DST and the Danish Health Data Authority publish more than one number for what sounds like the same thing, because the underlying population differs. For 2005, Hospital statistics 2005 reports 6,336,000 outpatient visits; the web-based Health data retrieval system reports 1,894,441 outpatient contacts for the same year, a difference of more than 3-fold. The first includes psychiatric wards and excludes private hospitals, the second does the opposite (Lynge et al. 2011, [The Danish National Patient Register](https://doi.org/10.1177/1403494811401482), Scand J Public Health 39(Suppl 7):30-33). Do not use a published aggregate as ground truth for your own extraction without checking its exact population. If your row count from lpr_a_kontakt does not match a number you found in a DST or Sundhedsdata- styrelsen publication, the mismatch may be the publication's population definition (which wards, which hospital types, which patient type), not a bug in your code. Check what the publication actually counted before assuming your extraction is wrong.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 13. lpr_a_kontakt/lpr_a_diagnose are not pure LPR3
sections.text: The name suggests these tables hold LPR3 data only. They do not: LPR_A also carries older LPR1, LPR2 and MiniPAS (private-hospital) rows, reloaded into the same table and tagged by lprindberetningssystem , for contacts that ended in 2017 or later ([DST's remark on LPR_A_KONTAKT](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Bemaerkning/LPR_A_KONTAKT%20-%20Landspatientregistret%20%28LPR3%29%20-Kontaktoplysninger%20omkring%20de%20enkelte%20kontakter.html)). See Understand LPR for what that means for your extract. If you combine LPR2 ( lpr_adm ) and LPR_A without filtering, the same contacts get counted twice - once from each table. Filter both lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" before using them alongside lpr_adm / lpr_diag : This filter is not free of its own problems. Your own lpr_adm delivery's actual coverage can end earlier than DST's own LPR2 files do (31 March 2019), in which case the simple filter above silently drops real, unique contacts along with the duplicates. See [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#lpr3-filter-caveat) for how to check your own delivery's coverage before trusting it. On DARTER specifically, see
sections.code: lpr3_k lpr_a_kontakt filter lprindberetningssystem lpr3 keep only genuine rows lpr3_d lpr_a_diagnose same column diagnosis table colnames there

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: Something actually broke?
sections.text: Every pitfall above is a case where the code runs and the answer is quietly wrong. If instead you have a red error message, or a result that came back empty, that is Troubleshooting.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.text: This is the last step of a project: taking your results home from Statistics Denmark (DST), which DST calls hjemtagelse (repatriation). Read it before you build the tables and figures you plan to export (Phase 13), and use the checklist at the bottom before you upload. The data on the research machine are microdata: they stay there, and results leave only through DST's repatriation tool, after you have checked them against DST's rules. This page is an overview. DST's own rules take precedence, and they can change: read them before you export. [DST: Rules for repatriation of analysis results (in Danish)](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-hjemtagelse-af-analyseresultater) [DST: guidance on the data security rules, with worked examples (PDF, in Danish, April 2024)](https://www.dst.dk/ext/158751994932/0/forskning/Vejledning-i-datasikkerhedsreglerne-under-Mikrodataordningerne-herunder-for-hjemsendelse-af-analyseresultater-og-sanktioner-ved-databru--pdf) The Danish quotes on this page are from those two sources.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: What may leave DST?
sections.text: DST lets you take analysis results and other material home when three conditions all hold: nothing at the level of individuals (or their pseudonymised keys) is left in it, it is aggregated enough that no person can be identified or recognised "hverken direkte eller indirekte" (neither directly nor indirectly), and the file is of an approved type and goes through the repatriation tool. What can meet those conditions: Aggregated tables Figures built from aggregated numbers (see figures below) Analysis results, such as model estimates with confidence intervals Scripts. Program code is an approved file type and goes through the same tool. It must not contain microdata either: DST's guidance (page 10) names code with microdata written into a condition, such as a pnr value in a filter, and log files that list observations. What never leaves: Individual-level data in any form, also with pnr removed Small cells, see the threshold below Results that could identify a person, directly or indirectly Copied notes, screenshots or photographs of the screen. DST's rule names them: no microdata may be taken home by copying information down, or by "et skærmprint eller et billede af skærmen med

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Which cell size applies to you
sections.text: DST's baseline is at least 3 observations per table cell. Some registers are stricter: > "Der skal være mindst 3 observationer pr. tabelcelle [...]. For enkelte > registre kan der være strengere krav, for eksempel mindst 5 observationer pr. > tabelcelle. Hvis dette er tilfældet, vil det fremgå i DDV App, når du > bestiller data." In English: at least 3 observations per table cell; for some registers the requirement can be stricter, for example at least 5; if so, it is shown in DDV App (DDV is Danmarks Datavindue at DST) when you order the data. Check there which rule applies to your project. The rule applies at the finest level of the table: if you cross two variables, every cell of the cross-tabulation must hold the minimum. DST also says the number is a guide and the responsibility is yours: if you doubt that 3 (or 5) is enough to keep people anonymous, aggregate further. This page uses 5 throughout, because it is the safe side of both rules and because health register data is usually in the stricter group. If your project is on the baseline of 3, nothing here breaks: you are reporting more conservatively than required.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: A hidden number must not be possible to work out
sections.text: Hiding the small cells is not enough on its own. DST's rules also say that a hidden number must not be possible to work out again from the rest of what you take home: > "Observationer, som er blevet aggregeret eller på anden vis sløret eller > fjernet i en tabel, graf eller figur, må ikke kunne udledes ved tilbageregning > eller krydslæsning. Hvis dette er muligt, skal der aggregeres yderligere." In English: observations that have been aggregated, blurred or removed in a table, graph or figure must not be possible to derive by back calculation or by reading tables against each other. If they can be, aggregate further. In plain words: no subtracting your way back to a hidden number, within one table or across tables. The usual way it happens is a total. Take two rows of a Table 1 with an overall column: Only 1 exposed person is aged 90+, so you hide that number. But the row still shows 18 overall and 17 unexposed, and 18 - 17 = 1. So you must hide a second number in the same row, the 17. Now the column gives the 1 back instead: the exposed column shows N = 282 and every other age group, so the missing 1 is what is left over. So a number in the same column must go too, and then one

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Min, max, median and percentiles can point to one person
sections.text: A minimum or a maximum is one person's actual value, and a median or another percentile is often one too. DST's guidance (PDF above, page 6) allows max, min and percentiles such as the median only when there is no risk of identifying individuals: > "Ingen personer må derfor kunne genkendes i det hjemsendte output." In English: no person may be recognisable in the output you send home. The guidance tells you to look for outliers first and remove them if needed, and for max and min it requires that the observations at each end of the distribution lie close together, so that no one stands out. If in doubt, they must not be sent home. In practice: a median and quartiles of age in a group of several hundred people are shared by many and point to no one. A maximum income, or the range of a variable in a small subgroup, can point to one person. Leave min and max out unless you need them, and ask your data manager when you are unsure.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Figures and curves
sections.text: A figure is judged as if it were the table behind it: > "For formater, der ikke indeholder tabelceller, såsom figurer eller grafer, > er en god tommelfingerregel, at de skulle have mindst 3 observationer pr. > tabelcelle, hvis de blev konverteret til tabeller." In English: for formats without table cells, such as figures and graphs, a good rule of thumb is that they would have at least 3 observations per cell if they were converted to tables. So every bar, point and histogram bin needs the minimum number of people behind it, and a plot with one mark per person (a scatterplot of individuals) cannot leave. DST's guidance (page 7) names three further things to watch: Outliers: a single extreme point or a long axis can show one person's value. Kaplan-Meier curves: "man fx med Kaplan Meier kurver skal være opmærksom på små populationer" (with Kaplan-Meier curves, for example, watch out for small populations). Each step in a curve is one or a few events, and the numbers in a risk table are table cells. Data stored inside the figure file: the file must not carry the observations the figure was drawn from. The guidance suggests PDF as one way to make sure. How to build figures that

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Missing values (NA) are cells too
sections.text: A count of missing values is a cell like any other. If 1 to 4 people are missing on a variable, that count may not be repatriated. Merge it into another category, or hide it the way you hide any other small cell (and check that it cannot be worked out from the total). Agree the solution with your data manager if neither fits. Make a quick overview of missing values, so you see the small cells immediately instead of adding figures up in your head: table() hides NA by default; useNA = "always" shows the NA row. See Phase 7 - table() hides NA.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: How the upload works
sections.text: You upload from the research machine. On its remote desktop there is a shortcut called "Hjemtag Filer" (retrieve files), which opens the repatriation tool of DDV App in the browser. There are three steps: upload the files, check them, then download them to your own computer through DDV App. The tool scans each file for possible microdata. The scan is a supplement: DST states that it "kan ikke erstatte manuel kontrol" (cannot replace a manual check), so the check on this page is still yours to do. If a file gets a risk message, you must add a remark saying what the file contains. DST's control staff read it. Before the files are released you confirm that they follow DST's rules. Afterwards DST checks files with a risk message, files over 1 MB, files that could not be scanned, and a random 10% of the rest. Give the files names that say what is in them ( table1_baseline.csv , not output.csv ): it helps the person who checks the file, and it helps you find it again. If you are in doubt about a file, DST's instruction is not to take it home until you have aggregated further or asked. General questions go to DDVHjemtag@dst.dk, described with made-up numbers, never with real data.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Checklist before uploading
sections.text: [ ] No individual-level data - only aggregated results [ ] All cells ≥ 5 observations [ ] No hidden number can be worked out from a total, a percentage, another table or an earlier export - merge categories, or hide more numbers so the hidden ones in each row and column add up to at least 5 [ ] Hidden numbers share one mark (e.g. .. ), so the small one cannot be told apart from those hidden to protect it [ ] Min, max, median and percentiles: no outliers, nothing that points to one person [ ] Figures: every bar, point and bin has at least 5 people behind it; no marks for individuals; the file does not carry the underlying data [ ] No count of 1-4 missing (NA): merge or hide it [ ] Descriptive filenames; no microdata in scripts or logs (no pnr values, no printed rows) [ ] File type is on DST's approved list, with the right extension: spreadsheets (xlsx, csv), text (txt), HTML, PDF, Word (docx), code (R, SAS, Stata), images (png, jpg, svg, eps and others), presentations (pptx)

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.text: This page has the code for pulling diagnoses out of LPR: for one outcome, for several outcomes at once, and as a reusable function, get_lpr_diagnoses() , that the later pages call. You need it whenever an outcome, an exposure or a comorbidity is defined by hospital diagnoses. When you are done you have one table with pnr , contact date and ICD code from LPR2 and LPR3 combined, and you know how to reduce it to one row per person. Read Understand LPR first. The code relies on what that page explains: the two periods (LPR2 and LPR3), the D-prefix, the diagnosis types (A/B/G) and the filter for retracted diagnoses. The extraction pattern itself (open lazily, filter, collect() ) is the one from [Phase 5](extraction-step-by-step.qmd) and Phase 6, applied to each LPR period. The examples assume you already have a cohort: cohort , a data.frame with pnr and index_date per person, built in [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd). That phase comes later and uses the pattern you learn here, so read them in order and come back to this code once your cohort exists. They also use inner_join() and bind_rows() , explained in [Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd).

sections.text: Check the column names in your own delivery. The examples use the names the registers typically have, but LPR_A renamed a number of them, and [what you were given is not what the register contains](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr-is-split-into-two-periods). List them with arrow::schema() , and look the confirmed ones up in Overview of registers. Two facts from Understand LPR that the code depends on. Use the LPR_A files and filter them with lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" (why), and expect a spike in diagnosis counts around 2019-2020 if your analysis counts diagnoses or looks at trends (why). Check that your LPR2 files reach the end of March 2019 before you rely on the lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" filter. The filter solves one confirmed problem: lpr_a_kontakt also holds older LPR2 contacts, which would be counted twice if you did not filter them out. It does not guarantee that your combined series has no gap around the transition. DST's LPR2 files end on 31 March 2019, but the files in your own delivery can end earlier. sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Private hospitals are in a separate register
sections.text: Private hospitals and clinics report to a separate system, MiniPas, which Sundhedsdatastyrelsen documents as a register of its own, [MiniPas - LPR](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=19), covering 2002 onwards. At DST the corresponding registers are priv_adm , priv_diag and their satellites (2002 to 31 March 2019, [DST's register overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html)). They are not part of lpr_adm and lpr_diag , and this page does not extract them. The exception is a small group of private or association-owned hospitals (mainly hospices) that report to LPR itself ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)). If your study needs private-hospital diagnoses from before 2019, check that the priv_ registers are in your delivery. They do not appear by filtering LPR2 or LPR3 differently. lpr_a_kontakt holds MiniPas rows under lprindberetningssystem == "MiniPAS" , but only for contacts that ended in 2017 or later ([DST's remark on

That is the worked example below. Several outcomes: pull all A and B diagnoses once into a table called all_dx , then filter that table per outcome. It is the same code with three small changes, see Several outcomes at once. You query LPR once instead of scanning the registers again for each outcome, and the function get_lpr_diagnoses() does it in one call. Either way the shape is the same, and it follows from [how LPR is built](understand-lpr.qmd#contact-and-diagnosis-tables): a hospital contact's pnr and date are in one table and the ICD code in another, so every extract is a join between a contact register and a diagnosis register, done once per LPR period and then stacked. The examples use read_register("name") (fastreg); without fastreg use open_dataset("path/to/<register>/") . LPR is one of the largest registers, so it must be in parquet: reading it from SAS pulls the whole thing into RAM. sections.heading: From all_dx to one outcome: first event per person
sections.text: all_dx has one row per diagnosis, so a person with five hip fracture contacts has five rows. An analysis dataset needs one row per person, with the date of their first qualifying diagnosis. The four lines from group_by() to ungroup() turn one into the other. [From event log to one row per person](#one-row-per-person) shows the other way of collapsing. What slice(1) does. slice(n) picks rows by position, not by value: slice(1) keeps the first row of each group. It only means "earliest" because arrange(date_contact) put the oldest first. With arrange(desc(date_contact)) the same slice(1) gives you the latest contact instead. See slice() . Three things to check in this block: Keep the ungroup() : a grouped table stays grouped, and every later mutate() or summarise() then operates per person instead of on the whole table, without telling you. Ties are broken arbitrarily: if someone has two qualifying contacts on the same date, slice(1) keeps whichever row came first. That does not matter for a first-event date, since the date is the same, but it does if you also keep columns that differ between the two rows, such as the hospital or the specific ICD code.

B) Many binary variables at once (e.g. comorbidity flags): build the flags, collapse with any() , and merge onto the cohort. any() returns TRUE if the person has at least one matching diagnosis in the window (0/1, not a count): It gives one 0/1 flag per comorbidity per person, ready to enter your model as covariates. If your cohort has one row per person, that gives the same result as pnr alone. If a pnr is repeated (e.g. a comparison group matched with replacement), it keeps each row's flags tied to that row's own index date, see [the callout on repeated pnr on Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-4---assemble-validate-and-save).

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.text: In Phase 4 you saw that registers are loaded lazily : you open a connection, not data. This page shows the working method that follows from that. It is the most important pattern in the guide - every extraction from Phase 6 onwards is this same structure, so learn it here once. Why can't we just load a register like a CSV file? Because the registers are too large. A CSV (or readRDS ) reads the entire file into memory at once - that works fine with your own small datasets, but BEF and LMDB have many millions of rows and would crash your session. The lazy connection lets you filter before you fetch, so only the rows you actually need ever reach memory.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: The pattern: open connection → filter → select → fetch
sections.text: Think of a supermarket. You can either buy the whole shop and sort at home - or send a shopping list and only have what is on the list delivered. Lazy loading is the latter: you describe what you want, and only fetch the items at the end with collect() . Step 1 - open the register as a lazy connection. Pick the way that matches your project (the rest of the pattern is identical whichever you choose): #### fastreg (recommended) This assumes you have pointed fastreg at your registers with one options() call at the top of the script - see [Point fastreg at your registers](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#fastreg-paths). That call is not repeated in the guide's examples: it belongs at the top of the script, once, not before each read. #### arrow (any parquet) Steps 2-3 - filter, select, then fetch. bef is now a lazy connection (no data has moved). The rest is the same regardless of how you opened it: Steps 1--2 are pure instructions - they cost almost no memory. collect() in step 3 is the only line that actually moves data. Why rename_with(tolower) as the first step? Raw column names in DST registers have inconsistent capitalisation - PNR , pnr , Pnr . By standardising to lower
sections.code: fastreg bef read_register rename_with tolower arrow open_dataset workdata projectnumber cleaned parquet registers dplyr filter select collect filter rows columns still bef_filtered year pnr koen foed_dag familie_id here selected moved into memory bef_data

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: The most important rule: filter and select columns BEFORE fetching
sections.text: BEF has millions of rows; LMDB has more than a billion. Calling collect() before you have narrowed the rows can crash your session - and because everyone shares the server's RAM, it makes the server slow for everyone else at the same time. The more you have filtered and selected columns in advance, the faster and more stably it runs. Rule of thumb: filter() limits rows. select() limits columns. Use both before collect() , never after.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: Very large registers: compute() instead of collect()
sections.text: On the very largest registers (LMDB, laboratory results), even a filtered result can be too big to pull into R comfortably, or you may need it as the input to several later queries. Then end the pipe with compute() instead of collect() : compute() does not make the data disappear: DuckDB still holds the result in the server's memory until your R session ends. It only saves you from copying it into R as well, and from re-reading the whole register for every later query. So the rule above still applies: filter() and select() first. It works on the DuckDB-backed tables that read_register() and read_parquet_duckdb() give you. On an open_dataset() table (arrow), add to_duckdb() before compute() . Later: keeping just your cohort. Once you have built a study population, you will usually want to keep only your cohort's people in a register. That is done with semi_join() against your cohort's pnr , and it first matters once the cohort itself exists ([Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd)). You don't need it yet. Never write actual CPR numbers (pnr) in your code - only variable names and vectors. Hardcoding real CPR numbers in a script violates DST's rules for handling

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: Check: do you have data or just a connection?
sections.text: Many errors arise because you think you have fetched data - but actually still have an unexecuted query. Ask the object what it is: A read_register() result says "data.frame" even though nothing has been fetched yet: look for "prudent_duckplyr_df" - as long as that is in the list, the data has not been collected. ( "Table" is an Arrow table that is already in memory, which you rarely meet in this guide.) On DST all users share the server's memory. When the memory bar in RStudio turns red, it slows everyone's sessions. rm() removes the object from your active session - it can no longer be used in code and disappears from the Environment panel (top right in RStudio). gc() ( garbage collection ) does not affect your session - all your other objects are still there. R normally holds on to freed memory a little longer, because it is faster to reuse than to request new memory from the operating system. gc() makes R free that memory now, so it can be returned to the operating system and become available to other users on the shared DST server (how much is actually handed back, and when, depends on the system). You lose nothing - it helps your colleagues. Always clean up after

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: What happens visually
sections.text: The blue steps are lazy - they only build up a query. Data moves into R only at collect() (orange). That is why filter() and select() must come before collect() . []{#arrow-vs-duckdb} You do not need to know these names to use the pattern above, but here is what happens under the hood. Parquet is a file format that stores data column by column rather than row by row. If you only want pnr and year , the computer reads only those two columns - not the rest. That is why it is fast. Getting your registers into parquet is Parquet and fastreg; on DARTER (708421) most of them are converted already, see DARTER - Register paths and datastores. Arrow and DuckDB are the two engines that run your query against the parquet. Both are lazy and both end at collect() , so your code looks the same either way. The difference is coverage: To move an Arrow connection over to DuckDB, pipe through to_duckdb() (from the arrow package): read_register() hands you a DuckDB-backed table already (a lazy duckplyr data frame), so this step is built in - you do not call to_duckdb() yourself. If you hit an error about an "unsupported function" in Arrow, that is the coverage gap:

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis is done and you want figures for the paper: bar charts of counts, proportions with confidence intervals, and forest plots of model estimates, built with ggplot2 and saved to a file. You start from the analysis-ready dataset ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)) or a fitted model (Regression, Time-to-event). On DST a figure is judged as if it were the table behind it, so you aggregate first and plot the aggregated numbers: a scatterplot with one point per person cannot leave. The rules are on [Export and repatriation](export.qmd#figures-and-curves). Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. ggplot2 must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.heading: Bar chart of counts
sections.text: Build the figure from your dataset. Here we count the number of people per group and draw a bar chart. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Bar chart produced by the code above. The numbers are simulated. The key parts: aes() maps columns to the figure's axes ( x , y ) and e.g. fill (colour). geom_col() draws bars from values you have counted yourself (unlike geom_bar() , which counts rows for you). labs() sets the title and axis/legend text; theme_minimal() gives a clean look.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Customise the look
sections.text: A figure is built up layer by layer with + : you start with ggplot(...) and add a new line for each thing you want to change. What a function should control, you write inside its parentheses as an argument, e.g. labs(title = "...") . Because we saved the figure in the object p in the code block above, you can build on it with + : you write only what you want to add or change, not the whole code again. (This requires that you have run the first code block, so p exists in your session.) Each line is one layer. The order mostly does not matter, with one exception: a complete theme such as theme_minimal() resets every theme setting, so put your own theme(...) after it, or the legend goes back to the right. A few typical moves: Colour by a variable goes inside aes() (e.g. fill = outcome as in the example at the top of the page - made a factor there, since a numeric 0/1 would get a continuous colour scale); you then control the colours with scale_fill_manual(values = ...) or a ready-made palette ( scale_fill_brewer() ). If you instead want one fixed colour for all bars, write fill = "steelblue" inside geom_col() , i.e. outside aes() . Axes:

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Figure with error bars (proportion and 95% CI)
sections.text: The bar chart above shows raw counts. In register work you will often rather show a proportion or rate with a confidence interval, so the figure also shows the uncertainty. Error bars ( geom_errorbar() ) draw the interval on top of each bar or point. Aggregate first again: one row per group with count, proportion and interval. Here we assume outcome is coded 0/1. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Bar chart with 95% confidence intervals as error bars, produced by the code above. The numbers are simulated. The key parts: geom_errorbar() needs ymin and ymax ; we computed them as prop ± 1.96 · se and put them in the dataset beforehand. The interval here is a simple Wald interval . It works when the group is large and the proportion is not close to 0 or 100 %, but it becomes unreliable with few people or few events, and it can go below 0. Output control only asks for 3 or 5 people per cell, so a group small enough for this to matter can still pass. In that case use prop.test(x, n)$conf.int , a score (Wilson) interval, by default with continuity correction, or binom.test(x, n)$conf.int for an exact (Clopper-Pearson) one. Same pattern for means: to show a

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Forest plot (estimates with 95% CI)
sections.text: A forest plot shows several effect estimates (hazard ratios or odds ratios) side by side with their confidence intervals and a vertical reference line at 1 (no effect). It is a common way to show the exposure estimate across models or subgroups. Plot the estimates you want the reader to interpret: the coefficients of the confounders in the same model are not effects of those variables, and showing them invites that reading (the "Table 2 fallacy", Westreich & Greenland 2013, doi:10.1093/aje/kws412). The code below pulls the estimates out of a fitted model with broom::tidy() and plots them. To show only the exposure, filter on its term. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Forest plot (simulated data): hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals and a reference line at 1. The key parts: tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE) converts the coefficients from the log scale to HR/OR ; conf.int = TRUE gives conf.low / conf.high (95% CI). The reference line at 1 is "no effect": if the interval crosses 1, the estimate is not statistically clear (here e.g. Low income ). scale_x_log10() puts e.g. HR 0.5 and HR 2 equally far from 1 - which is how ratios should be read.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Save the figure
sections.text: ggsave() writes the most recent (or a named) figure to a file you can send to output control. width / height + units ( "cm" , "mm" , "in" or "px" ) set the physical size; dpi = 300 is a good resolution for print. Choose .png (raster) or .pdf (vector, scales crisply) depending on the journal's requirements.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Check the figure before export
sections.text: Aggregating is not enough on its own. A bar or a point that covers very few individuals can still identify them, so check the group sizes behind every element of the figure the same way you would check the cells of a table. A single extreme value on an axis can show one person's value too. For Kaplan-Meier and cumulative incidence curves, see Time-to-event. DST's rule that a hidden number must not be possible to work out covers figures as well: a segment left out of a stacked bar can be read off from the bar's total height. See [Export - a hidden number must not be possible to work out](export.qmd#back-calculation). Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : ggplot basics ggplot tips

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.text: When you open File Explorer on the DST server, you encounter files with different extensions. This page is your reference tool: what file type is it, which function opens it, and does the data enter memory immediately or not? The last point - lazy vs. full loading - is the most important distinction here.

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: What a project folder looks like
sections.text: A typical project on the DST server is organised roughly like this. The registers live under cleaned-data/ ; your own scripts and results sit under workspace/[your-name]/ : The paths in the code examples follow this structure, but your own folder names may well differ - check with File Explorer. Two things are worth knowing: rawdata/ is read-only. You cannot edit or write to the raw register data DST delivers. You work in workspace/ , where each project member typically has their own subfolder ( [your-name]/ ) for scripts, intermediate results and output. Almost all the code in this guide assumes the registers are in parquet. If your project only has raw SAS files, converting them to parquet - and setting up a sensible folder structure for the project - is the first job. See [Convert SAS files to Parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet). How to name the scripts in R/ is covered in [Good code practice](good-coding-practice.qmd).

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Lazy vs. full loading - which file types behave which way
sections.text: Every file type below loads one of two ways. Full loading ( readRDS , read_sas , read_csv , read_xlsx ) reads the entire file into RAM straight away. Fine for your own intermediate results; it would crash your session on a whole register. Lazy loading (parquet) opens a connection instead, and fetches rows only when you call collect() . That is what lets you work with registers of millions of rows. For this page that is all you need: parquet is lazy, everything else is not. Why it works, and how to write a query against a lazy connection, is [Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd). SAS files are also large - and are shared with everyone on the server. On DST all users share the server's RAM. read_sas() on a large SAS file burdens the server for everyone at the same time. DST automatically kills processes (RStudio sessions, jobs, etc.) when RAM is close to full - so an oversized extraction can cost you your unsaved work. If you use a SAS file repeatedly, it is worth converting it to parquet once - this saves significant RAM and makes loading much faster. See [Convert SAS to parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) for the

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Overview - file type, package, function
sections.text: The last column is the lazy/full distinction from above: parquet is the only lazy format, everything else loads fully into RAM. What do you write in the parentheses? With open_dataset() (arrow) you write the path to the parquet folder - e.g. open_dataset("path/to/bef/") . It works on any parquet, on any project. With read_register() (fastreg) you write just the register name - e.g. read_register("bef") - because fastreg already knows where your parquet lives (you set that once during conversion). It also hands you a DuckDB-backed table (a lazy duckplyr data frame, like read_parquet_duckdb() below), so more dplyr functions work without an extra to_duckdb() step. It requires that the registers were set up with fastreg. With read_parquet_duckdb() (duckplyr) you write the path , like open_dataset() , but you get a DuckDB-backed table straight away. It is reported to be the fastest of the three and to keep memory use lowest, and to avoid the rapi errors that the arrow-to-DuckDB route ( to_duckdb() ) sometimes throws on very large registers. It does not make it safe to filter a datetime column such as kont_starttidspunkt with a date: that rule applies whichever of

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Reading a register that is split by year
sections.text: DST delivers registers as SAS files, often one per year. Converting them to parquet is a job the project does once, and fastreg writes the result partitioned by year - <register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet - so a converted register is a folder of yearly files. See [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet). You do not open those one at a time. Both open_dataset("path/to/bef/") and read_register("bef") read the whole folder, including the per-year subfolders, as a single combined dataset . So you pick years by filtering on the year column in the data : That column exists because of how the register was partitioned at conversion, not because DST supplies it - so its name can differ between projects. Confirm it against your own files rather than assuming. year says which folder a row came from, nothing more. It is not a date and it is not a DST variable. Because the files are split by year, filtering on it means the other years are never opened at all, which is what makes a query against a register with a billion rows finish in seconds. That is what it is for: limiting how much gets read . It is not for deciding when something happened. year ==

sections.title: Find your registers
sections.text: You can now inspect a dataset. The next step is to know where your variables come from: which register contains demographics, which contains diagnoses, which contains prescriptions. This page is your decision table. Once you know which register to use, you find the exact column names, types and code examples in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd), or search for a single variable across all of them in Find a variable. What a register holds is not what your project was given. The table below says which register covers what at DST. Which of its columns and years you actually received was decided when the data was ordered, so confirm with colnames() before you plan around anything here.

sections.title: Find your registers
sections.heading: What am I looking for? - decision table
sections.text: Know your question. Find the register. Look in the column. Some diagnoses sit in both the somatic and the psychiatric register before 2019. Dementia is the typical case: most dementia diagnoses are made in somatic departments (neurology, geriatrics), so you need lpr_diag and t_psyk_diag . The regions switched their reporting from LPR2 to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019, and DST's LPR2 files end on 31 March 2019 - see [Understanding LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr-is-split-into-two-periods). SKS (Sundhedsvæsenets Klassifikations System - the Danish Health Classification System) is the Danish system for coding operations and procedures in hospital - e.g. KJDF10 for Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Equivalent to the NOMESCO codes used in the other Nordic countries.

sections.title: Find your registers
sections.heading: The socioeconomic registers come as a set
sections.text: The three socioeconomic registers - UDDA (education), FAIK (income) and AKM (employment) - are extracted together in [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd). One trap worth knowing before you start: UDDA's hfaudd is a code for the specific education, not its level, so getting a level out of it needs a lookup - see [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd#udda---education-register).

sections.title: Find your registers
sections.heading: Join keys
sections.text: Wrong join keys produce silent errors: the code runs, but you lose rows - or duplicate them. Confirmed column names and join examples for each register are in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd). The mechanics of joins are covered in [Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset](data-manipulation.qmd).

sections.title: First extraction
sections.text: This page shows the complete process from a raw register to a saved dataset ready for analysis. You will see the pattern that recurs in almost every register extraction. These examples cannot be run on the DST server. The synthetic data package ( fiktive ) is not available there. You need RStudio installed locally on your computer : 1. Download R: cran.r-project.org 2. Download RStudio: posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop 3. Open RStudio, create a new script ( File → New File → R Script ), and copy the code there. When you are ready to work with real register data, you use the same pattern - but on the DST server and with your project's register data. The data is synthetic, from fiktive (MIT licence, Sara Schwartz): fictitious persons with the structure and column names of DST registers. load_registers_schema() , generate_background_population() , and generate_registers() return tibbles. You save those with write_parquet() , and you practise open_dataset() on the files. (These local examples use open_dataset() ; fastreg's read_register() is for a configured DST project, not ad-hoc local folders.) The example extracts from lpr_adm - hospital contacts , dates only, with

Here we build a small practice cohort directly from the BEF register. slice_sample(n = 30) draws rows. Because BEF is quarterly, the same pnr can appear more than once, so distinct(pnr) comes first - that way you sample 30 people, not 30 rows. In a real project, cohort_pnrs is a vector you built in a previous script and reload with readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") %>% pull(pnr) . The signs in filter() : , / & = AND, \| = OR, ! = NOT, plus == , != , > , >= , %in% . Examples and the parentheses pitfall are in [Combining conditions in filter() ](function-guide.qmd#filter-conditions). The BEF register stores koen , civst and reg as codes - not as text. This recoding translates them into analysis-ready variables: The code lists above are an excerpt, adapted from Anders Aasted Isaksen's dplyr practice vignette (MIT licence, Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus). The full vignette covers more variables and patterns. opr_land is entirely missing in this synthetic BEF, so the country-of-origin flag is replaced with partnered from civst .

sections.heading: Inspect the result
sections.text: Right after an extraction you should check that you got what you expected: If your extraction includes exclusion steps - e.g. "remove persons with an early diagnosis" - it is good practice to count N for each step. Replace raw and clean with your own variable names: These lines cannot be run with the synthetic practice data - they are a template for use when working with your own data and an exclusion sequence. The pattern is repeated for each exclusion step and forms the basis for a STROBE flow diagram (a standardised diagram showing how many were excluded at each step and why; STROBE is the reporting standard for observational studies, CONSORT is for randomised trials). The same attrition counting is used when you build the study population in Phase 10. This is a quick sanity check. The full toolkit for exploring data - summary() , table() , cross-tables and NA handling - is covered in [Phase 7 - Inspect your data](inspect-data.qmd).

sections.text: Step 1 (cohort construction from BEF) is adapted from Anders Aasted Isaksen's dplyr practice vignette (MIT licence, Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus). The synthetic tables come from fiktive . Steps 2--4 and the checklist are written for this guide.

sections.title: Format tables
sections.text: The format tables on the server are the authority, not this page. The examples and code lists here are a starting point. DST updates the format catalogue without this guide knowing, and a code can change meaning while keeping its number. Load the current table from E:/Formater/ and check the values in your own delivered data before you rely on a mapping. Several of the same code lists are also published outside DST, as [classifications with a CSV download](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer), which is the version Find a variable shows. Prerequisite: This page uses left_join() to attach format tables to your data. If you are not familiar with joins yet, read [Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset](data-manipulation.qmd) first. Many variables in DST registers are stored as codes - municipality numbers, education codes, employment codes. To give them meaningful labels you use DST's format tables : SAS files on the server that translate codes to text. A format table always has at least two columns: You join the format table onto your dataset with START as the key - exactly like a dictionary lookup. Rows in your dataset without a match in the

sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Where are the format tables?
sections.text: The Star ( ) on the Windows desktop inside the DST server opens an HTML guide for finding the right table. DST's written guides sit here: The one worth reading is Brugen af SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik.pdf (\~2 MB, DST Consulting). It explains the naming systematics used below and has a section per topic - Uddannelserne, Brancherne, DISCO, Sundhed, Geokoder, DREAM. The same folder holds dated older editions (2012-2019) and a set of Allokering af formatbibliotek ( ).sas scripts for pointing SAS at the format catalog - those are for SAS users and are not needed from R. Two more folders one level up are worth knowing: They let you look up what a code means without loading anything into R - useful when you just need to check a single value. Subfolders are organised by topic - including: Education sits in two places, and the naming is confusing. DST's guide says the formats for the current classification, DISCED-15 (used from 2015), are in the format catalog called DISCED , while the catalog called Uddannelser holds the older classifications it replaced (Forspalte, ISCED1997 and DUN). Look in both SAS_datasaet/Disced/ and SAS_datasaet/Uddannelser/ before you pick a
sections.code: formater sas formater danmarks statistik sas_datasaet vejledning html_oversigter browsable code lists pdf_lister same pdf geokoder municipalities regions times_personstatistik employment socio13 uddannelser education hfaudd brancher industries sundhed health disced format catalog see note more

The heaven package ships them as data, so you do not have to read a SAS format file at all: data(edu_code) : 4,621 education codes with hfaudd mapped to categories in English and Danish, a 5-level grouping and ISCED codes. kommuneRegion(kommune) : converts a numeric 3-digit municipality code straight to one of the five regions (valid from 2007). It gives you the region , not the municipality name - for the name you still need the format table below. heaven is pre-installed on DST, and elsewhere it installs from GitHub with pak::pak("tagteam/heaven") (it is not on CRAN, so install.packages() will not find it). The format tables below are still the route for every code heaven does not cover, and they are what DST itself publishes.

sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Education level (hfaudd)
sections.text: hfaudd is the four-digit code for the specific education . Its level - the thing almost every analysis actually needs - lives in a separate lookup, and the filename tells you exactly which lookup you are getting. These files are dictionaries, not data. A .sas7bdat in the format folders holds no people and no register records. It is a two-column translation table - one row per code, with the code and what it means - and they are tiny, a few hundred KB. You read one into R and left_join() it onto your own data, exactly like the municipality example above. Nothing about your cohort changes; you are only adding a column that says what a code stands for. What on this page has not been checked on the server. The naming rules below come from DST's own guide ( Brugen af SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik ) and DST's published DISCED-15 classification. The exact filenames in the education folders have not been listed and checked for this section, so treat every filename here as a pattern to look for, not a path to copy. Run list.files() on the folder first, as in the code below. How to read the file names. DST's guide gives the name for turning hfaudd into the main area as

sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Which variant to pick: _k, _t or _kt
sections.text: Every format comes in up to three output variants. DST's guide illustrates them with a municipality code turned into a region, using Copenhagen municipality ( 101 ): Use _k for the analysis variable. The code is short, it sorts correctly, and it does not change if DST rewords a label in a later version. You can filter and group on it directly ( %in% c("40", "50") ), and a model or a case_when() written against codes keeps working. Use _t for the labels in a finished table. Join it on at the end, when you build Table 1 or a figure, so the text never becomes something your code depends on. Use _kt for looking, not for analysing. It is the most readable while you explore, because you see what each code means and the values still sort by code. But "40 Korte videregående uddannelser, KVU" is code and text glued into one value: filtering on it means matching the whole string, and it breaks if the wording changes. Whichever you pick, the key is the same. All three join on START , the code in your own data. Only the returned column differs.
