sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.text: Know the function name? Use Ctrl+F (Windows) or Cmd+F (Mac) and search directly on the page. This is the data-handling toolkit (extract → clean → reshape → prepare). Statistical models - glm , coxph , lm ... - are explained in [Phase 13](analysis.qmd) where they're used. If you understand the 6 functions below, you can read most lines of register data code. The order is intentional: read_register / open_dataset → filter → select → collect is the pattern that appears in almost every script.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: What is a function?
sections.text: Think of a function as a machine on an assembly line. You send something in one end, it does something with it, and you get something new out the other end. filter() is for example a sieve: you send a large table in, specify which rows you want to keep, and get a smaller table out. All functions in R are written with parentheses: functionname(what_is_sent_in) . What you write inside the parentheses is called the arguments . Many functions have named arguments of the form name = value : on the left of = is the argument's name (fixed by the function, cannot be changed), and on the right is the value you supply, e.g. ratio = 5 or na.rm = TRUE . You do not need to memorize them: ?functionname shows which arguments a function takes and what they do. Want to see what a function does? Place your cursor inside the function name and press F1 - the help page opens with description, arguments and examples directly in RStudio's Help panel. You can also type ?functionname or help(functionname) in the console, or args(functionname) for a quick list of arguments. For packages on CRAN there is an online page with documentation and vignettes (e.g.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: The pipe - %>%
sections.text: The most important symbol in all the code is %>% , "the pipe". What it does: the pipe passes the result from the line on the left forward as the first argument to the function on the right. The two ways of writing do the same thing: Both versions give exactly the same result. The pipe version is easier to read because you can follow the steps in order - and easier to debug because you can add or remove one step at a time. A line break after %>% is not required - it is only for readability. You can write the whole chain on one line ( bef %>% filter(...) %>% collect() ) or split it with one step per line. The only rule: if you break the line, %>% must sit at the end of the line, not the start of the next one. R reads line by line, so a trailing %>% signals "more is coming": The same applies to |> and + in ggplot2. Analogy: Imagine cooking a meal. You chop the onions - and pass them on to the pot - which passes its contents on to the plate. The pipe does exactly that: it chains steps together so you can read the code from top to bottom like a recipe. %>% and |> are the same - just two different ways of writing the pipe. %>% comes from the magrittr package and
sections.code: lpr_adm semi_join tibble pnr my_pnrs copy select recnum collect without pipe inside out like russian dolls top bottom recipe works end line bef filter year fails thinks expression ended after

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: open_dataset("path") <small>- arrow</small>
sections.text: What it does: opens a lazy connection to a parquet file or folder. Analogy: Imagine calling the library and asking them to find all books about cardiac surgery from 1990 to 2020. The librarian says "yes, I'll find those" - but they have not arrived yet. That is exactly what open_dataset() does: it tells the computer what you want, but the data has not been fetched into memory yet. The rest of your commands ( filter , select ) add further instructions, before you finally say "send them now" - that is collect() . #### fastreg (recommended) read_register() finds the path from your project config (set once) - see Parquet and fastreg. It returns a DuckDB connection. It can only find registers in fastreg's own format ( <register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet ). If it does not know the name, list the available ones with list_parquet_datasets() , or point straight at the folder with read_parquet_dataset("full/path/to/folder") - see [When read_register() cannot find the register](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#when-read-register-fails). #### DST server (arrow) The confirmed paths for your project are in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd). #### Local (fiktive) Generate and
sections.code: fastreg bef read_register rename_with tolower knows path open_dataset workdata projectnumber cleaned parquet registers standardise column lowercase synth_data locally saved synthetic register arrow to_duckdb hand over duckdb

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: collect()
sections.text: What it does: executes the lazy query and pulls data into R's memory. This is the point where the librarian actually brings the books to you. Call it late - after all filter() and select() steps - so only the necessary data is moved. The concept of lazy evaluation - why data is not in memory before collect() - is explained in detail on the page [Extracting data step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd).
sections.code: result large_register semi_join tibble pnr cohort_pnrs copy only cohort select d_inddto two columns use collect pulled into memory

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: readRDS("path/file.rds")
sections.text: What it does: reads a saved R file from disk into memory. Analogy: It is like opening a Word file you saved last time. The .rds format is R's own save format - faster and more compact than CSV. It is used to pass data from one script to the next in the pipeline.
sections.code: full_cohort readrds path full_cohort.rds fetch saved dataset disk

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: saveRDS(object, "path/file.rds")
sections.text: What it does: saves an R object to disk. The opposite of readRDS() . Each pipeline script saves its result with saveRDS() , so the next script can fetch it.
sections.code: saverds full_cohort path full_cohort.rds save dataset disk

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: haven::read_sas("file.sas7bdat")
sections.text: What it does: reads a SAS data file into R. Used to load SAS files - e.g. DST's format tables or registers not yet converted to parquet. See File types and [Format tables](formatting-tables.qmd) for practical examples. read_csv("path/file.csv") (from readr ) is the equivalent for a .csv file - a plain text table, not a register format, but common for a code list or a small file someone hands you outside DST.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: arrow::write_parquet(df, "path/file.parquet")
sections.text: What it does: saves a data frame as a parquet file. Parquet is a particularly efficient file format for large datasets - it is far faster to read than CSV. Used when you want to save an R dataset as a parquet file, e.g. for use with open_dataset() or read_register() in another script.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: file.path(folder, "filename.rds")
sections.text: What it does: correctly assembles a folder path and filename into a full path. Analogy: Think of it as writing an address: file.path("C:/data", "results.rds") gives "C:/data/results.rds" . It is safer than just pasting strings together with paste0() , because it handles slashes correctly on all operating systems.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: file.exists("path")
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE or FALSE - does the file exist? Used to give an understandable error message before the code tries to open a file that might not be there.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: dir.create(path, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: creates a folder if it does not already exist. recursive = TRUE also creates any parent folders. showWarnings = FALSE suppresses the harmless warning you would otherwise get if the folder already exists.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: rename_with(tolower)
sections.text: What it does: converts ALL column names to lower case at once. Analogy: Imagine receiving a patient list from five different departments. One writes "CPR", another "cpr", a third "Cpr". It is the same thing - but the computer treats them as three entirely different things. rename_with(tolower) fixes it in one second: all names become consistent. Important: always call it on the same line as open_dataset() (or read_register() in DARTER). If you forget it, semi_join(..., by = "pnr") will fail because the column might be called PNR .
sections.code: bef open_dataset path rename_with tolower all columns become lowercase pnr koen foed_dag

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: rename(new_name = old_name)
sections.text: What it does: renames one or more specific columns.
sections.code: rename surgery_date index_date renamed

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: names(df)
sections.text: What it does: shows all column names in a data frame. Useful when you are not sure what a table contains. On a lazy connection names() is not always reliable - see arrow::schema() below.
sections.code: full_cohort prints all column

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: arrow::schema(lazy_table) <small>- arrow</small>
sections.text: What it does: lists the column names and their types of a lazy Arrow connection, without reading any data into RAM. Use it when you want to check what a register really contains before you write code against it - which you should, because a delivery only holds the columns your project ordered, and LPR_A renamed a number of them. For the DuckDB-backed objects that read_register() (fastreg) returns, use colnames() instead. Do not trust colnames() on a lazy Arrow query after rename_with() . It can return an empty vector silently, so a column that exists is reported as missing. The operations themselves are fine - it is only the name check that fails. (Seen on arrow 23.0.1 outside DST; not yet confirmed on the server.) Use names(collect(head(tbl, 0))) , which fetches the structure with zero rows.
sections.code: arrow open_dataset schema lpr path lpr_adm column types nothing read into memory

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: select(col1, col2, new = old, -remove)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the columns you name. Analogy: You have a large Excel file with 50 columns. You only need 3. select() is like saving a copy with only the three columns you need. It reduces the amount of data pulled from the server, and is one of the reasons the code is fast. When renaming inside select() , the direction is new_name = old_name - the new name on the left, the existing column name on the right.
sections.code: select pnr recnum d_inddto keeps three columns renamed year removes column all others

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pull(column)
sections.text: What it does: takes one column out of a data frame as a plain vector, instead of a data frame with one column. Analogy: select(col) gives you a one-column spreadsheet; pull(col) gives you just the values, no spreadsheet around them. Use it when the next step needs a bare vector, not a table - e.g. before %in% , or after summarise() when you only want the single number out.
sections.code: last_contact_date lpr_adm summarise max_date max d_inddto na.rm collect pull single tibble

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: mutate(new_column = expression)
sections.text: What it does: adds a new column (or modifies an existing one), computed from the columns you already have. The number of rows is the same - mutate() adds information, does not remove rows. ( df is just the name of your data frame - call it whatever you like.) You can create several variables in one call , and a variable you just made is immediately available further down (here obesity_class uses the just-computed bmi ): Check the units first. BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)². If height is in cm , weight / (height^2) is wrong. Convert height to metres in a mutate() step before you compute BMI: case_when() has its own entry below. More examples of mutate() :
sections.code: dplyr mutate bmi weight height new column computed two existing ones obesity newly created usable right away obesity_class case_when several conditions first one wins normal overweight obesity everything height_m height_cm then bmi correct icd3 substr c_diag icd code without prefix characters birth_year lubridate year foed_dag birth

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: transmute(new_column = expression)
sections.text: What it does: like mutate() , but keeps only the columns you name - the rest are dropped. Handy when you want a clean table with exactly the columns a function needs.
sections.code: mutate event keeps all columns new transmute pnr only

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: case_when(condition1 ~ value1, condition2 ~ value2, TRUE ~ default)
sections.text: What it does: an advanced if-else with many conditions. Analogy: Think of a traffic light: is it red → stop, is it yellow → be careful, is it green → go. case_when() works the same way: conditions are evaluated in order, and the first condition that is true determines the result. TRUE ~ default is the "in all other cases" arm.
sections.code: mutate education_cat case_when edu_level short medium long unknown

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: if_else(condition, true_value, false_value)
sections.text: What it does: a simple two-way condition. Stricter than base R's ifelse() - both values must have the same type. 0L and 1L are integers in R. The L suffix is R's way of specifying that a number is an integer rather than a decimal ( 0 and 1 without L are double by default). if_else() requires both values to have exactly the same type - use either 0L / 1L (integer) or 0 / 1 (double), but not a mix.
sections.code: if_else is.na death_date person has died

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: coalesce(x, replacement)
sections.text: What it does: replaces NA values with another value. Analogy: After a left join, many persons will have NA in flag columns because they did not have that condition. coalesce(mi_flag, 0L) says: "if mi_flag is NA, set it to 0 instead". Used systematically after each left join that produces flag columns.
sections.code: coalesce mi_flag found absent

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: replace_na(x, replacement) <small>- tidyr</small>
sections.text: What it does: the same job as coalesce() above - replaces NA with a value - but written for use inside across() , where you are naming a function rather than writing out one column at a time.
sections.code: mutate across starts_with dx_ replace_na every column match found

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: across(columns, function)
sections.text: What it does: applies the same function to many columns at once inside mutate() . ~ coalesce(.x, 0L) is an anonymous function: ~ means "function of", and .x is the current column. It is equivalent to function(x) coalesce(x, 0L) - but shorter. across() calls this function once per column in nmi_variables . starts_with("prefix") picks columns by name pattern instead of naming them one by one - across(starts_with("dx_"), ...) applies to every column that starts with dx_ , however many there are. Common inside across() when you built the columns yourself with a shared prefix ( dx_ , rx_ ).
sections.code: mutate across all_of nmi_variables coalesce replace all nmi flag columns

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: rowSums(matrix, na.rm = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: sums the values in each row across columns. Used in two places: 1. NMI score (Nordic Multimorbidity Index): sums the product of 0/1 flag columns and their individual weights → one weighted comorbidity score per person. A patient with cardiovascular disease and cancer scores higher than a patient with two milder conditions. 2. Multimorbidity count : sums all 0/1 flags → simple count of the number of conditions per person.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: filter(condition1, condition2, ...)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the rows that satisfy the conditions. Analogy: You have a patient list and only want to see women over 50. filter(koen == 2, alder > 50) is your sieve - everything else is removed. Signs for comparing a column with a value: Signs for combining several conditions: Pitfall - never mix AND and OR without parentheses. & binds before | , so filter(alder > 50 | alder < 18 & koen == 2) reads as alder > 50 | (alder < 18 & koen == 2) . If you mean "(over 50 or under 18) and woman", add parentheses: filter((alder > 50 | alder < 18) & koen == 2) .
sections.code: filter c_diagtype only action secondary diagnoses date_contact surgery_date post operative contacts icd3 s72 hip fracture codes

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: %in% - "is in the list"
sections.text: What it does: checks whether each element on the left side appears in the vector on the right side. Returns TRUE or FALSE for each element. %in% is optional: it is just one of filter() 's comparison signs (alongside == , > , < , etc.). You use it only when you want to match against a list of values rather than a single value - e.g. a code list. To match pnr against the cohort, use semi_join (see above). Analogy: Imagine a guest list for a party. icd3 %in% c("G30", "F00", "F03") is like standing at the entrance and checking: "is this diagnosis code on the list?" You will see %in% in almost every filter() call in the project. Sending a local list into a lazy query - two ways. The register is not in R yet. filter(c_diag %in% my_codes) usually works anyway - dbplyr and arrow use the local vector when no column is called my_codes - but if a column has that name, the column wins and you quietly get the wrong rows. !! forces the vector's contents into the query: filter(c_diag %in% !!my_codes) . Explicit, guards against that name clash, and what this guide uses throughout. semi_join() sends the list over as a temporary table: semi_join(tibble(c_diag = my_codes),
sections.code: icd3 g30 f00 f03 these three codes everything atc my_atc all atc local see below

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: distinct(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: removes duplicates - keeps only unique combinations. Analogy: A person may have received the diagnosis F00 ten times. You only need to know whether they ever had it. distinct(pnr, icd3) reduces it to one row per person per code. distinct(pnr) gives you just the list of unique person IDs.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: slice(n)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the nth row within each group (used after group_by() ). slice_max(column, n = 1) and slice_sample(n = 1) do the same job as arrange() %>% slice() above, without a separate arrange() step: slice_max(date_contact, n = 1) keeps the row with the latest date per group directly; slice_sample(n = 200) picks a random sample of rows instead (used for a practice cohort, not for choosing a real one).
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person arrange desc year newest first slice keeps record

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: group_by(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: divides data into groups so subsequent operations happen separately within each group. Analogy: Imagine you have a stack of patient records and sort them into piles by ID number. group_by(pnr) does exactly that - but only in memory. All subsequent steps ( arrange , slice , summarise ) now happen one pile at a time.
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person arrange date_contact oldest first slice earliest contact ungroup remove grouping afterwards

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ungroup()
sections.text: What it does: removes the grouping. Important: always call ungroup() after you are done with group_by() . If you forget it, data remains grouped, and later operations can behave unexpectedly.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: arrange(column) / arrange(desc(column))
sections.text: What it does: sorts rows ascending (default) or descending ( desc() ). Typically used with group_by() %>% slice(1) to find the first or newest record per person.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: summarise(new_col = function(col), .groups = "drop")
sections.text: What it does: reduces each group to one summary row. .groups = "drop" removes the grouping automatically afterwards.
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person summarise first_e66 min date_contact na.rm earliest e66

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: count(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: shorthand for group_by(col1, col2) %>% summarise(n = n()) how many rows share each combination of values. Analogy: You want to know how many contacts fall in each calendar year. count(year) gives you that table directly, without writing group_by() and summarise() yourself.
sections.code: all_dx mutate contact_year year date_contact count one row per number contacts arrange

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: n_distinct(column)
sections.text: What it does: counts how many different values a column has - not how many rows. Analogy: count(pnr) tells you how many rows each pnr has (useful for finding duplicates); n_distinct(pnr) tells you how many different people there are in total, in one number. Often used inside summarise() alongside other counts, or on its own: n_distinct(cohort$pnr) .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ntile(x, n)
sections.text: What it does: divides rows into n equal groups (quantiles). Not used for income quintiles in register-based studies following SEPLINE guidelines. SEPLINE recommends comparing against population-specific cut-points (Q20/Q40/Q60/Q80) stratified by sex × 5-year age group × reference year - not ntile() on your cohort alone. See SEPLINE. row_number() numbers the rows 1, 2, 3... within each group (after group_by() ), instead of dividing them into buckets like ntile() does - useful for keeping, say, only the first 3 contacts per person: filter(row_number() <= 3) .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Join - assemble tables
sections.text: This is one of the things that takes the longest to understand, but is essential for all register work. A join puts two tables together based on a shared key - typically pnr . The three joins below ( inner_join , semi_join , left_join ) are the ones this guide actually uses, and are explained here because each has a DST- or DuckDB-specific catch worth knowing before you rely on it. right_join , full_join and anti_join are real too, just rarely needed here - see Joins - link two tables for the full comparison table across all five, multi-key joins, and how to validate a join after running it.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: inner_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps only rows that exist in BOTH tables. Analogy: It is like a VIP list at the entrance. You must be on BOTH lists to get in. Used when a match is meaningful - e.g. inner_join(cohort) keeps only hospital contacts for persons who are actually in the study.
sections.code: inner_join cohort select pnr surgery_date only contacts members

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: semi_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps the rows from the left table that have a match in y - but adds no columns from y . So it is a filter where the list of allowed values lives in another table. Analogy: You have all of LPR and a list of your cohort. semi_join keeps only the LPR rows whose pnr is on the cohort list - the same result as filter(pnr %in% ...) , but faster and more reliable on lazy (Arrow/DuckDB) tables. Where is the local list? The list itself is the tibble you pass as the second argument ( y ); by = "pnr" only says which column to match on - not where the list is. Because y is an ordinary table, you do not need !! . That is the difference from filter(pnr %in% !!cohort_pnrs) , where the vector sits directly in the condition and !! is what injects it. Use semi_join to filter a register down to the cohort. Add copy = TRUE - it is cheap insurance, not just a fix for an error you already hit. y (your local tibble) and the left table (the register) can come from different connections - e.g. if read_register() routes through a database engine like DuckDB rather than plain Arrow, which depends on your fastreg version and setup. dplyr will not silently
sections.code: lpr_adm semi_join tibble pnr cohort_pnrs copy keep only cohort rows

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: left_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps all rows from the left table. Rows without a match in the right table get NA for the columns that came from the right. Analogy: It is like checking whether your patients have a particular finding, without discarding any of them. All patients are still there - those with the finding have a date, those without have NA . Used everywhere when adding flags and covariates to the cohort.
sections.code: full_cohort start all cohort members left_join hip_fracture pnr retained only those hip fracture get

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: bind_rows(df1, df2, ...)
sections.text: What it does: stacks data frames on top of each other (same columns, more rows). Analogy: Like taking three piles of paper and putting them in one pile. Used e.g. to combine LPR2 + psychiatric LPR2 + LPR3 into one combined diagnosis table.
sections.code: bind_rows lpr2_results lpr2_psyk_results lpr3_results combine all three source tables

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Reshaping
sections.text: pivot_wider() and pivot_longer() (below) are explained briefly here as functions; for when to reshape at all, and the group_by() + slice() alternative that avoids it for most cohort work, see [Long ↔ wide format](long-wide.qmd).

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = col)
sections.text: What it does: transforms a long format (one row per visit) to a wide format (one row per person with one column per time point). Analogy: Imagine a patient with five weigh-in visits - all in the same column with five rows. pivot_wider() transforms it into one single row with five columns: weight_3mo , weight_6mo , weight_12mo , etc. Used in extraction of weight and insulin outcomes.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pivot_longer(cols, names_to, values_to)
sections.text: What it does: the reverse of pivot_wider() - takes several columns and stacks them into two: one naming which column each value came from, one holding the value itself.
sections.code: pivot_longer cols starts_with weight_ names_to timepoint values_to weight

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: !! (bang-bang, two exclamation marks)
sections.text: What it does: injects a local R variable into a DuckDB/dplyr query. Analogy: Imagine asking an assistant to find all rows with a code from a list. If you say "find all with a code from the list my_atc ", the assistant first looks for a column in the database with that name, and only uses your list if there is none. You can say: "find all with a code from this list" and hold the list up. !! is the equivalent of holding the list up. You will see !! in front of local R variables (typically code and year lists) inside filter() calls.
sections.code: filter atc my_atc says column

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: !!column_name := value (inside mutate)
sections.text: What it does: creates a column whose NAME is determined by an R variable - not written directly in the code. Normally you write a fixed column name to the left of = in mutate() : But in the NMI calculation (Nordic Multimorbidity Index) we loop over a list of chronic conditions ( "mi" , "stroke" , "diabetes" , ...) and want to create one column per condition. The column name is therefore stored in a variable: Two things differ from normal: !! : as in filter() : injects the R variable's contents instead of interpreting it as a column name := : used instead of = , because R requires it when the left side of an assignment is dynamic. It is not possible to write mutate(!!name = 1L) - only mutate(!!name := 1L) works. 1L is an integer (see as.integer() / 1L ) - flag columns are stored as integers to save memory.
sections.code: mutate always creates column called condition_name variable contains string injects content equivalent next iteration stroke

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: substr(string, start, end)
sections.text: What it does: extracts part of a text string based on character positions. Analogy: You have the ICD code "DG30" . DST has prepended a "D" - it does not belong in standard ICD-10. substr("DG30", 2, 4) says: "give me characters from position 2 to 4" and returns "G30" . Register codes carry no decimal point. F00.1 is stored as DF001 , so the subtype digit is just the fifth character. Prefer substr(x, 2, 5) when you extract. substr() returns whatever is there when the string is shorter than the window you ask for, so it never pads and never errors: "DG30" gives "G30" and "DF001" gives "F001" . The shorter window is the lossy one, because substr(x, 2, 4) always returns three characters and therefore turns "DF001" into "F00" , discarding the subtype. Use the three-character version when you deliberately want a three-character grouping, and keep the original column beside it either way, so you can still tell F00.1 from F00.0 later without going back to the register.
sections.code: substr c_diag digit code dg30 g30 di110 i110

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: paste0(x, y)
sections.text: What it does: concatenates text strings without spaces. Used for compact construction of ICD code lists.
sections.code: paste0 creates c10 c11 c12 c43

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: paste(x, y, sep = "_")
sections.text: What it does: concatenates text strings with a chosen separator.
sections.code: koen birth_year sep creates e.g. matching key

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: toupper(x) / tolower(x)
sections.text: What it does: converts text to upper or lower case respectively.
sections.code: toupper c_opr ensures procedure codes match regardless capitalisation

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: grepl(pattern, x)
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE / FALSE for each element in x that matches a search pattern (regular expression). Analogy: It is like "Ctrl+F" on a text document, but applied to entire columns at once. grepl("^C34", icd4) finds all 4-digit codes starting with C34 . Used e.g. to match ICD codes against diagnosis patterns in comorbidity measures such as NMI (Nordic Multimorbidity Index).
sections.code: grepl c34 icd4 c340 c341 c342 etc.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: str_detect(x, pattern) <small>- stringr</small>
sections.text: What it does: the same job as grepl() above, just from the stringr package instead of base R, with the arguments in the opposite order ( str_detect(x, pattern) vs. grepl(pattern, x) ). Returns the same TRUE / FALSE per element. Used throughout the guide's diagnosis- and ATC-matching code (e.g. NMI) - functionally interchangeable with grepl() , pick whichever reads better in context.
sections.code: str_detect c_diag de1 any diabetes code e10 e14 prefix

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: as.Date(x)
sections.text: What it does: converts text or datetime to a simple date object. DST stores some date-times as "2021-03-15 14:32:00" . as.Date() removes the time parts and gives a clean calendar date. Use it after collect() , when the data are in R - see [DST pitfall 4](dst-pitfalls.qmd#4-date-columns-are-not-always-in-date-format) for why.
sections.code: as.date kont_starttidspunkt after collect

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ymd(x) / dmy(x) (from lubridate)
sections.text: What it does: reads dates that are not in ISO form ( "2021-03-15" ). as.Date() assumes ISO and returns NA on e.g. "15/03/2021" or "15-03-2021" ; the forgiving lubridate parsers infer the order from the name ( ymd = year-month-day, dmy = day-month-year, mdy = month-day-year).
sections.code: ymd year month day dmy as.date would

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: year(date) (from lubridate)
sections.text: What it does: extracts the year from a date.
sections.code: year surgery_date

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: difftime(date1, date2, units = "days")
sections.text: What it does: calculates the difference between two dates.
sections.code: as.numeric difftime surgery_date foed_dag units days age surgery years

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: min(x, na.rm = TRUE) / max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: finds the smallest/largest element in a vector and ignores NA .
sections.code: summarise first_date min date_contact na.rm earliest contact per person

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pmin(x, y) / pmax(x, y)
sections.text: What it does: compares two vectors position by position and returns the smallest/largest for each element. Analogy: Imagine two lists of dates - date of death and study end date. pmin(death_date, study_end) selects for each person what came first. The functions above are the building blocks. The concrete date tasks are shown where they belong in the workflow: Age at index ( /365.25 , leap years): [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) Baseline year for annual registers ( year(index_date) - 1 ): Socioeconomic variables SAS integer dates ( origin = "1960-01-01" ): [Pitfalls on DST](dst-pitfalls.qmd) Follow-up time and event variable ( pmin() ): Joins Start/stop format (time-varying covariate): [Time-varying variables](time-varying.qmd)
sections.code: pmin death_date as.date na.rm censoring either death study end alive

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: as.integer(x) / 1L
sections.text: What it does: converts to integer. The L suffix (e.g. 1L , 0L ) specifies that it is an integer rather than a decimal. Flag columns are stored as integers ( 1L / 0L ) to save memory.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: is.na(x)
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE for NA values (missing values).
sections.code: filter is.na pnr remove rows without person date_hip_fracture hip fracture

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: set.seed(n)
sections.text: What it does: fixes the starting point for random number generation. Analogy: Imagine shuffling a deck of cards. Without set.seed() you will shuffle differently every time. With set.seed(42) you always shuffle in the same way - and can thus reproduce your results exactly. Always call it before matching loops to ensure reproducibility.
sections.code: set.seed fix random seed reproducibility sample pool_pnrs size always selects same pnr

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: sample(x, size)
sections.text: What it does: draws random elements from a vector. Used in matching logic to select random control persons from a pool.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: split(df, group_vector)
sections.text: What it does: splits a data frame into a list of sub-data-frames, one per unique group. Analogy: Imagine sorting patient records into piles by year and sex. split(pool, paste(koen, birth_year, sep = "_")) gives you one pile per combination, so the matching code can work quickly within one pile at a time.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: vector("list", n)
sections.text: What it does: creates an empty list with space for n elements. Pre-allocation is faster than letting R expand the list one element at a time in a loop.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: seq_len(n)
sections.text: What it does: generates the sequence 1, 2, ..., n. Safer than 1:n in loops, because it handles the case n = 0 correctly.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: unlist(list, use.names = FALSE)
sections.text: What it does: flattens a list of vectors into one long vector.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Diagnostics and debugging
sections.text: The functions below help you find out what went wrong . For the actual list of known error messages and what fixes them - "code stopped" or "code gave nothing back" - see Troubleshooting; for "the code ran fine but the answer is wrong," see DST pitfalls.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: class(x)
sections.text: What it does: tells you what type of object x is. Always check class() first if you get a strange error.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: nrow(df)
sections.text: What it does: returns the number of rows. Used to print cohort sizes and verify that exclusions have worked. glimpse(df) (from dplyr ) gives a quick look at every column at once - name, type, and the first few values - transposed so it fits on screen even with many columns. A faster first check than head() when you just landed a new extract and want to see what you got.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: cat("text\n")
sections.text: What it does: prints text to the console without quotation marks. \n is a newline. Used for progress messages: cat("Extracting NMI score...\n") .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: stop("message")
sections.text: What it does: stops the code with an error message. Used to give an understandable error if a required file is missing.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: stopifnot(condition)
sections.text: What it does: a sanity check . If the condition is TRUE , nothing happens and the code continues. If it is FALSE , the code stops with an error. Use it for assumptions that MUST hold, e.g. "one row per person": What do you do if it stops? Then the assumption does not hold - e.g. there is more than one row per person. Find the duplicates and fix the cause: Duplicates often come from a join that multiplied rows, or from duplicate person-year rows in the source data.
sections.code: stopifnot n_distinct pnr errors there are duplicates count filter see which recur distinct keep_all keep one row per person correct

sections.heading: gc()
sections.text: What it does: releases unused memory back to the operating system. Use it after you are done with large registers - you share RAM with everyone else on the DST server.

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.text: You have built your cohort (Phase 10), assembled your extracts (Phase 12), and are now about to write the code that actually produces your results: descriptive tables, models, sensitivity analyses. The most important thing in register-based research is that your results can be reproduced - by a reviewer, a colleague or yourself in six months. That places demands on how you organise and write your code. The habits you adopt now will save you hours later. In short: One of the most important things is keeping an overview - e.g. via one script per step, run each script top to bottom (never across), give objects meaningful names, and comment the why rather than the what . The rest is polish.

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 1. Structure your scripts logically
sections.text: One script per step. Put each step of the analysis in its own .R file, named with a number that tells you the order to run them in: The script numbers tell anyone who sees the folder the order to run them in. Use subfolders as the project grows - e.g. R/ , output/ , datasets/ . A predictable order within each script. Whatever the script does, the same frame recurs: a header, load packages, import data - then the actual work - and finally save the result. Only the middle part changes from script to script: The same steps - header, packages, paths, data, save - recur in every script; only the actual work changes. The options() call belongs here, once, next to the library() calls: it is what lets read_register("bef") find a register by name, and it is the step people most often discover by getting an error. See Point fastreg at your registers. The header at the top tells you in five seconds what the script does, who wrote it and what it needs. More on good section headings and comments in section 5. Avoid jumping back and forth between cleaning, modelling and plotting. A script should read and run from top to bottom. If your code jumps around, it becomes impossible
sections.code: build_cohort.r build cohort pnr index extract_outcomes.r extract outcomes extract_covariates.r covariates data_management.r assemble clean derive variables descriptive.r descriptive analyses table analysis.r main models sensitivity.r sensitivity project bariatric surgery hip fracture example study illustration only author purpose main analysis cox model load packages tidyverse survival tableone createtableone point fastreg registers once per script right after calls before each read. only needed scripts read registers. see parquet fastreg. options fastreg.project_workdata_dir workdata projectnumber cleaned fastreg.project_rawdata_dir rawdata import analysis_data readrds path analysis.rds actual work varies

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 2. Run scripts top to bottom - never across
sections.text: A script should run from line 1 to the end without interruption and give the same result every time. Avoid running two lines from one file, jumping to another and back. Never run code manually across scripts. If your result depends on you having run line 14 in script 02 before line 7 in script 03, it is not reproducible. Instead, do a saveRDS() at the end of script 02 and a readRDS() at the start of script 03. When you think you are done: restart R ( Session → Restart R ) and run the whole script from line 1 again. Does it run clean? Then it is reproducible.
sections.code: end extract_covariates.r save result saverds covariates path covariates.rds start data_management.r load again readrds

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 3. Use meaningful object names
sections.text: The name should describe what the object contains . In six months you will not remember what a and b were. participant_data and bmi_model explain themselves.
sections.code: bad what are read_csv data.csv bmi age good speaks itself participant_data bmi_model

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 4. Use snake_case consistently
sections.text: Consistent naming makes code far easier to read. Pick snake_case (lowercase with underscores) and stick to it: What matters is not which style, but that you are consistent.
sections.code: good snake_case body_mass_index participant_age sweetener_intake avoid mixing styles bodymassindex pascalcase bodymassindex camelcase bmi_data mixed

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 5. Headings and comments make the code readable
sections.text: Headings and comments are what make a script navigable - for a reviewer, a colleague or yourself in six months. Three things to get into the habit of: A short description at the top of each script: what it does, what it needs as input, and what it produces (the header from section 1). Section headings that run out to the right margin: write the heading, then fill the rest of the line with dashes, as in the example in section 1. That one line does two jobs: it breaks the file up visually, and it makes the heading a section your editor can navigate to (see below). A comment on each substantial line of code: but explain why , not what . Comment the "why", not the "what". The code already shows what happens. A good comment explains why - the decision behind it. Explain choices, assumptions and sources - not the obvious. It takes five minutes to write a good comment now and an hour to understand the code again in three months.
sections.code: bad comment just repeats code calculate bmi bmi weight height better explains decision used adjustment variable primary models

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: Find your way around a long script
sections.text: Your editor keeps an outline of the file you are editing: an automatically generated table of contents. You do not write it. The editor builds it from your code, listing every function you define plus every comment line you have marked as a section heading. A 600-line extraction script stops needing to be scrolled. Where to find it. In RStudio the outline is a panel on the right-hand side of the editor. The same list also sits in the dropdown at the bottom left of the editor pane, the one that normally reads (Top Level) : it is clickable, and a lot of people have looked past it for years. Each entry in the outline is a comment line ending in dashes, and the small triangles in the left margin of the editor fold a section away. The dropdown at the bottom left shows the section the cursor is currently in. What turns a comment into a heading. A comment line that ends with four or more - , = or # characters. All three work and they are interchangeable; dashes are simply the most common. Whatever comes before that trailing run becomes the label in the panel: That trailing run is the entire mechanism. sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: Share functions across scripts with a separate file
sections.text: A function only helps within the script it is defined in. As soon as a second script needs it, you copy it over - and now you have two versions that drift apart. You fix a bug in one of them, months pass, and you can no longer tell which analysis was run with which version. The fix is one shared file that both scripts read. Three steps: 1. Put the definitions in their own file , e.g. 00_functions.R . The 00_ prefix places it first, before the numbered scripts (see [section 2](#run-top-to-bottom)). 2. Delete the definitions from the scripts and read the file instead, right after the library() calls: 3. Verify it before you trust it. Restart R completely first ( Session → Restart R , or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd>) so you know an old copy is not still sitting in memory: Move the constants too. get_prior_hip_fracture_pnrs() uses hip_fracture_icd3 . If you move the function but leave the constant behind in the old script, the function does not fail when you source it - it fails later , at a random point deep inside a run, with object 'hip_fracture_icd3' not found . Anything a function refers to but does not take as an argument has to move with it.

sections.title: Good code practice
sections.heading: 11. Mind your RAM in the shared environment
sections.text: On Forskermaskinen (the shared environment) all users share the same RAM. R loads data directly into RAM, so a single large extraction can slow the server for everyone. That is why DST automatically kills processes (RStudio sessions, jobs, etc.) when memory is close to full - and if your session is killed, you lose all unsaved work. There is a 250 GB limit per user session (on the STATA and R/Python servers). If you exceed it, you are logged off automatically and sent an email about the event. And if a server has less than 10 % free memory overall, the session with the largest usage is logged off - even if it is below 250 GB. Questions: servicedesk@dst.dk / +45 39 17 38 00. Save often, and write to disk along the way. Save your code continuously, and write intermediate results to disk with saveRDS() (cf. sections 2 and 10), so you do not lose hours of work if your process is killed. Concrete habits that keep RAM use down: Load only what you need. Select columns and rows before data lands in RAM - see Read only what you need ( open_dataset() + filter / select , read_sas(col_select=, n_max=) ). Clean up as you go. Delete large objects once you no longer need them:

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: Summarise data
sections.text: What is NA? NA ( Not Available ) is R's term for a missing or unknown value. A cell can have NA because the information was not recorded, not reported, or does not exist for that person. Most calculation functions return NA if there is one NA in the data - unless you write na.rm = TRUE ("remove NAs"). is.na(x) returns TRUE for NA values and FALSE for everything else. When is NA a problem? It depends on which column is missing: NA in a key variable (index date, pnr, outcome) is serious - these persons cannot be correctly included in the analysis, and you must decide whether to exclude them. NA in a covariate (e.g. income) can often be handled - e.g. with a separate "unknown" category or imputation. NA from a join usually means a person was not found in the right-hand dataset - e.g. no prescription record. Here NA is effectively a "no/none", not an error. Always check colSums(is.na(data)) immediately after an extraction or a join, so you detect unexpected gaps before they propagate silently through the analysis. For continuous variables:

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: Check missing values
sections.text: colSums(is.na(bef_data)) returns one line with a counter per column: Here foed_dag is missing for 3 - everything else is complete. A column with 0 has no NAs at all. colSums(is.na()) counts only true NA . In register data, "missing" is often stored as an empty or blank string (whitespace) or a sentinel code - not as NA . A column can therefore show 0 NAs and still be full of empty values: e.g. a fixed-width key field filled with blanks (a 13-character field that looks empty but is 13 spaces, not NA ). So also check for blank values - e.g. sum(trimws(bef_data$pnr) == "", na.rm = TRUE) - and look at nchar() / unique() on a slice. This matters most for join keys : a blank-but-not- NA key causes silent join errors (rows that look filled but don't match).

It may have been converted a year ago, ordered for fewer years, or be a register that has closed for good ( dodsaars stops in 2001, see pitfall 1). Nothing errors when your follow-up runs past the end of the data: people simply look as if nothing happened to them, which quietly skews censoring, outcomes and matching. So for every register you use, check its first and last year or date against your study period before you build anything on it: For event registers, use the date column rather than year : year is the folder the row was filed under, not when the event happened. The first and last date show only the two ends. One wrong date far in the future is enough to make a register look complete, so count the rows per year as well: a register that stops early has a last year with far fewer rows than the years before it. It also helps to know when the parquet copy was made. sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.text: Use this page to turn your cohort and your separate extracts into the one analysis-ready dataset that every analysis page starts from. Your extracts from Phase 6, Extract from LPR and Phase 11 are stored as separate RDS files. Once each extract is down to one row per person (Long ↔ wide format), you join them onto the cohort, check the joins, and calculate follow-up time and the event variable. When you are done you have analysis.rds . Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. First get each extract down to one row per person. left_join() only behaves predictably when the table you join on has one row per key ( pnr , or pnr + index_date ). Many register extracts have multiple rows per person (long format). Reduce them to one row per person with group_by() + slice() or pivot_wider() - explained in [Long ↔ wide format](long-wide.qmd). This page assumes your extracts are already in that shape.

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Joins - link two tables
sections.text: In register-based research you almost always work with data from two or more tables that need to be linked. All joins in dplyr take two tables and one key column they share (e.g. pnr ). When you join your finished person-level extracts onto the cohort , the key is usually pnr . Inside a register it is other keys: joining contact and diagnosis in LPR, for instance, happens on recnum or dw_ek_kontakt , not pnr (see the overview of LPR join keys). A value that is measured relative to the index date (socioeconomic position, a comorbidity score) is joined on pnr + index_date , so it still lands on the right row when the same person is in the cohort with more than one index date. The ER diagram below shows both - extracts joined onto the cohort: The key is marked PK (primary key) in the cohort and FK (foreign key) in each extract. The symbol ||--o| is standard ER notation ("crow's foot"): || = exactly one, o| = zero or one. So the line reads: each person in the cohort matches zero or one row in the extract. This describes the shape you must ensure before the join - not something left_join() checks or fixes. If an extract has several rows per pnr , left_join()

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Join with multiple keys
sections.text: Multiple keys only become relevant when at least one of the tables has several rows per person - otherwise pnr alone is enough. With multiple keys all the listed columns must agree before two rows count as a match ( pnr and year , not pnr or year ). The typical case is panel data: registers with one row per person per year . BEF, AKM and so on have a pnr row for every calendar year. Join two of them on pnr alone and each of the person's rows is paired with all of the person's rows in the other table: with 5 years in BEF and 5 in AKM you get every combination, 5 × 5 = 25 rows instead of 5. Add the year as an extra key and those 25 are filtered down to the 5 where the year also matches - 2018 against 2018: If instead you join two extracts that each have one row per person (e.g. finished person-level extracts onto the cohort), pnr alone is enough - there is no extra dimension to keep track of. Do not assume "one row per person per year" - check it. A BEF delivery can contain duplicate (pnr, year) rows (the delivery this guide was written from did), and adding the year as a key does not save you from those: a person with two 2018 rows still doubles. sections.text: bind_rows() and left_join() solve two fundamentally different problems : bind_rows() is not a join. It does not look at pnr and does not match. It simply places table 2's rows below table 1's rows - like pasting two Excel sheets together vertically. Columns missing in one table (e.g. a column that only exists in LPR3) are automatically filled with NA for rows from the other table. Counting diagnoses across this combined all_dx ? Expect a jump around 2019-2020 that isn't a real change in disease occurrence - see why. When do you use which? bind_rows() - when you have two versions of the same register (LPR2 + LPR3, exposed + comparators) and want to merge them into one. left_join() - when you want to attach a new variable (outcome, date of death, age) to your cohort table.

Date of death (DOD) Emigration date (VNDS) Emigration censors just like death - the person leaves the study on the day they emigrate. VNDS contains one row per migration event. Take the first exit after the index date , not simply the first ever: a person may have left and come back, and an exit before index censors nothing. Whether the person was resident at index at all is decided in Phase 10. The date of death is one date per person, so pnr alone is the right key. The emigration date depends on the index date, so it is keyed on pnr and index_date : a person who was drawn as a comparison person on two different dates then gets the right exit for each of them.

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Calculate follow-up time and event variable
sections.text: Before you can analyse, each cohort member needs a censoring date (when follow-up ends) and an event variable (did they experience the outcome?). The censoring date is the earliest of: event date, date of death, emigration date, the date a comparison person becomes exposed themselves (crossover) and end of study period. death_date and emigration_date were joined on above; the outcome date is joined on first here. pmin() compares vectors position by position and returns the smallest value per person - it is the vectorised version of min() . na.rm = TRUE ensures that a missing death date (= alive) does not make the censoring date NA . Crossover. A comparison person who later becomes exposed stops being a comparison person on that day, so follow-up is censored at crossover_date (made in Phase 10, NA for the exposed and for comparison persons who never become exposed). Without that line, time after their own exposure is counted as unexposed time. If your cohort has no crossover_date column (no comparison group, or one that can never become exposed), leave the line out. The alternative to censoring is to let the person switch group at crossover and contribute

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Assemble the final analysis dataset
sections.text: By now your cohort is built in Phase 10: a table with pnr and index_date (and exposed / case if you have a comparison group - renamed to exposure in the final select() ) - one row per person , unless your comparison group was matched with replacement , in which case the same pnr can carry several rows, one per index_date it was matched on. The recipe below works for both: everything measured relative to the index date is joined on pnr + index_date , see [comparison cohort's callout on it](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-4---assemble-validate-and-save). Your outcomes, covariates and censoring variables are extracted as separate RDS files (Phase 9, [Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd)). This last step joins them onto the cohort with left_join() , calculates follow-up time, and keeps only the columns the analysis needs. Cohort construction - including the matching - belongs to [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd). Here we assume the cohort already exists; this page only assembles the analysis dataset around it. Design choices (comparator, immortal time, matching ratio) are decided back in [Phase 1](plan-your-study.qmd#comparator-cohort). End with select() - keep only

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.text: Use this page when a laboratory value is part of your study: an exposure, a covariate at baseline or an outcome (for example HbA1c or creatinine). You need your cohort from Phase 10 and the list of analysis codes you want. You end with an .rds file of results for your cohort, one row per result, filtered to the cohort before collect() . The column dictionary is [Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel](register-reference.qmd#lab-forsker).

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: What the laboratory table is: LAB_F, not DST, not LPR
sections.text: LAB_F (Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel) is delivered by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (SDS) through Forskerservice. In the clinical epidemiology literature it is usually called RLRR (Register of Laboratory Results for Research). It is not on DST's register list. It is not LPR. LPR is hospital contacts. This table is one row per laboratory result. It is very large, so semi_join() and filter() have to run before collect() .

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: One delivery, several table names
sections.text: lab_dm_forsker , lab_forsker and laboratorieproevesvar are cuts of the same delivery, not separate registers. Using more than one double-counts. Column names are not the same in every cut. The dictionary section names the columns this extract uses on lab_dm_forsker : patient_cpr , analysiscode , samplingdate , value , unit . The Version 4 dictionary has more columns than that. A delivery may not include every column in the dictionary, so do not treat a full dictionary listing as the column list of the file you were sent. lab_dm_forsker : person column patient_cpr , result column value . lab_forsker : a narrower cut of the same delivery (fewer columns). laboratorieproevesvar : a narrow cut seen in at least one project delivery. The person column is cprnummer and the result column is samplevalue , not patient_cpr and value . The guide's schema describes this cut as four columns and names those two. It does not name the other two; check them with colnames() on your own file.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: The October 2025 delivery: table names may change
sections.text: Sundhedsdatastyrelsen updated the laboratory delivery on 3 October 2025 ([announcement →](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/forskerservice/om-forskerservice/nyheder-fra-forskerservice/2025/data_laboratoriedatabasen_031025)): "Det nye LAB erstatter den tidligere version af LAB" (the new LAB replaces the earlier version of LAB). The announcement names four tables, laboratorieproevesvar , Dimlaboratoriekoder , DimNPU and Proevesvar_optaelling , but never mentions lab_dm_forsker by name, and does not say what happens to projects already using it. The official data dictionary the guide is built from (PDF) is Version 4, dated 1 December 2023, nearly two years before that announcement, and it documents lab_dm_forsker only. Whether lab_dm_forsker is being retired, and what laboratorieproevesvar 's columns are after the October 2025 change, we do not know. Check the order sheet ("bestillingsark") on Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's site, or your own delivery, before relying on either name.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Extract lab results for your cohort
sections.text: You choose the analysis codes. Laboratory tests are coded in NPU (Nomenclature for Properties and Units), a terminology maintained by IFCC and IUPAC and used for laboratory results in Denmark, Norway and Sweden ([NPU leaflet, IUPAC 2019](https://iupac.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/NPUterminologi2019_Leaflet.pdf)). Look up the codes for your tests at npu-terminology.org, and write the list and its source into your code. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. The register name below is the lab_dm_forsker cut. If your file is laboratorieproevesvar , rename cprnummer to pnr and keep samplevalue instead of value . The table stays one row per result. Collapse to one row per person only when your definition needs that, the same way as in [Long and wide format](long-wide.qmd).

sections.text: fiktive can build a lab_dm_forsker table for local practice. It is not on DST. This synthetic table has not been run against a DST delivery, so do not treat it as a check that the pipeline works on the server. Install once with remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive") , as in Phase 6. To use real IFCC/NPU terms, set options(fiktive.labterm_fetch_ifcc = TRUE) before generating. That option downloads and caches a public IFCC code list. FIKTIVE_LABTERM (or options(fiktive.labterm) ) is the other route: a LabTerm or IFCC file you already have, not a download. Without one of those, fiktive does not invent NPU codes. Do not take column names from fiktive 's labka generator. That is a different database (LABKA, see Coverage).

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Which results reach the table
sections.text: NPU is not its own column. It sits inside analysiscode , together with Danish DNK codes. Only those coded results reach the table, about 95 per cent. A laboratory's own local codes never arrive. There is nothing to filter them in with. Patients who declined consent are absent from the table. That absence is not a coded value, so there is no code to filter on.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Coverage: from 2008, complete per laboratory by 2010-2016
sections.text: Coverage starts in 2008, not the 1990s. Complete coverage arrives per laboratory between 2010 and 2016. The start year, the table of periods per region and laboratory, the 95 per cent and the consent rule above are all in Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's [documentation of the research table](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638651043236441510/Dokumentation%20af%20Labdatabasens%20Forskertabel.pdf). See also [Laboratoriedatabasen →](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/nationale-sundhedsregistre/laboratoriedatabasen). For years before 2008, projects used the separate regional database LABKA (Arendt et al. 2020; [Grann et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S17901)). Neither paper gives literal column names, so the guide gives none.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Results are text: convert value with care
sections.text: value is text, not a number. Alongside numeric results the reference section lists POSITIV , NEGATIV , IKKE PÅVIST , INGEN VÆKST and the blood-type codes. as.numeric() turns every one of them into NA without warning, which drops exactly the samples where something was found. The same would happen to any result written with a sign, such as <5 . On laboratorieproevesvar the same column is called samplevalue . Before you convert, list the values that are not plain numbers, and decide what each should become: Do not compare a numeric result across laboratories, or across time, without unit . The same analysiscode can mean a different scale when the equipment or the sample material differs, including inside one laboratory over time. Keep unit in the extract.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.text: This page guides you from the very first login to having RStudio running and being ready to execute code. This guide assumes you are working with R . When you log in to DST, you choose "Python/R" - select R/RStudio.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 1 - Download Microsoft Remote Desktop (Mac only)
sections.text: Open the App Store on your Mac and search for "Microsoft Remote Desktop" . Download and install for free. Windows users have Remote Desktop built in - search for "Remote Desktop Connection" in the Start menu.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 2 - Log in
sections.text: 1. Go to remote.dst.dk in your browser 2. Log in with your ident (4 letters) and the one-time code you receive 3. Click Python/R 4. Log in with username dstfse\IDENT+PROJECTNUMBER (e.g. dstfse\abcd708421 ) and your chosen password You can also choose "FSE Windows" instead of Python/R - from there you land on a selection desktop and can click through to e.g. Python/R .

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 3 - Find/create your own project folder
sections.text: Open File Explorer and navigate to the workspaces folder under your project. Create a folder with your name or ident if it does not already exist: Recommended structure within your folder:
sections.code: workdata projectnumber workspaces project all scripts files datasets intermediate results rds local dst only output tables figures ready repatriation

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 4 - Mac keyboard fix (do this at every connection)
sections.text: Special characters such as , $ , \ , @ , { and } do not work correctly in Remote Desktop by default on Mac. Solution: Switch to Unicode mode with ⌃⌘U (Ctrl + Cmd + U) inside the Remote Desktop window. In RStudio, code is run with Ctrl+Enter (not Cmd+Enter). Project 708421 uses fastreg (on CRAN) to read the registers with read_register("name") - just like the general guide. See the complete guide: DARTER - overview and pipeline →

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Create your R project
sections.text: An R project collects all your scripts, output files and settings in one folder. Each study should have its own project. What does a project actually do? A project is first of all just a folder - you still save your own files in it (in R/ , datasets/ , output/ ). The point is the .Rproj file: when you open the project, RStudio automatically sets the working directory to the folder where .Rproj lives. So getwd() always points to your project folder, and you can use relative paths ( datasets/cohort.rds ) instead of writing the full path or setwd("E:/...") at the top of every script. Each project also keeps its own settings and history separate, so studies don't get mixed up. 1. Open RStudio 2. File → New Project → New Directory → New Project 3. Give the project a name and choose a location under your workspace folder 4. Click Create Project Run getwd() now and you get the path to your project, e.g. E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/workspaces/[your-name]/[your-project-name] Do not save workspace RStudio asks at close: "Save workspace image?" - always choose No . Set it permanently: Tools → Global Options → General → "Save workspace to .RData" → Never . Make RStudio

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: The rules you sign up to, in short
sections.text: You certify to these before you get access, and breaking them carries sanctions. The four that catch people out in ordinary daily work: No images of the screen: the ban covers photos and screenshots alike, so you cannot snap a console output to paste into a message to a colleague. Nothing leaves except through repatriation: not by email, not on paper, not by retyping it. See Phase 14 - Export and repatriation. Never put real data in a support question: when you write to a data manager or to DST, invent the numbers. A pasted error message with a real pnr in it is a rule breach. Work somewhere private: your institution or your home office. Not a train, a café or a library, and never leave the screen unattended. Screen sharing is allowed only with people who have access to that same project. The full text is short and worth reading once: [Rules for working with microdata →](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-arbejdet-med-mikrodata).

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Log off correctly when you are done
sections.text: Closing the RStudio window or simply disconnecting is not enough. You are sitting on two desktops nested inside each other plus a browser session - close all three, otherwise your session keeps running and holds the server's RAM (see Mind the RAM). Log off in this order: 1. Sign out of the Python/R desktop (the inner desktop where RStudio runs) - use Sign out in the Start menu, not just closing the window. 2. Sign out of the FSE Windows desktop (the outer choice desktop) - Sign out again. (skip this step if you went straight to the Python/R desktop) 3. Log out of remote.dst.dk in your browser. So: Sign out twice (once per desktop) plus log out in the browser.

sections.text: You are logged in and set up. Next is the data itself: which files you meet, and what opens them. → Phase 4 - File types and loading Project 708421: [DARTER - Register paths and datastores](darter-register-paths-datastores.qmd)

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.text: Use this page when an extract has many rows per person and you need it down to one row per person before you join it onto the cohort ([Link your extracts](joins.qmd)). The registers you extract from are almost always in long format with many rows per person. This page explains the difference and shows the two ways you reshape an extract: group_by() + slice() and pivot_wider() / pivot_longer() . Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Wide vs. long format
sections.text: Imagine three persons with weight measurements at two time points. Wide format - one row per person, one column per time point: Long format - one row per observation, one column for time point and one for value: Both formats contain the same information - they are just arranged differently.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Which formats are where?
sections.text: Registers are usually in long format. Your analysis dataset should typically be in wide format.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Two ways to get one row per person
sections.text: The key choice is what you want out of the long register: In register-based research group_by() + slice() is usually the one you need: you want "the newest" or "the first" value per person. You use pivot_wider() when you explicitly want to compare several time points.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: group_by() + slice() - one representative row
sections.text: The pattern is always the same: group by pnr , sort so the desired row is on top, take the first row per group. For baseline covariates you usually want the snapshot that applied at the index date, not the newest one: join on the index date and keep only snapshots on or before it before you take the first row. Always remember ungroup() . group_by() puts a "grouped_df" tag on your data.frame, which all subsequent operations inherit. That means: mutate() calculates per group, not across the entire dataset n() counts rows per group, not in total summarize() gives one result per group These errors are hard to detect because the code runs without error messages and produces seemingly reasonable numbers. ungroup() removes the tag and makes the data.frame normal again. Rule of thumb: always end a group_by() chain with ungroup() .

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Long → wide with pivot_wider()
sections.text: You CANNOT pivot_wider() an entire LPR table. LPR potentially has hundreds of unique ICD codes per person - pivot_wider() would give you one column per code, i.e. thousands of columns and a dataset that is impossible to work with. Instead use the pattern from Extract from LPR: extract the first date for one specific diagnosis group (with group_by() + slice() above), save as extract_hip_fracture.rds , and join it as one column with left_join() . AKM (the Labour Classification Module) stores one row per person per year - long format. If you want to compare employment status at baseline and follow-up side by side, you can pivot: In practice you would typically not pivot AKM - you filter to one specific year with filter(year == index_year) and use group_by() + slice() above. Pivot is relevant when you explicitly want two time points side by side in the analysis.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.text: Use this page to extract dispensed prescriptions for your cohort and turn them into a variable: a first dispensing date, a user/non-user flag, or the raw material for exposure time. You need your cohort from [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd), and you end with an .rds file of dispensings, one row per fill, that the later steps on this page reduce to one row per person. Prescriptions are in LMDB (Lægemiddeldatabasen). In the literature the same data are described as the Danish National Prescription Registry, the part of the Register of Medicinal Product Statistics that holds prescriptions filled by individuals at community pharmacies ([Pottegård et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)). LMDB has one row per dispensed prescription, so one person can have hundreds of rows. The two columns you almost always use are: atc : the drug's ATC code (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification), for example "A10BA02" for metformin. eksd : the dispensing date, the day the prescription was collected at the pharmacy. Use it as the prescription date, in the same way as date_contact in LPR (the National Patient Register). The full column list is in Overview of registers.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: What LMDB covers, and what it does not
sections.text: LMDB starts in 1995, and the data are considered complete and valid from that year (Pottegård et al. 2017). There is no medication history before 1995, so a lookback window that reaches further back is empty for everyone, and "no prescriptions" will look like "not a user". LMDB only holds prescriptions dispensed at community pharmacies. The following are therefore missing ([Pottegård et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)): drugs given during hospital admission; drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres (for example chemotherapy, immunosuppressants and methadone for substance use); drugs for certain institutionalised people (typically because of psychiatric illness); over-the-counter medicine. For a drug that can be bought both with and without a prescription, LMDB only shows the prescribed part. For in-hospital medication there is a newer Hospital Medication Register (Sygehusmedicinregisteret) with data from May 2018. Its data quality has not yet been evaluated, and some clinical specialties are missing ([Rosenkrantz et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S487838)). It is held by the Danish Health Data Authority. Until 1996, a child's prescriptions

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Exposure, outcome or covariate: one extract, different date filters
sections.text: Medication can be an exposure, a covariate or an outcome. As for diagnoses (Extract from LPR), you make one extract of the dispensings, and the role is decided by where eksd falls relative to index_date : If the first dispensing defines the index date, require a period before it with no dispensing of the drug (a washout). Otherwise people who have been on the drug for years enter as new users. LMDB starts in 1995, so nobody has a washout that reaches further back than that.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Extract the dispensings for your cohort
sections.text: ATC codes have no D-prefix (unlike ICD codes in LPR, see [Understand LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#icd-codes-and-the-d-prefix)), so you match directly on the start of the code. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. substr(atc, 1, 5) == "A10BJ" matches the whole ATC group (all GLP-1 analogues; GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1). For several groups at once, use a regular expression as in LPR: grepl("^A10BJ|^A10BA", atc) . Code matching (regex, %in% with a code list, !! ) is explained in [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd) and [Functions: overview](function-guide.qmd#filter-conditions). Reducing to one row per person is explained in Long ↔ wide format. Here it is slice(1) for the first dispensing, but it could also be ever/never or a count in a window (see the role table above).
