sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Define users: at least N dispensings within a window
sections.text: One dispensing is weak evidence of treatment, because some people fill a prescription once and stop. A common definition is therefore at least two dispensings within a window, with the onset date being the date the definition is first met. Sort with arrange() before lag() . lag() works on row order, not on dates. If the rows are not sorted by person and date, gap_days is computed against an arbitrary earlier row, and the result is wrong without any error. The two numbers are your choices, not standards, so write them into your methods. One dispensing can be enough for a drug taken once; for a chronic treatment two or more is the usual requirement. The same definition is how medication enters a comorbidity definition: for conditions treated largely outside hospital, LMDB catches people LPR never sees. Whether to define a condition from diagnoses, prescriptions or both is discussed on Comorbidity. The recipe above is the one to keep for one drug, or a few. It opens LMDB with read_register() , filters, collects, and calls flag_users() . Use this fold-out only when you need many ATC conditions, each with its own "N dispensings within a window" rule. Doing that with the recipe

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Which ATC column?
sections.text: LMDB does not hold the ATC code once. It holds it five times, at five levels, in five separate columns. DST's [variable list for LMDB](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/LMDB%20-%20L%C3%A6gemiddeldatabasen.html) labels them ATC-kode detaljeret and ATC-niveau 1 to ATC-niveau 4 . They are cumulative: each level repeats the levels above it and adds its own characters. The column names and their levels come from DST's variable list. The character counts are not stated there; they follow from the WHO standard, where level 2 is by definition the three-character code ([WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology](https://atcddd.fhi.no/atc/structure_and_principles/)). A pattern longer than the column can never match, and R will not tell you. atc2 holds three characters. grepl("N02A", atc2) compares a four-character pattern against three-character values, so it matches nothing: zero rows, no error, no warning. The same goes for filter(atc2 %in% c("A10A", "A10B")) . An empty result looks like a finding rather than a bug, and it is easy to write up as "no exposed patients" when the truth is that the filter could not fire. So filter on atc , not on the
sections.code: dplyr filter select collect ischaemic heart disease treatment defined organic nitrates c01da ihd lmdb grepl atc full definition one pnr eksd

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Which way should you write the filter?
sections.text: There are two ways to keep the codes you want, and the length of your codes decides which one to use. ATC codes are not all the same length: N02 is three characters, A10BA is five. All codes the same length. Cut atc down to that length, then check whether the result is on your list: substr(atc, 1, 3) means "the first three characters of atc ". Change the 3 to match your codes: use 1, 5 for five-character codes such as A10BA . Codes of different lengths. One substr() cannot serve N02 and A10BA at the same time, because they need different cut lengths. Use grepl() instead, which matches whatever you give it: In doubt? Use grepl() . It works for every code length, so it is never wrong. substr() + %in% was about twice as fast on a twenty-million-row test, which is worth having when you fetch many drug groups at once, but a correct slow filter beats a fast broken one. It is a reasonable thing to wonder, since atc2 is the short column, but the filter runs before anything is loaded: nothing reaches your memory until collect() , and what lands there is the rows that survived, which are the same rows either way. substr(atc, 1, 3) gives you exactly what atc2
sections.code: dplyr filter select collect four drug groups all three characters long my_codes a10 c09 n02 m01 lmdb substr atc keep first look them pnr eksd grepl a10ba c09aa means starts

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: What the level columns are for: grouping
sections.text: When you want a descriptive breakdown by therapeutic subgroup, atc2 is a ready-made grouping column and saves you a substr() : Two minutes, and it settles both whether the columns exist and how they are coded: Expect C / C09 / C09A / C09AA / C09AA05 across a row: each column repeating the one before it. If instead you see isolated fragments ( 09 in atc2 ), every ^ -anchored pattern in this section is wrong for your delivery and you should filter on atc only. Note that names(lmdb) may not answer this. sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Tell products apart when they share an ATC code: vnr and indo
sections.text: ATC classifies by active substance, not by product or indication. Two brands with the same substance therefore get the same ATC code and cannot be told apart on atc alone. Ozempic (semaglutide, type 2 diabetes) and Wegovy (semaglutide, weight loss) both have A10BJ06 : filter on ATC only, and you mix diabetes treatment with weight-loss treatment. Two columns separate them: vnr (varenummer): the unique key to the actual product (package). It is the only reliable way to isolate one specific product. The vnr -to-product lookup comes from the medicine taxonomy (KAT / Danish Health Data Authority); name / packtext hold the product text if you want to recognise it by eye. indo (indication code): a coded indication (from the Medicinpriser catalogue, LMS 25), not free text. The code is recorded only when the prescriber picks an indication from the drop-down menu in the electronic prescription. If the doctor types the indication as free text instead, it is not transferred to the register and indo is left blank. So it can in principle separate the same substance across indications, but it is often empty. Use vnr as the primary product key and indo as a supporting signal, not a

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: From dispensings to exposure time: DDD, PDC and MPR
sections.text: A dispensing is not the same as intake. eksd tells you the prescription was collected at the pharmacy, not that the patient took the drug, or for how long. For an exposure that lasts over time you need exposure windows built from the amount dispensed, not just a count of dispensings. That covers treatment episodes, grace periods (the gap allowed between two prescriptions before a person counts as having stopped) and adherence measures such as PDC (proportion of days covered: the share of follow-up time covered by medicine) and MPR (medication possession ratio: the amount dispensed divided by the length of the period). The LMDB columns for the amount are apk (number of packages), packsize (units per package) and strnum (the numeric strength; the unit is in strunit ). volume is the number of defined daily doses (DDD) per package (Pottegård et al. 2017, table of variables). The DDD is the WHO's "assumed average maintenance dose per day for a drug used for its main indication in adults", a unit of measurement and not necessarily the dose your patients were prescribed ([WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics

sections.title: Missing data
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis-ready dataset ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)) has missing values in covariates, exposure or outcome, before you fit the analysis model. It shows how to see where values are missing and how to run the two common approaches: complete-case analysis and multiple imputation with mice . When you are done you have either a complete-case dataset or a pooled estimate from imputed data. Register data almost always have missing values. Some are structural (a variable was not collected in all years) - that is not random, so think about why a value is missing before you handle it. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. naniar and mice must be installed in your R environment on DST. It shows how to run the methods, not when they are substantively defensible. Choosing between complete-case and imputation, and judging whether the missing mechanism allows either, is a methods question - read the theory elsewhere: Flexible Imputation of Missing Data : free online book by the mice author, Stef van Buuren. Sterne et al. (2009), BMJ: "Multiple imputation for missing data in epidemiological and clinical

sections.text: mice stands for Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations and is the most widely used R package for multiple imputation ([mice on CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mice)). sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: How does it find the values?
sections.text: For each variable with missing values, mice builds a regression model that predicts the variable from the other variables. A missing value is not filled in with a single "best guess", but with a random draw from the predicted distribution. That is why the 20 datasets differ. "Chained equations" describes how mice handles several variables with gaps at once: it takes them one at a time, imputes the first from the others, moves on to the next and now uses the just-filled first variable as well, and so on. It runs several rounds through (the chain) until the variables are imputed consistently from one another. Imputation affects both the estimate and the confidence interval . The estimate is the average across the 20 datasets. The confidence interval is built on Rubin's rules , the standard method for combining results from several imputed datasets ([Rubin 1987](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9780470316696)): it adds the spread between the datasets on top of the model's own uncertainty. The more the imputed values disagree from dataset to dataset, the larger that contribution, and the wider the confidence interval. That is exactly the point: if there is

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: When can you use it?
sections.text: Imputation makes most sense when a non-trivial share of the data is missing and complete-case would either be biased or waste too many rows. If complete-case is already unbiased (see the regression case below), the main gain from imputation is power, not correctness. mice rests on the MAR assumption ( missing at random ). MAR does not mean the gaps are pure chance. It means that the reason a value is missing lies in something you have measured, not in the missing value itself. Analogy: suppose older patients more often skip a question. As long as you have age recorded, this is no problem - within each age group, those missing the answer resemble those who answered, and mice can fill in from the observed ones. The gap is due to age (which you have), not the missing answer itself. The assumption cannot be tested in the data, only judged on substantive grounds. Missing covariates: the classic use. Here, include the outcome in the imputation model. It sounds backwards, but it is necessary: leave the outcome out and you pull the covariate-outcome association artificially toward null. Including the outcome adds no extra assumption, it simply respects the association you will

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: How much missing is okay?
sections.text: There is no real percentage threshold (5% / 10% / 40% are rules of thumb with no foundation). What matters is the mechanism and how well the missing values can be predicted from the rest. In practice: report how much is missing per variable (STROBE), treat results with very high missingness on a key variable as hypothesis-generating (a guide for randomised trials gives "more than 40%" as an example, Jakobsen et al. 2017, doi:10.1186/s12874-017-0442-1), and run complete-case and mice side by side as a sensitivity analysis. If they point the same way, you stand on firmer ground. The analysis models themselves are in Phase 13 - Analysis; fit them inside with(imp, ...) and pool as above. Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : Missing data

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.text: Use this page when you want to adjust for, or describe, mortality risk at baseline with one score. NMI (Nordic Multimorbidity Index) is a weighted score built from hospital diagnoses and filled prescriptions. It combines 50 mortality predictors, 29 diagnosis-based and 21 prescription-based, into a single continuous score. You need your cohort from [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd) ( pnr and index_date ), and you end with extract_nmi.rds : one score per person and index date. Article: Kristensen et al. Clinical Epidemiology 2022 - doi:10.2147/CLEP.S353398 Important: NMI is a mortality index, not a measure of comorbidity burden. NMI was developed and validated to predict 5-year mortality (Kristensen et al. 2022, \~425,000 Danish residents aged ≥40), and its predictors were selected for how much they added to the mortality model - not to cover disease burden. As a result: Several common chronic diseases are not included in the model (e.g. hypertension and type 1 diabetes). Some items are mortality proxies, not diseases in their own right (e.g. laxatives, iron). Some weights are negative (e.g. statins -3, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) -2), which only makes sense in

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: What NMI gives you
sections.text: A continuous mortality-risk score per person. It was developed and validated in Danish data to predict 5-year mortality, where it discriminated better than the Charlson and Elixhauser indices; the authors say it should still be validated in other Nordic countries (Kristensen et al. 2022, abstract). Use it as: A covariate: summarising mortality-associated illness in a Cox or logistic model. A summary variable: for mortality risk in Table 1.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: Leave out predictors that are your exposure or outcome
sections.text: Your own exposure or outcome should not be one of the score's predictors. The article advises avoiding items closely related to the exposure under study. In a dementia study, for example, drop the dementia predictors ( dx_F00_G319 and rx_N06D ), since dementia would otherwise be part of the score you adjust for. Say in your methods which predictors you dropped.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: R implementation
sections.text: There is no official R package; the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) publishes a Stata implementation. The R version below runs in two steps: extract, then compute. These code examples are based on Pernille Errebo Tonnesen's translation of the SDU Stata code to R. How far this has been checked, and how far it has not. Checked (30 August 2026): every one of the 50 indicators and all 50 weights below were compared against SDU's own online_nmi.do , character by character. All 29 diagnosis patterns and 21 ATC patterns match, the weights match (including the two negative ones, C09C/C09D at -2 and C10AA at -3), and both assessment windows match: 5 years before index for diagnoses, 6 months for drugs. Not checked: we have not run the two implementations on the same people and compared the resulting scores. Matching code is not the same as matching output. Differences can still arise upstream of the patterns - in which diagnosis sources you feed in, how dates are handled, and how the tables are joined. So this is a faithful transcription, not a validated implementation. If the score carries weight in your analysis rather than serving as a covariate among many, compare a sample

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.text: Use this page when diabetes is part of your study: as an exposure, an inclusion or exclusion criterion, or a covariate, and especially when you need to tell type 1 from type 2 diabetes, which diagnosis codes in LPR (the National Patient Register) alone do not do reliably. OSDC is an open source algorithm, published as the R package osdc , that classifies diabetes from diagnoses, prescriptions, podiatrist services and HbA1c results. You need access to five registers (listed below). You end with one row per person with diabetes, their type and the date they enter the diabetes population. Article: doi:10.2147/CLEP.S407019 Documentation and code: steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc The package README says that minor changes have been made to the algorithm since the validated version in the article, and that more are expected; the changes are listed in the repository.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: What OSDC gives you
sections.text: classify_diabetes() returns one row per person classified as having diabetes, with five columns. People without diabetes are not in the output: "no diabetes" means "not in the table". The inclusion events are HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more, a hospital diagnosis of diabetes, a diabetes-specific podiatrist service and a purchase of glucose-lowering drugs. The dates are inclusion dates, the date a person enters the diabetes population, not a date of disease onset, and there is no age at onset. Choosing between the two dates is a study decision. Before 1998 the register data may not be good enough to tell new (incident) cases from existing (prevalent) ones, so stable_inclusion_date is blank for inclusions before then. The 1998 default is one year after pregnancy data in LPR became usable for dropping purchases related to gestational diabetes. Filter on stable_inclusion_date and every case included before 1998 leaves your cohort without an error. Use raw_inclusion_date and you keep them, at the cost of dates the package's authors flag as uncertain. Decide which, and say which in your methods section. The cutoff is an argument, stable_inclusion_start_date , if your LPR and LMDB

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: Run osdc on your project
sections.text: osdc is on CRAN. Install it, then load it: install.packages() installs dependencies that are missing, but it does not update ones that are already installed; R's own help advises running update.packages() first. The pre-installed packages on DST may be old, so if library("osdc") stops with a version error, update the package it names. classify_diabetes() takes one argument per register ( lpr , hsr , lab_forsker , bef , lmdb ). Each must be a DuckDB table covering all the years you have, for example a connection to your parquet files. LPR must first be combined into one table, and so must the two health insurance registers, with join_registers() . The getting-started guide, steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc/articles/osdc.html, walks through this step by step. Is osdc available on your project? It is confirmed on DARTER (project 708421). It is likely available on other projects too, but this has not been verified. Check with "osdc" %in% rownames(available.packages()) on your own server (the package is not pre-installed, so available.packages() shows whether it can be installed). If it is missing, you can ask DST to install it.
sections.code: install.packages osdc

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: The registers osdc needs
sections.text: classify_diabetes() uses BEF, LPR, LMDB, the health insurance registers ( sysi / sssy ) and laboratory results, and needs all five: it has one argument for each ([osdc design vignette](https://steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc/articles/design.html)). Missing one of the five? Two different reasons, two different fixes: sysi / sssy : these are ordinary DST registers. If they are missing, your project has not requested them; ask for them to be added. Laboratory results: these are not a DST register. They come from the Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen) through a separate Forskerservice application, so they never appear in DST's own overview. See Laboratory results for the table names and how the data are reached. Not every purchase of a glucose-lowering drug (ATC A10 ) counts: All GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1) are dropped, because this drug class is used extensively for weight loss in people without diabetes. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, two SGLT-2 inhibitors (sodium-glucose co-transporter 2), are dropped when bought on their own, because Danish guidelines recommend them for heart and kidney failure in people without diabetes.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: The type is decided with data from after your index date
sections.text: Run on all years, the type classification uses information from after your index date. Type 1 versus type 2 is decided from the person's whole record: the share of diagnoses that are type 1, and insulin purchase patterns. A person's type can therefore depend on events that had not happened on your index date. If you use the type as a baseline variable, you classify people with information from the future (look-ahead misclassification). This applies to a pre-computed population too, since it is run on all years. To avoid it, run classify_diabetes() yourself on register data filtered to before your index date, so the classification only sees pre-index information. If you change the algorithm itself, for example to count GLP-1 receptor agonists, the published validation no longer applies.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: On DARTER: a pre-computed population
sections.text: On DARTER the OSDC classification is already computed, so you do not need to run the algorithm yourself unless the look-ahead problem above matters for your study. The path and the name osdc (and read_register("osdc") ) are DARTER-specific; on other projects the file is named differently and lives elsewhere. The 2024 population was generated, on the latest data, after the package was updated and released on CRAN. It is valid for inclusions until the end of 2024 and replaces the previous population file: use one or the other, never both. The previous files are kept for reproducibility. sections.title: Outcomes
sections.text: Use this page to extract the dates a time-to-event analysis needs: the date of the first outcome event after index, and the dates of death and emigration that end follow-up. It builds on Extract from LPR, which explains the diagnosis extraction and defines the helper used below. You finish with one small .rds file per date ( pnr plus one date column), ready to be linked onto the cohort in Phase 12. In a time-to-event study you follow each person from the index date until the outcome occurs, or until the outcome can no longer be observed. A person who dies or emigrates disappears from the Danish registers, and you cannot know whether they later developed the outcome. So you censor them on the death or emigration date. Follow-up then ends at the earliest of outcome, death, emigration and end of study. If a competing event (for example death) precludes your outcome rather than just ending follow-up, it is a competing risk. That is handled in the analysis, see Competing risks.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Extract the first outcome event after index
sections.text: The outcome is typically the first hospital diagnosis after index, taken from LPR (Landspatientregisteret, the Danish National Patient Register). read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. group_by(pnr) , arrange() and slice(1) keep only the first event per person, which is what most outcome definitions need. The pattern is explained in Long ↔ wide format. The join inside get_lpr_diagnoses() assembles one extract: it puts LPR's contact and diagnosis tables together so that pnr , date and diagnosis sit in one table. Linking the finished extract onto your cohort is a separate step that comes later, in Link your extracts, once all your extractions are done.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Death and emigration dates for censoring
sections.text: Extract the date of death from DOD (the register of deaths, column doddato ) and emigrations from VNDS (the migration register, rows with indud_kode == "U" ), each as its own table filtered to the cohort. The worked code for both, including keeping only the first emigration after index, is in Link your extracts; the column names are in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd). Follow-up time is then calculated from the outcome, death and emigration dates in [Calculate follow-up time and event variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time).

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Misclassification: a diagnosis code is a proxy
sections.text: A register diagnosis is a proxy for the real condition, with its own validity (sensitivity and positive predictive value, PPV). How wrong it is shapes your result: Non-differential misclassification: errors unrelated to exposure (the same code validity in both groups) usually bias the effect toward the null, so a real effect looks weaker than it is. Differential misclassification: the outcome is captured more completely in one group (for example, exposed people are in contact with the health system more often and so get diagnosed more). This can bias the estimate in either direction. What you can do about it: use validated code definitions where they exist, look up the PPV of your codes, and run a sensitivity analysis with a stricter or looser definition. For the validity of LPR diagnoses, start with the review by [Schmidt et al. 2015, Clinical Epidemiology ](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S91125) (the Danish National Patient Registry). Background on measurement bias: [Hernán & Robins, What If , chapter 9](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook).

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Where does your codelist come from?
sections.text: Applying a codelist (regex, %in% ) is the easy part. Deciding which codes make up your condition is the hard part. Use a published, ideally validated list where one exists, and document and share your own so others can reproduce it. ICD-10: for example mltc-codelists, ICD-10 codelists for many chronic conditions, with the accompanying methods paper ([Prigge et al. 2025, Communications Medicine ](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-025-00995-4)). ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes, for medication): define drug groups from the WHO ATC/DDD index and published drug-class definitions. See Medication (ATC).

sections.text: (GitHub only - local use only - github.com/sara-schwartz/fiktive) Fictitious register tables for practising and testing code locally without DST access. Not used on the server. sections.heading: fastreg - SAS → parquet (and reading registers back)
sections.text: (CRAN; install.packages("fastreg") - dp-next.github.io/fastreg) The recommended tool for converting SAS registers to parquet. It converts ( convert() , partitioned by year, with a use_template() targets pipeline for the whole workspace) and reads back ( read_register("bef") returns a lazy DuckDB connection, reading all yearly subfolders as one dataset). Set options(fastreg.project_rawdata_dir=, fastreg.project_workdata_dir=) once, then refer to registers by name. See [Parquet and fastreg - SAS → parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet). read_register() only finds registers in fastreg's own format ( <register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet ). For any other parquet the package has list_parquet_datasets() , read_parquet_dataset() and read_parquet_file() - see [When read_register() cannot find the register](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#when-read-register-fails).

Published in R Journal 2021. Output control: counts below DST's threshold (fewer than 5) must not be exported, and a suppressed cell must not be recoverable from totals or other cells. It rounds every count in the table, N included, so its "<5" does not sit next to an exact total. Exact numbers for the same people elsewhere (a flowchart, the text, another table) can still give it back - see A hidden number must not be possible to work out.

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.text: Everything about getting registers into parquet and reading them with fastreg , in the order most people need it: 1. Point fastreg at your registers - one options() call at the top of each script. Every read_register() example in this guide assumes you have done this. If a colleague already converted the registers, this is the only section you need. 2. Convert SAS files to Parquet - when your project received .sas7bdat and nothing has been converted yet. Done once per register, usually by one person for the whole project. 3. [When read_register() cannot find the register](#when-read-register-fails) - reading parquet that is not in fastreg's layout. 4. Several registers on one DuckDB connection - for heavy work across the whole population, where everything has to stay in the database until the result is small. Which file types you meet on the server, and what opens each one, is [Phase 4 - File types and loading](file-formats.qmd).

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: What is parquet, and why use it?
sections.text: Parquet is a file format built for exactly the kind of work this guide does: a large table, read many times, usually filtered down to a few columns and a cohort's worth of rows. Unlike SAS ( .sas7bdat ) or .rds , which store data row by row and load the whole file before you can use any of it, parquet lets you open a connection and read only what you actually ask for. Think of a supermarket. You can either buy the whole shop and sort through it at home, or send a shopping list and only have what is on the list delivered. A SAS or RDS file is buying the whole shop. Parquet is sending the list first filter() , select() - and only paying for delivery ( collect() ) once you know exactly what you want. That is why a filtered, cohort-sized extract from a register with tens of millions of rows can come back in seconds, without ever loading the whole register into RAM. See [Phase 4 - File types and loading](file-formats.qmd) for the mechanics behind this (lazy vs. full loading). This is why almost every register on DST is worth converting to parquet once the rest of this page shows how.

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Point fastreg at your registers
sections.text: If someone else already converted the registers, you do not convert anything. You tell fastreg where they are, once per script , and then read them by name. Ask whoever set the project up for the exact paths: After that, read_register("bef") works by name, with no conversion and no path in each call. Set it once, at the top of the script, next to the library() calls. Every read_register() example in this guide assumes it has been set, and none of them repeat it: two lines of someone else's project paths in every code block would be noise, and it would suggest the call belongs next to each read rather than once at the top. Two things that otherwise cost you time: Write E:/ with the colon : the DST server is Windows, also when you log in from a Mac. fastreg's own guide shows E without the colon, but only because the example writes to a temporary folder with fs::path_temp() . The folder does not have to be the innermost one : you can set the path to cleaned-data/ even though it holds several subfolders ( parquet-registers/ , parquet-external/ ). read_register() searches further down for the register name.

After that you use them exactly like any other register. Relevant for most projects outside DARTER. If you are working on a project where the registers have not already been converted to parquet, this step is necessary before you can run extractions. Done once per register - after that the normal extraction pattern applies.

sections.text: The recommended tool is the fastreg package (dp-next, on CRAN). It converts SAS registers to Parquet (partitioned by year) and lets you read them back by name . Use fastreg's own guide for the conversion code. The exact commands are documented - and kept up to date by the maintainers - in fastreg's [Getting started vignette](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/articles/fastreg.html). We link to the relevant section below instead of reproducing code that could drift out of date. sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: When read_register() cannot find the register
sections.text: This is the direct consequence of how the parquet was laid out, which is why it sits on the same page as the conversion. read_register() can only read registers that sit in fastreg's own format: That year= level is what produces the year column you filter on later. It is a partition marker, not a DST variable and not a date - see [Phase 4 - reading a register split by year](file-formats.qmd#year-column). Both halves count: the year= subfolder and the part- filename. This is not a bug but a deliberate choice. The function is built for data converted with fastreg's convert() , and is not meant to guess every way parquet files might otherwise be named. If the register is laid out differently - say as one flat folder of parquet files, or with filenames without part- - read_register() cannot see it, no matter how correctly you set the path. In that case you use one of fastreg's two other reading functions: All three hand you a DuckDB table (a lazy duckplyr data frame - its class() starts with "prudent_duckplyr_df" ), so the rest of your code is exactly the same whichever one you use. read_parquet_dataset() does not use your options() path. Only read_register()

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Several registers on one DuckDB connection
sections.text: read_register() is the right tool for most extractions in this guide: a cohort-sized filter, a few columns, collect() . Some steps are different. They work on the whole Danish population and join two large registers before anything can be reduced, for example the income cutpoints in [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income). For those, open the registers yourself as views on one plain DuckDB connection : Edit the paths to your own project. If a register sits in one flat folder with no year subfolders, use '.../faik/ .parquet' and leave out hive_partitioning . Why this, and not read_register() , for these steps: Nothing is computed in R behind your back. read_register() hands you a duckplyr table. duckplyr uses the same DuckDB engine, but when it cannot translate a step it falls back to computing that step in R's memory instead, with no warning. fastreg opens registers as "thrifty", so for a large table that fallback stops with a materialization error rather than running in the database; for a smaller one the data quietly ends up in RAM. A tbl() on a plain DBI connection uses dbplyr , which only ever sends SQL to DuckDB, and show_query()

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.text: Register-based research does not start in R. It starts with pen and paper. This page guides you through the things you should have in place before writing a single line of code. In short: Settle four things on paper before you code - a precise research question, your data model (which registers cover exposure, outcome and covariates), your covariates chosen with a DAG, and your comparison cohort.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: What type of study are you doing?
sections.text: Almost all register-based research is observational and analytical : you observe what has already happened, without intervening. Registers record the past, so you cannot randomise anyone. The two classic analytical designs are case-control and cohort ; Phase 10 shows how to build a matched cohort study. The two analytical designs differ in which end you start from : Cohort follows persons forward in time from the index date and measures how many develop the outcome - which is why you can compute incidence and risk. Well suited when you have multiple outcomes (cf. the all_dx approach in Extract from LPR). Case-control starts from those who already have the outcome and matches them with controls without it - efficient for rare outcomes, but cannot compute absolute risk. With register data you can do both, because the entire population's history is available. Phase 10 shows a matched cohort study step by step.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.text: Before planning a study it is worth knowing these terms - they are used throughout the guide. Cohort A group of people followed over time because they share a particular characteristic at a particular point in time. Example: all patients who underwent bariatric surgery in the period 2010--2020. Index date The start date of follow-up - the point from which you begin counting. For operated patients this is typically the date of surgery. For matched comparators the same date as the matched operated patient is assigned. Exposure The factor whose effect you are investigating - e.g. a surgery, a medication, or a diagnosis. Outcome What you are measuring - e.g. onset of a disease, a hospitalisation, or death. Covariates Variables you include to account for confounding - factors that affect both exposure and outcome. Examples: age, sex, comorbidity, socioeconomic status.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 1. What do I want to investigate?
sections.text: Formulate your research question precisely before looking at any data. A vague question produces a messy dataset. A precise question produces a clear plan. Ask yourself: Example study (illustration only). The examples on this page, and in many code examples across the guide, use one made-up study: does bariatric surgery change the risk of hip fracture ? It is not a real project. The choices in it are there to show the method, not as recommendations for your study. Make sure follow-up starts at the same moment eligibility and exposure are decided. When those drift apart you get [immortal time bias](dst-pitfalls.qmd#immortal-time-bias).

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 2. Which registers cover what?
sections.text: Before mapping your data model it is useful to know which registers exist. A complete description of all registers with column names and join keys is in Overview of registers →

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 3. Choose your covariates using a DAG
sections.text: Which variables should you adjust for? The answer is not "as many as possible". Adjusting for the wrong variables can introduce bias rather than remove it. A DAG (directed acyclic graph - a causal diagram) is a drawing of your assumptions about how exposure, outcome and other variables relate to each other. It makes your assumptions explicit and helps you choose the right set of covariates. Rules of thumb: Adjust for confounders: variables that affect both exposure and outcome (e.g. age, comorbidity). Do NOT adjust for mediators: variables that lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome (this removes part of the effect you want to measure). Do NOT adjust for colliders: common effects of two variables (this opens a spurious association). You do not have to work the rules out by hand. dagitty.net takes your drawing and returns the minimal adjustment set : the smallest group of variables that removes the confounding without opening a new bias through a collider. A concrete example: does bariatric surgery affect the risk of hip fracture ? !DAG of surgery → hip fracture with a confounder (age), a mediator (bone loss) and a collider (hospitalisation).{#fig-dag

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 4. The comparator cohort
sections.text: Many studies compare an exposed group with a comparator cohort . How you build it is a design decision to be made on paper - before writing code. At this stage you only need to settle four things: Who is an appropriate comparator? An active comparator (people with the same indication starting an alternative treatment - reduces confounding by indication), or a matched background population (maximal contrast). What decides the comparator's index date , since the exposure does not give them one. Which variables you match on, and at what ratio (e.g. age, sex and calendar year, 1:5). What happens if a comparator becomes exposed later. → Each of these, plus eligibility at index, the shared exclusions and the immortal-time trap, is worked through in [Phase 10 - Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd) and [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd).

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 5. Get an overview - pen and paper
sections.text: Before opening R, answer these questions in writing: 1. Which variables do I need? (patient information - age, sex, diagnoses etc. - and for which years) 2. Which registers contain this information? (LPR, BEF, LMDB, ...) 3. In what order should data be assembled? (define population → extract outcome → extract covariates) A solid overview on paper saves many hours of debugging in code.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 6. Write an analysis plan
sections.text: An analysis plan is a document you write before looking at your data. It forces you to commit to design, statistics and variables before results can colour your decisions. Use the STROBE checklist as a skeleton: [STROBE Statement - checklists →](https://www.strobe-statement.org/checklists/) For register-based studies, RECORD extends STROBE with items on routinely collected data, and RECORD-PE covers pharmacoepidemiology specifically: [RECORD-PE (EQUATOR Network) →](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/record-pe/) Pre-register your analysis plan on e.g. OSF - this is good scientific practice and required by many journals: [Open Science Framework - registration templates](https://help.osf.io/article/330-welcome-to-registrations) Power and sample size. Even large registers have limited power (the ability to detect an effect that is really there) for rare outcomes or small subgroups. Already in the plan, consider the smallest effect you could meaningfully detect with your expected number of events. The pwr package does simple power/sample-size calculations; for survival and rate designs it is often the number of events (not the number of people) that

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.text: You do not need to learn R from scratch. This phase gives you the minimum you need in order not to feel lost when you meet the extraction code later in the guide. Data structures and commands for exploratory analysis come in Phases 7 and 11 - they make no sense until you have data to look at.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: Download R and RStudio
sections.text: Both are already installed on the DST server, so you do not have to do anything here. If you want to practise locally first, install R and then [RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/), both free. If you want to learn R properly alongside this guide, the courses and books are in [Learning resources](learning-resources.qmd).

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: RStudio for the first time
sections.text: RStudio is divided into four panels: !RStudio's four panels{fig-alt="RStudio interface with four panels"} Source: Wikipedia / RStudio, CC BY-SA 4.0 Top left - Script editor This is where you write and save your code. You can have multiple scripts open at once and switch between them using the tabs at the top of the panel. Remember to save changes regularly - Ctrl+S (Windows) / CMD+S (Mac). Top right - Environment / History / Connections Environment: shows all objects you have created in the current R session - data frames, vectors, lists. Functions from packages (e.g. filter() from dplyr) are not shown here; only what you have created yourself. It also shows how much memory each object takes, which matters on a shared server - see [Seeing your memory use from inside R](good-coding-practice.qmd#see-ram-in-r). History: a log of all commands you have run in the console. Bottom left - Console Code is executed here and output and error messages are shown here. You can type commands directly in the console - but they are not saved. All work you want to keep must be in a script. Bottom right - Files / Plots / Packages / Help Files: a file browser for your folders and files on

[]{#what-is-an-object} What is an object? x <- 5 creates an object . The arrow <- means "store what is on the right under the name on the left". From now on x stands for the value 5 - until you overwrite it yourself. The pattern is always the same: You name something so you can reuse it later without writing it out again. Almost everything in R is an object: a single number, an entire table, a model. When you fetch (part of) a register with collect() , for example, you typically store it in an object so you can keep working with it: The objects you create appear in the Environment panel in the top right of RStudio.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: What is a function? A package? What does library() do?
sections.text: A function is a command that performs an action. filter(data, age > 50) is a function. sum(c(1, 2, 3)) is a function. You recognise functions by their parentheses. What is inside the parentheses? The parentheses are always there - but they are not always filled. It depends on whether the function needs input to know what to do: filter(age > 50) - requires you to specify the condition; otherwise it does not know what to filter on open_dataset("E:/workdata/...") - requires the path; otherwise it does not know what to open collect() - requires nothing ; it already knows what to fetch, because it is the pipe that has sent data forward to it Rule of thumb: in a pipe , empty parentheses usually mean the function acts on what has been passed forward via the pipe , without needing anything extra from you. Outside a pipe, empty parentheses just mean the function needs no input, e.g. getwd() , Sys.Date() or gc() . A package is a collection of functions written by others that you can load. R comes with base functions, but most of what we use is in packages such as dplyr and arrow . library() loads a package so its functions are available in your session. You will see
sections.code: install.packages dplyr install package once after server reset load start each session

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: 6 functions and symbols you'll meet throughout the guide
sections.text: You will see these in almost every extraction. You do not need to understand them in detail now - just recognise them. A symbol you will see everywhere is %>% (the pipe). It passes the result from one line forward as input to the next. df %>% filter(age > 50) means: "take df , and pass it to filter() ". This makes it possible to chain steps together and read code from top to bottom. The pipe %>% is explained in detail in [Functions: overview](function-guide.qmd#the-pipe), and collect() in [Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd).

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.text: Use this page when you want an adjusted incidence rate ratio from your cohort: Poisson regression with person-time, when to choose it over Cox, its assumptions, and where to go when the rate changes with age or calendar time. You start from the analysis-ready dataset with event status and follow-up time (Phase 12), and you end with rate ratios ready for a results table. A rate is the number of events divided by the time people were at risk ( person-time ). An incidence rate ratio (IRR) compares the rate in two groups: if the rate is twice as high among the exposed, the IRR is 2. Rates fit register data well, because registers follow people over time and count events. In Descriptive tables you computed a crude rate per group. A Poisson regression gives an IRR that is adjusted for confounding (age, sex, other covariates), the same way logistic regression gives an adjusted odds ratio. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. survival , gtsummary and MASS must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Poisson, Cox or logistic regression: which to choose
sections.text: Three models can be used on a "did the event happen?" outcome. The difference is whether time enters, and how : Logistic regression (Regression) only looks at yes/no and ignores time. Gives an odds ratio . Fits when everyone is followed equally long, or when time is irrelevant. Cox regression (Time-to-event) looks at the time until the first event per person and gives a hazard ratio . It models the rate without assuming a particular shape over time. Poisson regression (this page) looks at the number of events per person-time and gives a rate ratio (IRR) . It is strong when you want to work with rates across age groups or calendar periods , or when you have counted-up events and person-time rather than one time-to-event per person. Cox or Poisson? They often answer almost the same question, and HR and IRR agree closely when the Poisson model lets the baseline rate vary over follow-up (follow-up split into time bands, see below); with a single constant rate they can differ if the hazard changes over time. Choose Cox if you think in individual follow-up time and time-to-first-event. Choose Poisson if you think in rates per person-year split by age/calendar time

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: You need two things per person, exactly as for [the crude rate](descriptive-tables.qmd#crude-rate): the number of events ( outcome , here 0 or 1) and the person-time ( followup_years , follow-up time in years). Both are built in Phase 12.
sections.code: dplyr pipe gtsummary tbl_regression tidy output readrds path analysis.rds analysis ready dataset one row per person index matched replacement

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Poisson regression: rate ratio (IRR)
sections.text: The model is a glm with family = poisson . The new part, compared with logistic regression, is the offset : it tells the model how long each person was at risk , so it models the rate (events per time) and not just the number of events. family = poisson makes it a rate model. offset(log(followup_years)) is the person-time. It must be logged ( log() ), because the Poisson model works on the log scale. Without the offset you model the number of events, not the rate - and that is almost never what you want. Zero follow-up gives log(0) = -Inf , which is why the Phase 12 recipe drops people with no follow-up. exponentiate = TRUE shows rate ratios (IRR) instead of log-rate coefficients. An IRR reads exactly like an OR or HR: 1 = no difference , above 1 = higher rate, below 1 = lower. See [Reading your result](regression.qmd#read-the-output). Here outcome is 0/1 (one row per person), and the offset is the person's total follow-up time. That gives a valid IRR adjusted for the covariates you have at baseline (at study start/index) - not one that changes as people age. For that, see Rates that vary over time below.
sections.code: model glm outcome exposure age sex event count explained covariates offset log followup_years person time turns counts into rate needs see phase family poisson rate send table tbl_regression exponentiate ratios irr

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.text: The Poisson model rests on a few assumptions. If they fail, the confidence intervals in particular become misleading: Constant rate within each "band". The model assumes the rate is the same throughout the person-time a group contributes. If the rate changes strongly with e.g. age, you satisfy the assumption by splitting the person-time into age groups (see below), so the rate only has to be constant within each narrow band. Events are Poisson-distributed (mean = variance). If the variance is larger than the mean ( overdispersion ), the standard errors become too small and the confidence intervals artificially narrow. This is common in register data - see the fold-out below. Independent observations. One row (or one cluster of person-time) per person. If the same person appears several times (e.g. matched with replacement or recurrent events), use cluster-robust standard errors as in Regression. Log-linearity. Continuous variables are related to the log rate in a straight line. Check as for logistic regression, e.g. with splines. Overdispersion means the events vary more than a pure Poisson distribution allows. The consequence is confidence intervals that are too narrow.
sections.code: mass glm.nb negative binomial regression df_agg one row per group outcome number events followup_years person years model_agg glm exposure age sex offset log family poisson sum residuals type pearson df.residual about fine well above overdispersion negative like poisson but extra parameter allows tbl_regression exponentiate irr confidence intervals account

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Rates that vary over time
sections.text: The model above assumes one rate throughout the person's follow-up. But in a register study the person ages along the way, and the calendar year changes - and the rate of e.g. cancer or death changes strongly with both. If you want the rate to vary with attained age or calendar period , the follow-up time must be split into intervals : one row per person per interval, so each row sits in one age band and one calendar year. You then count up events and person-time and fit the same Poisson model with age and period bands as covariates. This is a standard move in register epidemiology, but it needs a bit more machinery than this page covers. Use survival::survSplit() or Epi::splitLexis() (Lexis objects), or the popEpi package, which is built for exactly rates, person-time and standardisation on register data. See [Read more](#read-more). SMR and SIR. If you want to compare your population's rate with a reference population (e.g. the rates for all of Denmark from Statistics Denmark), you use indirect standardisation : the standardized mortality/incidence ratio (SMR/SIR) is observed events divided by those you would expect from the reference rates. sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.text: A starting point, not an authority. This page can be out of date or simply wrong, and your own delivery may differ from it. Verify against your files with colnames() (see Phase 7 - Inspect your data) before you rely on anything here. Found a mistake? [Open an issue](https://github.com/steno-aarhus/registers-guide/issues) or use the feedback box at the bottom - corrections are genuinely welcome. The tables on this page are generated from a schema built out of DST's published documentation: the [variable list](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html) for each register and DST's [order list](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Bestillingsliste.xlsx), which names every variable in every DST register with its period. The health registers - LPR, LMDB, the death registers, the cancer register - are documented by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen on esundhed.dk instead, which is also the only source that publishes data types. Each register links to its own source, and every value set says underneath where its codes come from. Those sources change. Registers are extended, columns are added and retired, and a code can change meaning without

sections.text: This page shows the columns most studies use. When you need more than that, the question you are asking decides where to go: All of it hangs off [Dokumentation af data →](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/generelt-om-data/dokumentation-af-data), DST's own hub, if you would rather start there. sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Overview - all registers
sections.text: The Often used column is the handful of columns most studies reach for, not the full list: follow the register link for every column DST documents, or the section below for the ones this guide explains. lab_dm_forsker is in the schema but not in this table, because it is reached through Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's Forskerservice rather than DST.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: BEF - Population Register
sections.text: Status register - one snapshot per person per reference time point. Delivered quarterly since 2008 (March, June, September, December); before 2008 December only. Whether year == 2020 corresponds to a particular reference time point depends on the project convention - confirm in your project guide. A person is in a file only if they were alive and living in Denmark on that file's reference date, so someone who dies after that date is still in the file - use DOD to determine whether a person was alive on a specific date. BEF cannot on its own answer whether a person was resident in Denmark on a given date: between two snapshots people can both leave and come back. To decide residence on an index date, combine BEF with VNDS - see [Phase 10 - the source population](build-study-population.qmd#step-1). BEF does not contain date of death. Use DOD ( doddato ) for censoring, not DODSAARS, which stops in 2001 (see below). DST's own documentation: [statistikdokumentation/befolkningen →](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/befolkningen).

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: DOD - Death Register
sections.text: Døde i Danmark. One row per deceased person, covering 1970-2025 and still updated ([DST register overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html), last reference date 31 December 2025). This is the register you use to censor at death. It is a short one: DOD is sometimes delivered only as a raw SAS file, in which case read_register("dod") will not find it and you read it with haven::read_sas() instead. Ask your data manager for the path. And check the span of your own delivery, which is the years your project ordered rather than everything DST holds:
sections.code: dod summarise min doddato max collect

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: DODSAARS - Cause of Death Register (ends 2001)
sections.text: Dødsårssagsregistret. One row per deceased person, with the cause of death. It carries a death date too, in d_dodsdto , which is why it is so often used for censoring - but its coverage stops on 31 December 2001 . Use it for causes of death up to 2001, and use DOD for the date. Censoring on dodsaars silently treats everyone who died after 2001 as alive. No error, no warning: they simply stay in your risk set to the end of follow-up, so survival looks better than it is and rates come out too low. The full version of this is [pitfall 1 - four death registers](dst-pitfalls.qmd#death-registers). #### DODSAASG - the 2002-2022 link in the chain Coding of the underlying cause changed again in 2007, mid-register. Until then, trained coders at the National Board of Health interpreted each death certificate. From 2007, certificates are submitted electronically and it is the certifying doctor who assigns the ICD-10 code directly, with no central review of that classification afterwards. dodsaasg covers both halves of this change (2002-2022) with nothing in the data to tell them apart. See Helweg-Larsen 2011, [The Danish Register of Causes of

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: VNDS - Migration Register
sections.text: One row per migration event per person. VNDS was closed in February 2026 and split into three registers ( VNDS_ind , VNDS_ud , VNDS_hist , described below). It is still documented here because it is the only migration register many projects have: a delivery made before the split will not contain the replacements. Check colnames() or your project's register list to see which you have. If you have both, use the new ones and do not mix them with VNDS , or you will count the same migration twice. For emigration dates used in censoring, combine VNDS_ud (2005+) and VNDS_hist (1973-2004) in place of the old VNDS . VNDS_ind : immigrations to Denmark from 2005 onwards. VNDS_ud : emigrations from Denmark from 2005 onwards. VNDS_hist : historical migrations 1973-2004, no longer updated. The split reduces duplicates that arose because immigration and emigration data came from different sources over the years. The earliest data is now frozen in the historical register. Source: [DST notice, 19 February 2026](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2026/VNDS). Use: filter(indud_kode == "U") → min(haend_dato) per pnr for first emigration date.

sections.heading: 2. LPR2 - Somatic (up to March 2019)
sections.text: The register itself is owned by the Danish Health Data Authority, whose documentation covers what is reported and how it changed over time: Landspatientregisteret →. Join: lpr_adm LEFT JOIN lpr_diag ON recnum .

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 3. LPR2 - Psychiatric (1995 -- March 2019)
sections.text: Psychiatric contacts before March 2019 are in separate registers from somatic LPR2. From March 2019, LPR3 covers both in one table. []{#psyk-before-1995} The Danish Psychiatric Central Register is electronic from 1969, but covers only inpatients until 1995 (outpatient visits were added from 1995), and diagnoses before 1994 are coded in ICD-8 (numeric codes, e.g. 290-315, where 290 covers dementia) - not ICD-10 F-codes. These older data are normally not part of the standard extract and are requested separately, via Rigsarkivet or [NCRR, Aarhus University](https://ncrr.au.dk/danish-registers/the-danish-psychiatric-central-research-register). If your study covers that period, you have to map ICD-8 to your F-code groups yourself. If you forget to query the psychiatric registers for the period 1995--2019, you miss all dementia diagnoses (F00--F03) recorded at geriatric psychiatry outpatient clinics and memory clinics. Those patients will appear dementia-free and remain in the cohort as false negatives.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 4. LPR3 (March 2019 and onwards)
sections.text: Before you join these two tables: lpr_a_kontakt / lpr_a_diagnose are not pure LPR3. They also hold LPR1, LPR2 and MiniPAS (records from private hospitals) rows, tagged by lprindberetningssystem , going back to around 2017. Filter both tables on lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" first, or you will double-count contacts already in lpr_adm . See Understand LPR for why, and Extract from LPR for open problems with that filter. LPR3 covers both somatic and psychiatric contacts in one table. Join: lpr_a_kontakt LEFT JOIN lpr_a_diagnose ON dw_ek_kontakt . The "a" in lpr_a_diagnose does not mean A-type diagnoses. DST describes the LPR_A tables, released in June 2025, as an "LPR analyse model" ([Nyt om grunddata, 2nd quarter 2025](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2025/nyt-om-grunddata-2-kvartal-2025)). The table contains all types: A (main) and B (secondary), plus add-on codes (G, grundmorbus, is LPR2 only), so you still need to filter on diag_kode_type .

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 5. LPR - SKS procedure codes
sections.text: SKS (Sundhedsvæsenets Klassifikations System - the Danish Health Classification System) is the Danish classification system for operations and procedures - equivalent to the NOMESCO codes used in the other Nordic countries. Bariatric surgery has e.g. codes KJDF10 (RYGB) and KJDF40 (sleeve gastrectomy). Look up codes in the SKS browser → (in Danish). SKS codes are split across two registers depending on period. For full coverage both must be queried and the results bound together. Neither procedure table holds pnr . It is fetched by joining to lpr_adm (LPR2) or lpr_a_kontakt (LPR3).

sections.text: The LPR3 procedure table. It sits alongside lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose , and joins to contacts on dw_ek_kontakt exactly like the diagnosis table does. Column names confirmed against [DST's variable list →](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/LPR_A_PROCREGISTRERING%20-%20Landspatientregisteret%20%28LPR3%29%20-%20Oplysninger%20om%20procedureregistreringer.html). There is no pnr here , as in every LPR procedure table: it identifies procedures, not people. Join to lpr_a_kontakt to get one. A few rows have no contact to join to, and DST flags them for you in flag_proc_uden_kont . Count them before you drop them.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: MFR - Medical Birth Register
sections.text: One row per birth, carrying both mother and child. The mother appears once per birth, so a mother of three has three rows; the register is keyed on the child through cpr_barn . Three eras, three different data models, not one register with minor revisions. 1973-1996 was paper form reports; not an "MFR" table, but not undocumented either - DST's own ftbarn / ftforael / ftnaevn ("Fertilitet - børn/forælder/Nævner") datasets cover 1973-2025 and explicitly incorporate MFR content ( ftbarn 's weight/length columns are documented as matching MFR, alongside its own MFR_OPLYSNING column). These are demography datasets (parity, birth spacing, fertility-rate denominators), not a clinical birth-event table - see below. 1997-2018 is the wide DST table below ( mfr ), marked closed by DST with no successor named on DST's own overview - because the successor is delivered by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's Forskerservice , not DST, the same pattern as lpr_a_kontakt . Nineteen of mfr 's own columns are flags backed by their own separate DST datasets, plus a full stillbirth detail table - see [MFR marker sub-cuts](#mfr-markers) and MFRDFOED below. From 2019 onwards the register was fully

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: FTBARN / FTFORAEL / FTNAEVN - the pre-1997 period
sections.text: Three separate DST datasets, not one register split three ways: ftbarn (one row per child), ftforael (one row per parent-child link, up to two per child), and ftnaevn (one row per person per year - the fertility-rate denominator , not a birth-event table at all). All three cover 1973-2025, so they overlap with mfr and mfr_nyfoedte in time; use them for the years those two do not reach, 1973-1996. DST's own variable-list pages for these three give a short Danish label for some columns and none at all for others - no value/code definitions anywhere. Unlike mfr_nyfoedte , there is no code_system on any coded column here ( KOEN , LEVENDE_ELLER_DOEDFOEDT , CPRTYPE , MOR_FAR , and more): inventing a lookup neither DST nor any other source confirms would be actively misleading. Confirm actual values with count() / table() on real data before writing code that filters or recodes on any of them. ftforael 's four parity/spacing variants ( DEMOGRAFISK_ / ENKELT_ / FAMILIE_ / MEDICINSK_PARITET , and the matching _SPACING columns) are not further defined by DST relative to each other or to the simpler PARITET column - see ftforael.yaml 's reader_note before picking one

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: MFRHJMFO - home births, 1997-2018
sections.text: Supplementary clinical detail for the home-birth subset of mfr , joined via FK_MFR - not a separate population: mfr already includes home births, flagged via its own FOEDESTED and MARKOER_HJEMMEFOEDSEL_BEREGNET columns. This is the DST-native counterpart to a data-management convention of splitting the 1997-2018 era into "home" and "not-home" deliveries. DST's page gives no Danish label at all for any column here , not even the partial labelling ftbarn / ftforael / ftnaevn have - the thinnest documentation of any register in this schema. Every reader_note on this register's columns is an informed guess from the variable name alone (Danish administrative/clinical vocabulary), not a sourced fact.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Nyfoedte - Medical Birth Register, 2019 onwards
sections.text: The current MFR. One row per newborn, live-born or stillborn, in one table (for 1997-2018 DST delivers two datasets, see MFRDFOED ). Join Barn_ satellite tables via DW_EK_Nyfoedt , Mor_ satellite tables via DW_EK_Foedsel (see the ten satellite tables below). Nyfoedte itself already carries a curated subset of medical facts (diagnosis, weight, Apgar score, smoking status) that Sundhedsdatastyrelsen resolves from the underlying LPR3 contacts. Numeric fields use -1 as "not stated", not NA . Vaegt_Barn , Laengde_Barn , Hovedomfang , Abdominalomfang , Placentavaegt , Paritet , Apgarscore and BMI_Mor (as -1.0 ) all use this sentinel. A mean computed without recoding it first will be pulled sharply downward. Every stillbirth also gets Apgarscore = 0 by definition, not -1 - filter on LevendefoedtDoedfoedt before summarising Apgar scores. Mother's smoking status ( Tobaksforbrug ) uses two SKS code families for the same nine categories. DUT before the LPR3 cutover (Feb/March 2019), RGAB from it onwards - DUT20 and RGAB20 mean the same thing. See tobaksforbrug.yaml for the full mapping (resolved via the sksr package, since Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's own

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: MFR marker sub-cuts - the detail behind the flags
sections.text: Nineteen of mfr 's own MARKOER_ columns above are flags only - the actual SKS-coded finding behind each one is published as its own separate DST dataset, joined back to mfr via FK_MFR . Confirmed against DST's full 531-register order list (Bestillingsliste.xlsx) on 2026-09-12, the same "home births" relationship MFRHJMFO already has to mfr (see above). DST publishes no labels or value definitions for any column in any of these 19 datasets. Two carry a genuine extra measurement alongside the SKS code ( MFRBLODM 's measured blood-loss amount, MFRNVLAN 's pH/base excess); the rest are three columns wide: the SKS code, its type, and the foreign key back to mfr . Every row joins to mfr via FK_MFR . Full column-by-column detail for each is in the schema ( schema/registers/mfraccre.yaml etc.) and searchable on Find a variable; it is not repeated here as 19 near-identical three-column tables.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: MFRDFOED - stillbirth detail, 1997-2018
sections.text: For 1997-2018 DST delivers two datasets from the Medical Birth Register: mfr , which DST titles "Levendefødte fra det medicinske fødselsregister" (live births), and mfrdfoed , titled "Dødsfødsler fra det medicinske fødselsregister" (stillbirths) ([DST's register overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html)). Both have a column LEVENDE_ELLER_DOEDFOEDT , for which DST gives no values, and mfrdfoed has the key FK_MFR , same as the marker sub-cuts above. DST's documentation does not say whether stillborn children also have rows in mfr , or whether every row in mfrdfoed has a matching row in mfr . Check both in your own delivery before you count births. DST gives no label or value definition for any column here , the same thinness as MFRHJMFO . Do not confuse this with LPRMFRDF ("Dødfødte ud fra LPR"), a separate DST register deriving stillbirth data from LPR rather than MFR - not modelled in this schema.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: The Cancer Register
sections.text: The gold standard for incident cancer diagnoses - more complete and precise for cancer than LPR diagnoses. Running since 1943, which makes it one of the longest continuous cancer registries anywhere. Use it for cancer as an outcome or an exclusion. It is not a DST register. The Cancer Register is held by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen and does not appear in DST's register list at all: a project reaches it through Forskerservice, on a separate application. The person key is k_cprnr , not pnr , so rename before joining. One row per tumour, not per person. Somebody with two primary cancers has two rows, distinguished by k_tumornr . Deduplicating on the person alone collapses second primaries and undercounts incidence.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Primary sector - sysi and sssy (Health Insurance Register)
sections.text: Contacts and services in the primary sector (general practice, practising specialists, physiotherapy etc.). As with LPR, the register is split over time: sysi covers the older years, sssy the newer. Join via pnr . Use it for e.g. GP/specialist contacts, screening or vaccinations billed in primary care. Key fields are named the same in both, but the two registers do not carry an identical column set, so verify with colnames() . They overlap in 2005: both report that year, so reading both without picking a source double-counts it. No validation studies of this register have ever been published. Coverage is assumed to be high because registration is tied to the provider's reimbursement, but that is an inference, not a measured validity, and sysi/sssy record almost no clinical information to begin with. Treat diagnoses and reasons for contact with more caution than in registers that do have published validation studies. See Sahl Andersen et al. 2011, [The Danish National Health Service Register](https://doi.org/10.1177/1403494810394718), Scand J Public Health 39(Suppl 7):34-37. sysi (1990-2005): sssy (2005-2025):

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Laboratory results - Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel
sections.text: Laboratory and blood test results: HbA1c, lipids, creatinine. A very large register , so filter with arrow or duckplyr before you collect() into R. It is not a DST register. This is Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel (LAB_F), held by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen and reached through Forskerservice. It is not in DST's register list. The exact table name can still differ by project: lab_forsker and laboratorieproevesvar are narrower cuts of the same delivery as lab_dm_forsker (fewer columns, some renamed - see the reader notes on the columns below for the exact differences), not separate registers. In the clinical epidemiology literature it is usually called RLRR, Register of Laboratory Results for Research (see e.g. [Arendt et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S245060), Clinical Epidemiology 12:469-475). The columns are named in English: patient_cpr , analysiscode , samplingdate , value , unit . NPU is the coding system used in analysiscode , not a column name. sections.heading: Healthcare costs (under development)
sections.text: Under development - confirm everything in your own delivery. This section describes cost sources at the register level. Exact table and column names and the available years change from year to year (the DRG rate system is updated annually) and are not verified here. Use it as a pointer, and clarify the specific files with your data manager. To compute healthcare use/costs per person, they are typically assembled from several sources: Somatic hospital contacts: DRG-grouped rates from the Danish Health Data Authority (DRG = inpatient, DAG = outpatient). Rates express average operating expenses per DRG group and are computed annually - see [SDS DRG rates](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/sundhedsoekonomi/drg/drg-takster). Psychiatric hospital contacts: are not billed by DRG. The main principle is a bed-day rate for inpatients and a visit rate for outpatients - keep somatic and psychiatric separate. Primary sector (general practice, specialists etc.): fees in sysi / sssy (see the section above). Medication: patient co-payment vs. reimbursement in LMDB (section 7). Availability of cost data varies (some years/sources are missing, e.g. more recent DRG

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 7. LMDB - Prescription Register
sections.text: Owned by the Danish Health Data Authority as the Prescription Register: Lægemiddelstatistikregisteret →. One row per dispensed prescription. Covers 1995 onwards: data were also collected in 1994 but are not made available to researchers. Over-the-counter medicine and medicine given during a hospital admission are not in it (Pottegård et al. 2017). pnr , eksd , ekst , atc , atc1 , atc2 , atc3 , atc4 , indo , vnr , apk , aldr , bald , eksp , korr , rinr , name , streng , packtext , volume , voltypecode , voltypetxt , dosform , strnum , strunit , packsize , cprtjek , cprtype , year , etid , ovnr , patt , doso , reca , abc Filtering on atc2 fails silently. The level columns are shorter than the full code: atc2 holds three characters, so grepl("N02A", atc2) matches nothing and returns zero rows without an error. Filter on atc and keep the level columns for grouping. Details, and a check you can run on your own extract, are in Medication (ATC). indo (indication code) is recorded only when the doctor picks an indication from the drop-down menu in the electronic prescription; typed as free text, it is not carried over.
