sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 8. Socioeconomic registers
sections.text: All three registers are used for SEP extraction following SEPLINE guidelines (Hjorth et al. 2025). No single combined SEP variable is calculated - three separate dimensions.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: UDDA - Education Register
sections.text: One record per person per year - updated when the education level changes. This is the single easiest mistake to make with UDDA, and it produces wrong numbers without any error message. There are two different code systems , and they look confusingly alike: hfaudd is an identifier , not a scale. The first two digits are simply the start of a serial number, and there is no arithmetic relationship between the two systems. Taking substr(hfaudd, 1, 2) and treating it as the level is wrong, and it fails in both directions: hfaudd = 4272 is an electrician - vocational, level 30. Reading 42 and comparing it to 40 makes it a long higher education . hfaudd = 0141 is genuinely level 40, short cycle higher education . Reading 01 (or 14 , if the column is numeric and the leading zero is gone) matches no level at all, so a real education becomes missing data . UDDA does not contain the level. DST's education register holds only HFAUDD , HF_KILDE , HF_VFRA , HF_VTIL and INSTNR - there is no level column to read. The level has to come from a lookup table that maps each education code to its level. See [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#education) for

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: FAIK - Family Income
sections.text: Household-equivalised disposable income per year. Link: join BEF ( pnr , familie_id , year ) with FAIK ( familie_id , year ). The structure can differ from DST's documentation. DST documents FAIK with no pnr , but in the DARTER delivery FAIK from 2022 onward also carries pnr , and the family's row is repeated once per family member instead of appearing once. Joining on familie_id alone then multiplies your rows silently. Check your own delivery before you rely on the join - how, and what to do about it, is in [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income). SEPLINE classifies income as a 3-year mean against quintile cutpoints from the whole population with the same sex and 5-year age group, per year: Low, Medium or High. The recipe is in [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income).

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: AKM - Labour Classification Module
sections.text: Labour market status per person per year. SEPLINE's main groups for socio13 (Table 6, with the corrigendum): A: Working: 110-114, 120, 131-135, 139, and students (310) B: Unemployed: 210, 410 C: Outside workforce: 220, 321, 330 D: Retired: 322, 323 Missing/other: 0, 420 (children under 15), or no record The recipe, with the subgroups, is in [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#employment).

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 9. Project-specific registers
sections.text: Many projects have access to registers beyond the standard list above - e.g. quality registers from clinical databases or pre-computed classification files. These are project-specific and not available in all projects on DST. Examples are private hospitals ( priv_adm , priv_diag , priv_skspor - structured in parallel with LPR) and various clinical quality registers. Availability varies from project to project. The project uses among others DBSO (the Danish Obesity Treatment Database) and OSDC (Open Source Diabetes Classifier). All applied-for variables and registers in a searchable table: [steno-aarhus.github.io/darter-project →](https://steno-aarhus.github.io/darter-project/) Confirmed paths and column names: [DARTER - Register paths and datastores →](darter-register-paths-datastores.qmd)

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Data resource profiles and reporting
sections.text: Data resource profiles are the papers you cite when you describe a register in your methods section: they document the register's content, coverage and validity. Cite the profile for each register you use. Reporting: report observational studies following STROBE. For register-based / routinely-collected-data studies, RECORD extends STROBE, and RECORD-PE covers pharmacoepidemiology specifically - see [RECORD-PE (EQUATOR Network)](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/record-pe/).

sections.title: Regression
sections.text: Use this page when you have the analysis-ready dataset ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)) and want an adjusted estimate for an outcome without follow-up time: logistic regression for a binary outcome, linear regression for a continuous one, and conditional logistic regression for a matched case-control study. It also covers interaction, splines, how to read the output, and robust standard errors when the same person is in the data more than once. If your outcome is time to an event, go to Time-to-event or Rates and rate ratios (Poisson) instead. Regression relates an outcome to one or more explanatory variables (your exposure plus covariates), and is how you adjust for confounding in the analysis. The outcome is also called the dependent variable and the explanatory variables the independent ones. Explanatory variables can be continuous (e.g. age) or categorical (e.g. sex). Linear regression ( lm ): when the outcome is continuous (e.g. BMI or blood pressure). Gives differences in means. Logistic regression ( glm with family = binomial ): when the outcome is binary (yes/no, e.g. whether a person got a diagnosis). Gives odds ratios . Conditional logistic regression (

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Logistic regression (binary outcome)
sections.text: family = binomial makes it logistic regression. exponentiate = TRUE shows odds ratios (OR) instead of log-odds coefficients. Assumptions: the observations are independent (one row per person - otherwise use robust standard errors, see below), and continuous variables are linearly related to the log-odds . If linearity does not hold, you can let the variable enter as a smooth curve instead of a straight line - see Non-linear relationships (splines) below. Logistic regression ignores time. In a cohort where people are followed for different lengths of time, or are censored by death or emigration before they could have the outcome, use Cox or Poisson regression instead.

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Linear regression (continuous outcome)
sections.text: Assumptions: a linear relationship, constant variance (homoscedasticity), roughly normal residuals and independent observations. Save the model to a variable and check with plot(model) , which gives the classic residual plots; if they look skewed, a transformation of the outcome or a different model may be needed.

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Matched case-control: conditional logistic regression
sections.text: When you have matched in a nested case-control design (Case-control), the analysis must respect the matching with conditional logistic regression. Use clogit() with a strata() term for the matched set. strata(match_id) tells the model which rows belong to the same matched set ( case.id from incidenceMatch() or Set from Epi::ccwc() ). case = 1 for a case, 0 for a control. What the odds ratio estimates depends on how the controls were sampled. With risk-set (incidence-density) sampling, where each case's controls are drawn from those still at risk on the case's date, the matched odds ratio estimates the incidence rate ratio (hazard ratio), and no rare-disease assumption is needed (Greenland & Thomas 1982, doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a113439). Report it as an odds ratio, but interpret it as a rate ratio. Assumptions: as for logistic regression (continuous variables linear with the log-odds; the matched sets independent of one another). The matching itself is handled by strata() .
sections.code: survival clogit case exposure age sex strata match_id matched set control dataset case page tbl_regression exponentiate odds ratios

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Interaction (effect modification)
sections.text: Sometimes an exposure's effect depends on a third variable : a drug may work more strongly in younger than older people, or a risk factor may hit men harder than women. This is called effect modification (or statistical interaction ), and you examine it with a product term in the model. exposure sex means "both variables plus their interplay". It is the interaction term exposure:sex that you read off. If the interaction term's OR sits close to 1 (and p is large), you have no clear evidence that the effect differs between the groups - which is not the same as showing it is equal (interaction tests have low power), so report the stratum-specific estimates regardless. If it differs clearly from 1, the effect (on the odds ratio scale) depends on sex, and you should then report group-specific estimates (e.g. by running the model separately for each sex, or with emmeans / marginaleffects ). A product term tests interaction on the multiplicative (ratio) scale: does the exposure change the odds ratio differently between groups? For public health the additive scale (differences in absolute risk) is often more relevant, and it is measured with RERI (relative excess risk due

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Non-linear relationships (splines)
sections.text: By default, the models above assume a continuous variable is related to the outcome in a straight line on the model's scale: in logistic regression each extra year of age changes the log-odds by the same amount (multiplies the odds by the same factor), whether you go from 30 to 31 or from 70 to 71. That often fits poorly - the risk of many outcomes rises only slowly at young ages and steeply later. That is a curve , not a straight line. A spline lets the variable enter as a smooth curve instead of a straight line, so the model finds the shape itself. You only decide how bendy the curve may be (via the number of degrees of freedom - how many "bends" the curve may have). ns(age, df = 3) replaces the straight line for age with a smooth curve. df = 3 controls the bendiness: more degrees of freedom = a more flexible curve. 3-4 is a common starting point. It works in all the models on these pages (logistic, linear, Cox, Poisson) - just wrap the continuous variable in ns(...) . Especially useful when the variable is your exposure (so you see the dose-response shape itself) or a strong confounder (so a too-rigid straight line does not leave residual confounding , i.e.

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Reading your result
sections.text: For each variable the regression table gives an estimate , a confidence interval and a p-value : The estimate is the effect measure. For logistic regression it is an odds ratio (OR) , for log-binomial a relative risk (RR) , and for Cox (Time-to-event) a hazard ratio (HR) - all are ratios , where 1 means no difference (above 1 = higher odds/risk/rate, below 1 = lower). For linear regression the estimate is instead a difference in means, where 0 means no difference. Example: OR = 1.5 → 50% higher odds; OR = 0.8 → 20% lower. The 95% confidence interval shows the effect sizes that are compatible with your data, given the model: an interval built this way covers the true value in 95% of repeated studies. Narrow = precise, wide = much uncertainty. For a ratio: if the interval includes 1, the effect is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The p-value is the probability of seeing an effect at least as extreme as yours if there were truly none (and the model is right). A small p (typically < 0.05) argues against "no effect", but does not tell you how large or important the effect is - the estimate and confidence interval do. In very large register datasets

sections.title: Regression
sections.heading: Robust (clustered) standard errors
sections.text: When the same person appears several times in the dataset - e.g. if the comparison cohort is matched with replacement , or a comparison person later becomes exposed (crossover, see Comparison cohort) - the rows are not independent. If you ignore this, the confidence intervals come out too narrow. The fix is clustered (robust) standard errors : a way of computing the uncertainty that accounts for rows from the same person being linked. If each person appears only once, you do not need this. vcovCL(model, cluster = ~ pnr) is the cluster-robust covariance matrix (clustered on pnr ). "Sandwich" only refers to the shape of the formula - the point is that it does not assume independent rows. For a Cox model you do it with the cluster argument in coxph() instead (see Time-to-event). A cluster is a group of rows that belong together and are therefore more alike than two random rows - a group of rows , not necessarily of people. It can be several rows from the same person (e.g. repeated measurements over time), all patients at the same hospital , or siblings in the same family. So a person is a cluster only if they appear in several rows; if you have exactly one row per

sections.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections.text: Use this page once your main analysis runs and you want to know how much the estimate depends on the choices you made. It covers changing one choice at a time, and two design checks for confounding you cannot measure. You need your main model from Regression, Time-to-event or Rates and rate ratios; when you are done you have a set of supplementary estimates to report next to it. Register data lacks important lifestyle variables (smoking, BMI, alcohol, diet), so reviewers will ask how robust your result is. A sensitivity analysis repeats the main analysis under a different but plausible assumption and checks whether the conclusion holds. If it holds, the result stands stronger; if it collapses, you know a particular assumption is carrying the result, and you should be honest about that. Two principles: pre-specify your sensitivity analyses in the analysis plan (otherwise they look like fishing for a nice number), and report them alongside the main estimate, not instead of it. Variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. You rarely need new packages here: a sensitivity analysis is usually your main model run again with one changed choice.

sections.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections.heading: Robustness checks: change one choice at a time
sections.text: Most sensitivity analyses consist of changing one choice at a time and seeing whether the conclusion moves: The conclusion need not be numerically identical across the analyses - it just has to point the same way . A hazard ratio moving from 1.8 to 1.6 is robust; one shifting from 1.8 to 0.9 means the changed choice is carrying the result.

sections.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections.heading: Probe for unmeasured confounding
sections.text: The checks above vary your choices . But register data also lacks variables you do not have at all (smoking, BMI, etc.). Two design checks are widely used against that kind of unmeasured confounding: a negative control outcome can reveal it, and an active comparator can reduce it.

sections.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections.heading: Negative control outcome
sections.text: Idea: pick an extra outcome the exposure cannot possibly cause , but which is hit by the same hidden confounders as your real outcome. Run your main model on it. If you still find an "effect", that is a warning flag : the groups are systematically different ( residual confounding , i.e. confounding left after adjustment), and your main result is probably coloured by it too. If the estimate instead sits close to 1, it supports your main analysis, but it cannot rule out confounding that affects only your real outcome. Example (healthy-vaccinee bias). Studies often find that influenza-vaccinated older adults have markedly lower all-cause mortality . But if you look at mortality outside the influenza season - a negative control outcome, because the vaccine cannot protect against influenza when there is no influenza - they are still "protected". That reveals the vaccinated are healthier and more resourceful to begin with ( healthy-vaccinee bias ), not that the vaccine itself lowers all-cause mortality that much. Jackson and colleagues ran this check, as described by Lipsitch et al. (see Read more).

sections.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections.heading: Active comparator (new user)
sections.text: Idea: instead of comparing drug users with non-users (who are wildly different - they do not even have the indication), compare them with new users of an alternative drug for the same condition . Both groups then share the indication, so confounding by indication is sharply reduced. "New user" means both start treatment at index, so you do not mix newly started and long-term users ( prevalent-user bias ). Example. You study whether glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (glucose-lowering drugs for type 2 diabetes, usually added to metformin) affect the risk of an outcome. If you compare against non-users , you are really comparing people with and without treatment-requiring diabetes - two wildly different groups, where the disease itself confounds the picture. If you instead compare against new users of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (another add-on drug for the same condition), the groups are far more alike on indication and disease severity, and the estimate is less coloured by why people are on treatment. Active comparator is about how you build the cohort ([Phase 10 - Build your study population](build-study-population.qmd)) - see the new-user

sections.title: Socioeconomic variables
sections.text: Use this page when you need socioeconomic position as a covariate (or an exposure): educational level, labour market affiliation or household income at baseline. You need your cohort from Phase 10, one row per person and index date. The page gives you three stand-alone recipes, one per dimension, and you end with extract_ses.rds : one category per cohort row in education_cat , occupation_cat and income_cat . Run the setup once, then any recipe on its own, in any order. Every recipe follows the same pattern: open the register → fetch → attach to the cohort → categorise → check. The steps are numbered in the code comments ( # 1. , # 2. , ...), and the text between code blocks refers to them by number.

sections.title: Socioeconomic variables
sections.heading: SEPLINE: the guideline these recipes follow
sections.text: SEPLINE is a 2025 Danish national guideline for measuring socioeconomic position (SEP) in register-based research: which register variables to use, when to measure them, and how to categorise them, so that studies saying "adjusted for socioeconomic position" mean comparable things. Hjorth et al. Clinical Epidemiology 2025, doi:10.2147/CLEP.S520772, with a corrigendum (Hjorth et al. 2026). The table numbers on this page refer to that article. The recipes show how to implement SEPLINE's recommendations. They are not validated, and where SEPLINE leaves a choice open, the page says which choice it made. Review them against your own analysis plan before you use them. Have working code, or input on the categorisations? Get in touch. Four SEP dimensions, three here: SEPLINE covers educational level, labour market affiliation, income and wealth. Wealth (Table 7: FAMFORMREST_NY05 , FGNF_2020 ) is not built out on this page yet. Related factors are not SEP: SEPLINE also covers cohabitation or marital status, ethnicity and area-level characteristics, as sociodemographic factors that sit alongside SEP. For Denmark it recommends cohabitation over marital status, because many

sections.title: Socioeconomic variables
sections.heading: When each dimension is measured
sections.text: All three registers are annual. Taking the value from the index year itself risks measuring status after your exposure (a job lost because of the illness you study), which is reverse causation. SEPLINE sets the timing per dimension: For education the year before index is not a stricter choice than SEPLINE's: UDDA holds the status on 1 October each year (Table 1), so for an index date before 1 October the index year's value does not yet exist at index. If your index dates fall on or after 1 October, you may include the index year (see the education recipe).

sections.text: Every recipe starts from cohort , one row per person and index date, with pnr and index_date . Two columns are added once and used everywhere: Every join uses row_id (to attach a finished category back to the cohort) or pnr + a year (to pull a value out of a register), never pnr alone. If your cohort has one row per person, this changes nothing. If a pnr can appear more than once (for example controls matched with replacement, see Comparison cohort), row_id keeps each row's own index date apart.

sections.text: The recipes read the registers through one DuckDB connection instead of read_register() . Only the income recipe requires it; the fold-out says why, and what to do if you cannot use it. Only the income recipe requires it. Education and employment filter to your cohort before collect() , so only a cohort-sized extract reaches R, and they would work just as well with read_register() , as on the guide's other pages. They use the same connection here so that all three recipes are opened the same way. Income needs it so R does not run out of memory and crash. Its cutpoints come from the whole Danish population: step 7 joins BEF and FAIK for everyone and computes the quantiles before anything can be reduced. Pulled into R, that is one row per person per reference year (about six million), which is more than R's memory holds on DST: R stops with a memory error, or the whole session freezes and you lose what you had not saved. With both registers on one DuckDB connection the work happens inside the database instead, only the small table of cutpoints comes back to R, the quantiles are exact, and DuckDB writes to disk rather than filling the memory. sections.title: Socioeconomic variables
sections.heading: Missing is a category, not a dropped row
sections.text: A register extract only holds people who have a record. Someone with no record is absent from it, and after a left join onto the cohort they have NA . Most model functions, including survival::coxph() , then drop that person without a warning, and your model's N no longer matches your cohort's. Each recipe therefore joins onto the full cohort by row_id before it categorises, turns NA into an explicit "Missing" category, and checks with stopifnot(nrow(...) == nrow(cohort)) that nobody has been lost. SEPLINE recommends exactly this: people with missing values "may constitute a vulnerable group", so keep them as a category and look at them separately in relation to the outcome.

sections.text: hfaudd is the highest completed education (højest fuldførte uddannelse): a four-digit DISCED-15 code (DST's education classification) for the specific education a person completed ( 4272 is an electrician, installation technology). It is an identifier, not a scale, so the level has to be looked up. SEPLINE names DST's own format for it (Table 3), always the newest version: AUDD..._HOVED_L1L5 for the main groups, which turns the four-digit code into a two-digit main area ( 10 Grundskole, primary and lower secondary school; 20 Gymnasiale uddannelser, general upper secondary; ... 80 Ph.d.), or AUDD..._HOVED_L1L2 for a more detailed grouping. This recipe uses the main groups. How to read those file names on the server is in [Format tables](formatting-tables.qmd#education-level). Do not take the level from the first two digits of hfaudd ( substr(hfaudd, 1, 2) ). They look like the main-area codes but are wrong for roughly 4 codes in 10, without any error. Why is in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd#udda---education-register). sections.title: Socioeconomic variables
sections.heading: Imputed education and hf_kilde
sections.text: DST collects immigrants' education from abroad through surveys. For those who do not answer, it imputes the education with a model (a random forest) built on earlier survey answers and background variables from other registers. SEPLINE describes this in its section on education and gives the details of the models in its supplementary Table S2. The imputed education is one of the sources DST builds hfaudd from ([DST's documentation of HF_KILDE ](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/generelt-om-data/dokumentation-af-data/hoejkvalitetsvariable/Hoejst-fuldfoerte-uddannelse/HF-KILDE)). It is written into hfaudd as an ordinary code, so an imputed record looks exactly like an observed one, and every delivery with hfaudd contains them. The only marker is hf_kilde , the source of the record: in DST's value set, 9 , 10 and 18 are immigrants' education imputed by DST. SEPLINE recommends grouping these as Missing in individual-level analyses (Table 2 and 3): imputed values are reliable for groups, where the errors even out, but less reliable for single people. Not every delivery has hf_kilde , so check yours:

They all belong to immigrants, so a sensitivity analysis can set every immigrant's education to Missing and compare the result with your main analysis. This is deliberately too broad: it also removes immigrants' own answers about their education and Danish education taken after immigrating. Use it as a sensitivity analysis to see whether the result moves, not as the main analysis. Realskole (middle school): People whose highest education is realskole fall in main area 10 and are therefore Short. SEPLINE suggests considering them Medium, depending on your population (Table 3, note c). sections.heading: Income - FAIK via BEF (famaekvivadisp_13)

Time: the mean of the three calendar years before the index year. If one year is missing, the mean of the other two; if two, the one that exists; if all three, missing. Standardisation: quintiles of the general population with the same sex and 5-year age group, not of your own cohort. The cutpoints are also computed per calendar year: SEPLINE's text describes income "calculated in income quintiles by calendar year", and incomes rise every year. A person's family comes from BEF, so the recipe goes person → BEF → family → FAIK. Use the _13 version of the variable for the whole period: in DST's variable list for FAIK the older famaekvivadisp runs 1990-2012 and has a different definition, while famaekvivadisp_13 runs from 1987 on one definition. sections.title: Self-controlled and family-based designs
sections.text: Use this page when you are deciding whether a self-controlled or family-based design fits your question, instead of a [comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) or matched controls. Those designs find a group to compare against and then adjust for confounding. The designs here let the person themselves, or the family, be the control, so confounding by what does not change over time (genes, fixed socioeconomic status (SES), unmeasured lifestyle) is removed without you having to measure it. The page tells you when each design applies and what it assumes; it has no worked code, and the packages that do the work are linked in each section.

sections.title: Self-controlled and family-based designs
sections.heading: Self-controlled designs (SCCS and case-crossover)
sections.text: Idea. The person is their own control: you look at whether the outcome happens more often in a short period right after a transient exposure than in the person's other time. Because it is the same person, all confounding that does not change over time (genes, sex, fixed SES, unmeasured lifestyle) disappears, without you measuring it. When. Transient exposure and acute outcome. Classic: a drug or vaccine and an acute adverse event. SCCS was developed for vaccine safety ([Farrington 1995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7766778/)); the case-crossover design was introduced for transient triggers of acute events such as myocardial infarction (Maclure 1991). Two variants: SCCS (self-controlled case series): models the rate of the outcome within each person's follow-up and compares exposed vs. unexposed periods. Case-crossover: compares the exposure in a "hazard window" just before the event with the exposure in earlier reference windows in the same person. Assumptions (otherwise the estimate is biased): the exposure is transient (not permanent); the event does not affect the probability of future exposure (and preferably not the length of follow-up either, e.g. if the outcome is

sections.title: Self-controlled and family-based designs
sections.heading: Family- and sibling-based designs
sections.text: Idea. Compare siblings (or twins) within the same family. That holds what siblings share, such as genes and upbringing environment, constant, and you isolate the effect of what differs between them. Families are linked via the parents' personal numbers, mor_id and far_id in BEF ([DST, Nyt fra Forskningsservice 4/2019](https://dst.dk/ext/2940168985/0/forskning/Ekstra-Nyt-fra-Forskningsservice-4-kvartal-2019--pdf)). Analysis. Conditional logistic regression or stratified Cox on the family ID: the same strata idea as matched case-control, just with the family as the matched set. R. Building the family links is the first job: kinship2 handles pedigrees and fmn_siblings() from the experimental GitHub package famnet finds all sibling pairs from father and mother IDs; both are described in [Algorithms and packages](packages-overview.qmd), and famnet is not confirmed on DST. The analysis itself is survival::clogit() with a strata() per family, or coxph() stratified by family ID (see Regression). A sibling design only removes shared confounding. Non-shared confounding, what differs between siblings (e.g. different birth weight or differences in upbringing over time),

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.text: Use this page when your cohort is built and you want to analyse the time until the outcome: Kaplan-Meier curves, a Cox model for the hazard ratio, the check of proportional hazards, and what to do when death (or another event) can come first. Time-to-event analysis (survival analysis) handles the fact that not everyone reaches the event during follow-up (censoring). You need the analysis-ready dataset with follow-up time and event status from [Phase 12](joins.qmd#follow-up-time); when you are done you have curves and estimates to take through output control. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. survival , survminer and tidycmprsk must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: You need two things per person: follow-up time (how long the person was followed) and event status (whether the event/outcome occurred in that time: 1 = yes, 0 = censored, i.e. not seen during follow-up). Follow-up time is stop date minus index date , where the stop date is the first of outcome, death, emigration or end of study; see [Calculate follow-up time and event variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time) in Phase 12 for the construction itself.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Kaplan-Meier curves
sections.text: survfit() computes the Kaplan-Meier estimate (the event-free proportion over time), and ggsurvplot() draws it nicely. With simulated numbers the curves look like this (here the exposed drop faster, i.e. they get the outcome more often): !Kaplan-Meier curves with simulated data. ggsurvplot() typically also adds a risk table below the figure.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Before you export a Kaplan-Meier curve
sections.text: The curve and its risk table are output like any table. Each step in the curve is one or a few events, and each number at risk is a table cell, so check them against the small-cell rule (3 or 5, see Export). In the tail of the curve, where few people are left, this usually fails: one way out is to cut the x-axis ( xlim = in ggsurvplot() ) where the number at risk falls below your threshold. One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve also overestimates the risk when a competing event (typically death) can preclude your outcome: see [Competing risks](#competing-risks) below.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Cox regression (hazard ratio)
sections.text: coxph() gives hazard ratios (HR) adjusted for covariates. tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) shows them as HRs instead of log-hazards. A hazard ratio is a ratio of rates (hazards) over follow-up: 1 = no difference, above 1 = higher rate in the exposed, below 1 = lower. It is not a ratio of risks. See [Reading your result](regression.qmd#read-the-output). The difference with replacement. If the comparison cohort is matched with replacement (or there is crossover), the same person appears several times and the rows are not independent. Then you add one argument, cluster = pnr , to exactly the same model. It does not change the hazard ratio estimate; it replaces the standard errors with robust (sandwich) standard errors that allow for the repeated person, so the confidence intervals are no longer too narrow. Same idea as in Regression. Note the syntax: coxph() takes the cluster variable as an argument without a tilde ( cluster = pnr ), whereas sandwich::vcovCL() on the Regression page uses a formula with a tilde ( cluster = ~ pnr ). Same idea (cluster on person id), just two functions' different ways of receiving the variable. What is your time scale? The time axis

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Check the assumption: proportional hazards
sections.text: The Cox model assumes proportional hazards (PH): that the hazard ratio is constant over follow-up. If it is not, a single hazard ratio does not describe an effect that changes over time. Check it with cox.zph() , which is based on the scaled Schoenfeld residuals (in short, whether the effect drifts over time). With register-sized data the test has the power to flag even a tiny departure, so a small p-value alone says little. Judge the plot: how much the curve slopes, and whether that changes what you would conclude. If a variable violates the assumption, you can e.g. stratify on it ( + strata(variable) in the model, giving it its own baseline hazard) or model a time-dependent effect (let the effect change over follow-up). A third alternative is to drop the hazard ratio and use RMST ( restricted mean survival time ): the average event-free time within a fixed window (e.g. "months alive within 5 years"). You compare groups by the difference in RMST , measured in time units instead of a ratio, and it is valid even when PH is violated. In R: the survRM2 package.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Competing risks
sections.text: If another event can preclude your outcome (classically death, before the outcome can occur), it is a competing risk . One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve then overestimates the risk, because it treats those who died as if they were merely censored and could still get the outcome later. In register cohorts with older people or long follow-up this is common. Each person ends up in one of three places, and only the first thing that happens counts: (1) they never reach an event during follow-up ( censored ), (2) they get your outcome, or (3) they have the competing event (e.g. death). Someone who dies first can never reach the outcome, and the analysis must reflect that.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 1. Set up the data
sections.text: You need the same two variables as for an ordinary Cox model - but the status variable now takes three values instead of two (so we call it status instead of outcome ): time_days - the time from index to the first thing that happens (outcome, death or end of follow-up). status - what happened: censored, outcome or death. status must be a factor , and tidycmprsk requires "censored" to be the first level . The order of the levels is also where you tell R which level is your outcome and which is the competing risk: You build status_code (0/1/2) from the dates - what happened first : 0 = censored (e.g. end of follow-up, emigrated or otherwise lost), 1 = outcome, 2 = death. The construction lives in [Calculate follow-up time and event variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time) (Phase 12). The number you give censoring does not matter - what matters is that the censored level is listed first in levels = (which is why it is 0 here).
sections.code: tidycmprsk cuminc crr mutate status factor status_code raw code one per person e.g. levels order sets meaning labels censored level must first outcome models death competing risk

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 2. Describe the risk over time (CIF)
sections.text: Instead of Kaplan-Meier , use the cumulative incidence function (CIF, also called Aalen-Johansen). It allocates people correctly across the competing outcomes, so death no longer "steals" risk from the outcome. (This is about the curve ; the regression itself is still done with Cox, see step 3.)
sections.code: surv time status factor cumulative incidence each event type cuminc time_days exposure one curve per group also gives gray test difference

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 3. Regression: pick the model to match your question
sections.text: There are two regression models, and they answer different questions: The rate of the outcome among those still alive and event-free: run an ordinary Cox model and censor the competing event. You do that by setting the event to status == "outcome" : both censored and dead people then become "no event". This is the cause-specific hazard, the usual choice for an etiological question. The cumulative incidence (absolute risk) of the outcome: use Fine-Gray ( crr ), where the dead stay in the risk set. crr by default models the first event type after "censored" (here "outcome") and treats the rest ("death") as competing. This is the subdistribution hazard. Neither hazard ratio is a risk ratio. The subdistribution hazard ratio tells you the direction in which the exposure shifts the cumulative incidence (if the model fits), but not by how much; for the absolute risk, report the cumulative incidence (CIF) at fixed time points, for example at 1 and 5 years. If you want to describe or predict risk (e.g. "what is the 5-year risk of the outcome?"), use the CIF and Fine-Gray. If you want to know whether the exposure changes the rate of the outcome in those still at risk, use the

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Time-varying covariates (briefly)
sections.text: If a variable changes during follow-up (e.g. a blood test or BMI), it cannot be a single value per person. It must be in start/stop format (one row per interval), built with survival::tmerge() and analysed with coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, outcome) ~ ...) . The reshaping itself is in Time-varying variables. Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : [Survival analysis](https://www.epirhandbook.com/en/new_pages/survival_analysis.html)

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.text: Almost everything else in this guide builds on one row per person with variables measured at index (baseline). Use this page when something changes during follow-up and you need to decide whether that matters. It helps you decide when the baseline setup is enough, shows how to build start/stop data for a time-varying covariate with survival::tmerge() , and tells you when the problem is beyond a reshaping. You need the analysis-ready dataset from [Phase 12](joins.qmd#follow-up-time). This is a short orientation to a hard topic. Time-varying analysis ranges from a simple reshaping of the data (what we show here) to the causal methods for time-varying treatments ; for the latter, see for example [What If, Part III](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook). Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. survival must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: What can vary?
sections.text: Three different things can vary over time, and they call for very different answers: Time-varying covariate / confounder: a background variable that changes (e.g. BMI, a blood test, a medication status, marital status). It cannot be a single value per person if it changes along the way. Time-varying exposure / treatment: the exposure itself starts, stops or switches during follow-up (a treatment the person goes on and off). A common register use is an exposure that starts after cohort entry: counting the person as exposed from entry creates [immortal time bias](dst-pitfalls.qmd#immortal-time-bias), while letting exposure switch on at its start date in start/stop data avoids it. Exposures that go on and off are where it gets causally hard, see the feedback section below. Censoring is also time-varying: people leave follow-up at different times (emigration, death, loss to follow-up). This is already handled in your follow-up time and time-to-event setup, see Time-to-event.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: When is the baseline setup enough?
sections.text: Often. If your exposure is fixed at index (e.g. a diagnosis or a surgery on a given date) and you adjust for confounders measured at baseline , then the ordinary setup from Phase 10-12 - one row per person, covariates frozen at index, one follow-up interval - is the right one. You do not need time-varying analysis just because the data span time. Only consider it when a variable that matters for the analysis actually changes value after index. Rule of thumb: ask whether the extra complexity changes the answer. If a covariate drifts a little but is not a strong confounder, its baseline value is usually fine. If the exposure itself changes, or a strong confounder changes systematically with the exposure, read on.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: A time-varying covariate
sections.text: If you have a covariate that changes along the way (and that is not caught in feedback with the exposure, see the next section), the fix is mechanical: you build start/stop format (also called counting-process format). Instead of one row per person you get one row per person- interval , where the variable is constant within the interval. You build it with survival::tmerge() and analyse it with an ordinary Cox model. A person with two measurements becomes two rows, each with its own tstart / tstop interval and the value that applies within it:

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: Build start/stop data with tmerge()
sections.text: event(time, status) marks when the event occurs. tdc(day, value) lets measure change value on each measurement day.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: Analyse in a Cox model
sections.text: The time-to-event analysis itself (Kaplan-Meier, Cox, assumptions) is in Time-to-event. The detailed recipe for tmerge() and time-dependent effects is in [the survival package vignette Counting process and timeline data sets (CRAN PDF)](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survival/vignettes/timeline.pdf).
sections.code: coxph surv tstart tstop outcome measure age time varying cox model

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: Treatment-confounder feedback
sections.text: The start/stop Cox above is not always enough - and can even be wrong. The most important trap in time-varying analysis is treatment-confounder feedback : when a time-varying variable is both a confounder for the exposure and itself affected by past exposure. Classic example: a treatment (exposure) affects a biomarker, the biomarker affects whether the person gets more treatment, and the biomarker also affects the outcome. The variable is at once a confounder (normally handled by adjustment) and an intermediate variable / mediator on the path from past treatment to outcome (adjust for it and you block part of the effect you want to measure, introducing bias). In that situation you cannot simply put the variable into an ordinary Cox model, the way we did above. Adjusting and not adjusting both give a wrong answer. The solution is a whole different family of methods, g-methods : the g-formula (standardisation step by step over time) IP weighting / marginal structural models: the most accessible g-method. The guide introduces the weighting idea for a fixed exposure in [IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)](weighting-iptw.qmd); marginal structural models extend it to a

sections.text: [What If (Hernán & Robins), Part III - Causal inference for time-varying treatments](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook) (free PDF): the standard reference. Ch. 19 (time-varying treatments), ch. 20 (treatment-confounder feedback), ch. 21 (g-methods) and ch. 22 (target trial emulation). [survival package vignette: Counting process and timeline data sets (CRAN PDF)](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survival/vignettes/timeline.pdf): the technical recipe for tmerge() and start/stop data. IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW): the guide's introduction to IP weighting (fixed exposure), the foundation under marginal structural models. Time-to-event: Kaplan-Meier, Cox and assumptions. sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.text: This page is for when something has already gone wrong: a red error message, or a result that came back empty. If your code runs fine but you suspect the answer is wrong, that is the other page: DST pitfalls collects the traps that produce a plausible-looking result and never say a word.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Start here: six steps
sections.text: Before you go looking in the code, do this in order: 1. Read the error message: which line is mentioned? Which object name appears? 2. Run class(object) : is it data ( "data.frame" ) or still a connection ( "prudent_duckplyr_df" from read_register() - even though it also says "data.frame" - or "arrow_dplyr_query" , "tbl_duckdb_connection" )? See [Phase 5 - do you have data or just a connection?](extraction-step-by-step.qmd) 3. Run names(object) : is the column named exactly what you think? A single letter or difference in capitalisation is enough to fail. 4. Isolate the failing line: run it alone and see what happens. 5. Restart the R session (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10) and run from the top. This clears stale objects left behind by earlier runs, which is a surprisingly common cause. It also throws away everything in memory, so read [The console is stuck](#console-stuck) first if you have unsaved results. 6. Use ?functionname : type e.g. ?colSums in the console to open the help in the Help panel (bottom right) - what the function does, its arguments, and examples. Still stuck after that? Where to ask is at the bottom of this page.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: The console is stuck
sections.text: Before any of the above: if the console will not give you a > back, there is no error message to read. R is waiting, not failing.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: R shows + instead of >
sections.text: R could not finish reading your command and is waiting for the rest of it. Everything you type next is swallowed as a continuation, which is why the commands after it appear to do nothing at all. Press Esc to get out ( Ctrl+C if you are running R in a terminal rather than RStudio). The half-finished command is thrown away and the > comes back. What usually causes it: A missing ) or ] : put the cursor next to a bracket and the editor highlights its partner, or shows nothing if there is not one. An unclosed quote: "dementia instead of "dementia" . A trailing %>% with nothing after it: the pipe promises another step, so R waits for it.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Something has been running too long
sections.text: Press Esc , or click the red stop sign that appears in the console toolbar while R is busy. That sends an interrupt and usually returns you to > . If nothing happens, R is inside compiled code that is not checking for interrupts. Large collect() calls on arrow or DuckDB do this. Then: 1. Session > Interrupt R. 2. If that does not work either, Session > Restart R (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10). Restarting throws away everything in memory. On DST that can mean running an extraction again that took an hour the first time. Save anything expensive with saveRDS() before you start something long, so a restart costs you minutes instead of the morning. The same point, from the other direction, is in [File formats](file-formats.qmd): a full load of a large SAS file can cost you your unsaved work.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Common R error messages
sections.text: Most R errors are small typos. Quick self-check of the code: A missing comma or pipe ( %>% )? Unclosed ( , [ or { ? Capitalisation ( PNR vs. pnr )? Are the data and packages loaded in this session? For a fuller walkthrough of debugging ( traceback() , browser() , print-debugging and reading error messages), see Debugging from Zheer's R Coding Café, and the DDEA course's [troubleshooting guide](https://r-cubed-intro.rostools.org/appendix/troubleshooting).

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Error messages specific to register work
sections.text: These are the ones you meet in a DST workflow rather than in R generally: unsupported function in Arrow is not a mistake in your code - it is a gap in what the Arrow engine covers. Switch the connection to DuckDB with to_duckdb() , or collect() into R first and do the operation there. See Arrow vs. DuckDB.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: No error, but zero rows
sections.text: This is the failure mode that does not announce itself. A filter that cannot match returns an empty result, R reports success, and the empty table looks like a finding: "no patients were exposed". Two ways to produce it: A pattern longer than the column: atc2 in LMDB holds three characters, so grepl("N02A", atc2) compares four characters against three and matches nothing. See Medication (ATC). A type mismatch in a join or filter: a join on a character pnr and a numeric one usually fails (see the table above), but converting one side can still leave values that never meet - a code stored as a number loses its leading zero ( 0001 becomes 1 ), so it no longer matches the text "0001" , the same way a format table joined on the wrong type does (see [Format tables](formatting-tables.qmd#education-level)). So treat an empty result as a bug until proven otherwise . Count the rows before and after the filter, and check that the values you filter on actually occur: If the second line shows three-character values and your pattern is longer, you have found it.
sections.code: dplyr count filter collect lmdb rows before atc2 what column really contains

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Where to ask
sections.text: Follow this order. AI is at the bottom for a good reason. Two ready-made references worth bookmarking: [Common errors](https://www.epirhandbook.com/en/new_pages/errors.html) and [Getting help](https://www.epirhandbook.com/en/new_pages/help.html), both in The Epidemiologist R Handbook. On DST there is an extra rule: no data in the question. Not a value, not a row, not a pasted error message that happens to contain one. This applies to colleagues, to DST support and to any AI tool. When you need to show the problem, build a small fake dataset that reproduces it. Avoid AI as your first stop if you are new. AI can generate plausible-sounding code that does not work - or works but gives wrong results. Use it as a supplement to your own understanding, not as a substitute. A good help question is minimal (the smallest code that still shows the error), complete and reproducible . Bad: "My code fails, what is wrong?" (no code, no error message) Good: > "I get the error Error: object 'pnr' not found - what is missing?" > > r > library(dplyr) > df <- data.frame(PNR = 1:5, age = 20:24) > df %>% filter(pnr > 3) # error here > > > Expected: rows where PNR > 3. Actual: error that

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.text: The National Patient Register (Landspatientregisteret, LPR) is where hospital diagnoses, contacts and procedures come from. It holds inpatient contacts from 1977, and outpatient, emergency department and psychiatric contacts from 1995. Private hospitals and clinics report through a separate system, see [Private hospitals](extract-from-lpr.qmd#private-hospitals). Read this page before you write code against LPR. It explains how the register is laid out: the two periods (LPR2 and LPR3), which tables hold what, how the diagnosis codes and diagnosis types work, and the breaks in 1994, 1995 and 2019 that change what a count means. When you are done you know which tables your study period needs and which filters to apply. The code is on the next page, Extract from LPR. In short: LPR changed format in 2019: use LPR2 (up to March 2019) and LPR3 (after) and combine them. All ICD codes carry a D prefix you usually strip, and you choose diagnosis types (A/B for outcomes; G for baseline comorbidity exists only in 1995-2003).

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: LPR is split into two periods
sections.text: In early 2019 LPR changed format, from LPR2 to LPR3. Two dates matter, and they are not the same thing: When the hospitals switched their reporting. Region Hovedstaden, Region Sjælland and Region Midtjylland switched to LPR3 on the weekend of 2-3 February 2019, Region Nordjylland and Region Syddanmark on the weekend of 2-3 March 2019 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's data quality report on LPR3, April 2019](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/media/16452/Datakvalitetsrapport%20om%20LPR3%20pr.%2012.%20april%202019.pdf)). Where DST's LPR2 files end. lpr_adm , lpr_diag and the other LPR2 registers at DST end on 31 March 2019 ([DST's register overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html)). A study period that crosses early 2019 needs both systems, combined. ¹ ³ These are DST's names. Check whether your variables have been changed during delivery or data preprocessing: in DARTER the join key arrives as k_recnum in t_psyk_adm and v_recnum in t_psyk_diag , and the person column as v_cpr . Check colnames() and rename to recnum and pnr before joining. ² datetime format - convert with as.Date() . ⁴ LPR2 does not hold

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Contact table and diagnosis table: every extract is a join
sections.text: LPR splits each hospital contact into two tables. The contact register (e.g. lpr_adm ) has one row per contact with pnr , dates and hospital, but not the diagnoses. The diagnosis register (e.g. lpr_diag ) has one row per diagnosis with the ICD code, but neither pnr nor a date. One contact can have several diagnoses. You join the two on the contact key ( recnum in LPR2, dw_ek_kontakt in LPR3) to get pnr , date and diagnosis in one table. The recipes in Extract from LPR are built on that join. Operations and procedures work the same way: lpr_sksopr (LPR2) has the SKS code (SKS is the Danish health care classification system) and recnum , but not pnr or date, so it is joined to lpr_adm when you want to find who had an operation and when.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Psychiatry: separate tables in LPR2, combined in LPR3
sections.text: Before 2019, contacts at psychiatric departments and their diagnoses (typically F-codes such as dementia and depression) were stored in separate registers ( t_psyk_adm , t_psyk_diag ). The structure resembles somatic LPR2, but column names can differ (see the table footnotes above). LPR3 combines both: somatic and psychiatric contacts and diagnoses are in the same tables, and no separate psychiatric query is needed. Psychiatric data older than 1995 exists but is not part of a standard LPR extract, see Overview of registers.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Timeline of the LPR tables
sections.text: The figure shows two breaks that are easy to miss: outpatient, emergency and psychiatric contacts only start in 1995 (footnote 4 above), and the LPR_A files overlap the LPR2 files from 2017 to early 2019 (the callout below).
sections.code: gantt title lpr registers dateformat yyyy axisformat section lpr2 somatic lpr_adm lpr_diag inpatient only done plus outpatient emergency psychiatric t_psyk_adm t_psyk_diag lpr_a files rows tagged lpr1 minipas overlap crit lpr3 active

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: LPR3 is delivered in the LPR_A files
sections.text: You access LPR3 through the LPR_A files ( lpr_a_kontakt , lpr_a_diagnose ). Use the LPR_A files, and filter them. Two things, both easy to get wrong. 1. LPR_A, not LPR_F. LPR3 has been delivered as two sets of tables: the older LPR_F ( kontakter , diagnoser , forloeb ) and the current LPR_A ( lpr_a_kontakt , lpr_a_diagnose ). DST released LPR_A in June 2025 and has closed LPR_F for ordering. DST writes that the LPR_A tables largely correspond to the LPR_F tables but hold considerably more variables (LPR_A has 12 tables, LPR_F had 14), and that LPR_A, unlike LPR_F, also holds LPR2 rows from 2017-2019 ([DST, Nyt om grunddata, 2nd quarter 2025](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2025/nyt-om-grunddata-2-kvartal-2025)). Every example on this site uses lpr_a_ . An older project may have both sets in its folder. They hold the same LPR3 contacts, so use one of them: stacking both gives you duplicated rows. 2. LPR_A holds four reporting systems in one table. Besides LPR3 contacts, lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose hold contacts from the older systems that ended in 2017 or later. Every row is tagged by lprindberetningssystem (reporting system):

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: ICD codes and the D-prefix
sections.text: ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision) is the WHO's system for classifying diseases and conditions. Hospital diagnoses in Denmark have been coded with ICD-10 since 1994 (earlier years are ICD-8), e.g. G30 for Alzheimer's disease and F00 for dementia in Alzheimer's. ICD-10 codes in LPR have a prepended "D" : "DG30" (Alzheimer's), "DF00" (dementia), "DI21" (acute myocardial infarction). The D is a Danish addition from SKS, not part of the WHO code. The examples on this site strip the D-prefix before comparing codes, so that a code list reads like the ICD-10 codes in a paper and can be reused across registers: substr(x, start, stop) keeps characters from position start up to and including stop (counted from 1). substr(c_diag, 2, 4) skips position 1 (the D-prefix) and keeps characters 2, 3 and 4: "DG30" → "G30" . Use 2 to 5 for 4-digit codes: "DI219" → "I219" .
sections.code: mutate icd3 substr c_diag dg30 g30 digit code icd4 di219 i219

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Only the patient registers have the D-prefix
sections.text: The prefix belongs to the patient registers. Other registers store the plain WHO code, and stripping the first character there removes a real one: Run substr(x, 2, 4) on "E119" and you get "119" . It matches nothing, it raises no error, and the result looks like an empty subgroup rather than a bug. A leading D is not always a prefix. ICD-10 has codes of its own that begin with D: D46 (myelodysplastic syndromes) and D32 (benign meningeal tumour) are whole codes. In the cancer register they are stored exactly like that. Strip the "prefix" and D46 becomes 46 .

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Before 1994 the codes are ICD-8
sections.text: LPR2 starts in 1977, and Denmark did not move to ICD-10 until 1994 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)). The early years hold ICD-8: pure digits, no letter and no decimal point, so 446.30 is stored as 44630 . You get no error or warning from this. An ICD-10 code list matches no rows before 1994, and substr(c_diag, 2, 4) on "44630" returns "463" , which is not a code in any classification. A study whose period starts before 1994 reads two classifications out of one column and needs a code list for each. The same applies to dodsaars , which runs from 1970 and changes over in the same year.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Diagnosis types
sections.text: LPR2 ( c_diagtype ) has six diagnosis types, and three of them were only in use for some years: The codes and years are from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's [code sheet for LPR](https://www.esundhed.dk/-/media/Files/Dokumentation/Landspatientregisteret/5_Kodeark_LPR---pdf.ashx); the explanations of A, H and M follow [Schmidt et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S91125). G was voluntary to record in 1995-2001, was recorded only for psychiatric patients in 2002-2003, and is not used after 2003 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)). H and M are usually left out of outcome and comorbidity definitions: a referral diagnosis is what the referring unit suspected, and a provisional diagnosis is not final. That follows from what the two types are; it is not a rule from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, so say in your methods what you chose. LPR3 ( diag_kode_type ) has only two diagnosis types: action diagnosis (A) and secondary diagnosis (B) ([reporting guideline for LPR 2025, section 6.1.3](https://cdn.sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638955095432142451/LPR-indberetningsvejledning_2025_v.5.1.pdf)). Keep the
sections.code: outcomes exclusion diagnoses filter c_diagtype baseline comorbidity note only exists

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type: inpatient, outpatient or emergency
sections.text: Some studies need to tell inpatient contacts apart from outpatient and emergency-room visits, for example to count only admissions as an outcome. LPR2 has a field for it, LPR3 does not, so you derive patient type differently in the two. c_pattype and c_indm have to be in your extract. DST documents both for every year of LPR_ADM, but a delivery only contains the variables the project ordered. In the DARTER delivery, for instance, lpr_adm has neither, while t_psyk_adm has both - the same register family, two different extract scopes. Run colnames() on your own lpr_adm first. If the columns are missing, no filtering trick recovers them: you have to ask DST to add them to the delivery. Check the column names and codes below against your own extract with arrow::schema() or colnames() , and look them up in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd): the column names in LPR_A may differ from the example. The pattern is adapted from [the Plana-Ripoll group's code on OSF](https://osf.io/zhfyp/overview).

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type in LPR2: c_pattype
sections.text: Patient type is in c_pattype , but the coding changed twice ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5), under "Kendte databrud/ændringer", known data breaks): Emergency room, 2014: code "3" was discontinued, and emergency-room visits are from then on registered as "2" (outpatient) with an acute admission mode ( c_indm == "1" ). Part-day patients, 2002: code "1" was discontinued. After that, hospitals registered these patients differently: some as outpatients, some as inpatients. The code below groups "1" with inpatients; whichever you choose, inpatient counts are not directly comparable before and after 2002.
sections.code: dplyr mutate case_when lpr2_type lpr_adm extract patienttype c_pattype inpatient full admitted part day emergency explicit discontinued c_indm became acute outpatient na_character_

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type in LPR3: derived from duration
sections.text: LPR3 has no c_pattype . The kont_type code ALCA00 means physical attendance (not admission): the patient came in, whether for an outpatient visit or an admission. The other contact types are ALCA01 home or outreach visit, ALCA03 virtual contact, ALCA10 death and ALCA20 a pseudo-contact for reporting diagnoses only (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, [LPR reporting guide, Bilag 1](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638955095266548367/Bilag1_model_og_regler_v.5.1.pdf)). The prioritet (priority) code ATA1 means acute. The example below derives patient type from the contact's duration plus an emergency-room marker ( skadestue is Danish for emergency room): The 8-hour cut-off is a heuristic, not an official definition. LPR3 has no "inpatient" field. Other cut-offs are in use: DST's hospital statistics report stays under and over 12 hours ([DST, documentation of the hospital utilisation statistics](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/sygehusbenyttelse/statistisk-behandling)). Pick a threshold, write it in your methods, and clarify it with your data manager.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Retracted diagnoses in LPR3 (senere_afkraeftet)
sections.text: LPR3 flags diagnoses that were later retracted in the column senere_afkraeftet ("later disproved"). The filter used on this site: The is.na() part is needed. In R, NA != "Ja" returns NA , not TRUE , and filter() drops rows where the condition is NA . filter(senere_afkraeftet != "Ja") alone would therefore remove every diagnosis with an empty flag. With is.na(...) in front, the row is kept if the flag is empty or is not "Ja" . The filter thus assumes that a diagnosis with an empty flag was not retracted.
sections.code: filter is.na senere_afkraeftet

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Diagnosis counts jump around 2019-2020
sections.text: The move to LPR3's contact-based model also changed how outpatient diagnoses are registered, and this can distort diagnosis counts across the transition. In LPR2, a course of outpatient visits was typically summarised with a single (action) diagnosis for the whole course. In LPR3, each contact can carry its own diagnoses. So a patient with 10 outpatient visits for depression that produced one diagnosis row in LPR2 can produce ten rows in LPR3: the same illness, many more registrations. Count-based analyses are clearly affected. Number of contacts or diagnoses per person per year, healthcare utilisation or recurrence measures, episode counts, or anything comparing volume before and after 2019: the same clinical course can turn into many more registrations, and the apparent "spike" is a registration artifact, not a real change in disease incidence. Whether first/last-diagnosis-date outcomes are also affected is not yet resolved. In principle, fragmentation alone should not change a "first diagnosis of X" date - the earliest matching row is still the earliest row, whether the underlying course produced one registration or ten. But that relies on every row still carrying its true

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Check your own diagnoses across the transition
sections.text: There is no single agreed fix, and the problem is largest for analyses that rely only on hospital diagnoses. Count the diagnoses used in your study per calendar year and look at the result: Most diagnoses show the spike. A few are stable across the transition (type 1 diabetes, for example) and make a useful sanity check: if even a stable diagnosis jumps in your data, something else is wrong. For inspiration and for evaluating diagnostic stability across the transition, see Aarhus-Psychiatry-Research/diagnostic-stability-lpr2-lpr3 (methodological inspiration, not code for reuse).

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.text: Use this page when you want to control confounding by weighting instead of matching or regression adjustment (IPTW), or to correct for people whose outcome you do not observe (IPCW). You start from the analysis-ready dataset ([Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd)) and end with a weighted estimate, a balance check and robust standard errors. The page does two related jobs, one per part. IP weighting (inverse probability weighting) is one technique with two applications. You model the probability of whatever skews the comparison and weight each person by its inverse . This creates a pseudo-population in which the skew is gone: IPTW (treatment weighting) against confounding : weight by the probability of being exposed . IPCW (censoring weighting) against selection bias from censoring, dropout or missing outcomes: weight by the probability of being observed . Both are handled in the analysis rather than by design. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. WeightIt , cobalt , sandwich and lmtest must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Part 1: IPTW - weighting against confounding
sections.text: Where matching (Phase 10) balances the groups by selecting people, IPTW weights them: each person gets a weight based on their probability of being exposed (the propensity score), so exposed and unexposed become comparable on the measured confounders. The propensity score (each person's probability of being exposed given the confounders) can be used by weighting (IPTW, this page), by matching exposed to unexposed on the score, or by stratifying / adjusting on it. They are alternative routes to the same end, balancing measured confounders, and all share the same positivity diagnostic: poor overlap shows up as extreme weights or as people who cannot be matched. See Hernán & Robins, What If , ch. 15. Three assumptions for IPTW to work (the general identifiability conditions for any causal estimate, introduced in [Phase 1](plan-your-study.qmd#covariates-dag)): 1. Exchangeability: you have measured and included the main confounders (no substantial unmeasured confounding). 2. Positivity (overlap): within each combination of confounders, both exposed and unexposed must be possible. Very large weights are a warning sign of poor overlap. 3. Consistency: the exposure must

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Step 2: check balance
sections.text: The weights are only good if they actually balance the confounders. Check that before looking at the outcome. bal.tab() / love.plot() show how far each confounder is from being balanced (SMD = standardised difference between the groups) - before and after weighting. The goal is for all of them to sit close to 0 after weighting. If some are still skewed, or a few weights are very large, reconsider the model (more/other confounders) or consider stabilising/trimming the weights.

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Step 3: weighted outcome model
sections.text: Once balance is acceptable, fit the outcome model with the weights . Weighting requires robust standard errors (same idea as in Regression). Expected warning. With non-integer weights, glm(..., family = binomial) prints the warning "non-integer #successes in a binomial glm" . It is harmless here and can be ignored: the estimates are correct, and the robust standard errors take care of the uncertainty. (Don't switch to family = quasibinomial to remove it - that changes the model's variance assumption.) The robust standard errors treat the weights as fixed. To account for the weights being estimated too, WeightIt::glm_weightit(outcome ~ exposure, data = df, weightit = W, family = binomial) computes them by M-estimation by default, or you can bootstrap the whole procedure. If the same person is in the data more than once, cluster on pnr as in Regression. IPTW has a twin for confounding control: standardization (also called g-computation or the parametric g-formula). Instead of weighting, you fit an outcome model and average its predictions over the confounder distribution. It often gives more stable estimates and lets you report marginal risk differences and ratios, not

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Part 2: IPCW - weighting against censoring and missing outcomes
sections.text: The same machinery can fix a different skew: selection bias from censoring, dropout or missing outcomes. Think of censoring as a "second treatment" : instead of asking "what is the effect of the exposure?" (which requires complete data) you ask "what would the effect be if nobody had been censored? ". This converts selection bias into a confounding problem for censoring, and confounding can be weighted away. Each observed person is weighted by 1/Pr(observed), so they stand in for the similar people who dropped out. This rebuilds the full population. Example (from [Hernán & Robins, What If , ch. 8](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)): a randomised trial of wasabi and death. Dropout is highest among precisely the exposed and the sick, so censoring becomes uneven : The completer analysis gives RR = 0.89 - wasabi looks protective . But that is an illusion created by the uneven dropout: the exposed who stayed are systematically healthier. Weighted back to the full population, the risk is 57% in both groups, RR = 1.00 - no effect. This code handles an outcome that is missing for some people.
